Z06-P09:action3 Handle sharp-toothed esocids with wet hands and long-nose unhooking tools—never grip gill arches—to prevent severe lacerations and fish mortality.
Z06-P12:action2 Handle catfish and bullheads carefully to avoid venomous-mucus puncture wounds from locked dorsal and pectoral fin spines.
Z06-P12:failure Pulling a protected sturgeon out of water for prolonged photos or mishandling bullhead spines causes illegal take and infected puncture injuries.
Z06-P12:stop Stop handling if a fin-spine puncture causes worsening swelling, redness, or fever; clean thoroughly and seek medical evaluation.
Z07-P18:action2 Recognize that even gentle dogs in sudden pain or panic frequently bite owners during stressful incidents; protect hands/face, stay calm, and call for immediate assistance if an incident occurs.
Z07-P22:action3 If any bite, scratch, or saliva exposure occurs, wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water immediately and seek urgent medical evaluation for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis and tetanus.
Z10-P20:action1 Wash your own hands (or wear clean gloves) first, then rinse the minor wound thoroughly under steady clean potable water to flush out dirt, grit, and surface debris.
Z10-P20:action2 Wash surrounding intact skin gently with mild soap and safe water, avoiding pouring harsh alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, or full-strength iodine directly inside open tissue where they irritate healing cells.
Z10-P20:action3 Pat surrounding skin dry with clean gauze, cover the wound completely with a clean sterile dressing, and re-check daily for moisture, dirt breakthrough, or infection signs.
Z10-P20:failure Rinsing an open scrape in untreated creek water or sealing muddy grit inside a wound with tight tape.
Z10-P20:verify Confirm only confirmed potable/boiled-and-cooled water touched the wound, visible grit is flushed out, and the dressing stays clean and dry.
Z10-P20:stop Deep gaping cuts, heavy dirt that will not flush clean, hand/face/joint wounds, or unknown tetanus status require prompt clinical care.
Z10-P21:action1 If an object is impaled deeply in the body, do NOT pull it out—the object may be plugging a severed blood vessel, and removing it can trigger fatal internal or external hemorrhage.
Z10-P21:action2 Control bleeding around the base with gentle pressure on either side without pressing on the object itself, build bulky donut-style padding around it to prevent movement, and activate 911/EMS.
Z10-P21:action3 Treat all deep puncture wounds (even small ones that barely bleed, such as stepping on a rusty nail or deep stick puncture) as high-infection and tetanus hazards requiring clinical cleaning and evaluation.
Z10-P21:failure Pulling a wooden branch out of a thigh or chest in the backcountry and triggering massive uncontrollable arterial bleeding.
Z10-P21:verify Confirm impaled object is padded immobile without shifting, surrounding bleeding is monitored, and clinical evacuation is underway.
Z10-P21:stop Any impaled object in the head, neck, eye, chest, or abdomen is an immediate life-threatening emergency requiring urgent EMS extraction.
Z10-P22:action1 Irrigate accessible superficial lacerations thoroughly with clean potable water, approximate edges only lightly with clean dressings if needed for bleeding control, and arrange clinical evaluation within standard medical windows.
Z10-P22:action2 Never stitch wounds with improvised sewing needles, staple skin, or seal dirty, jagged, puncture, or animal-bite wounds shut with household superglue—trapping bacteria inside an airtight wound causes severe deep abscess and sepsis.
Z10-P22:action3 Keep the wound moist-clean under sterile gauze protected from dirt, elevate an injured limb if comfortable, and monitor closely for infection during exit.
Z10-P22:failure Sealing a muddy trail laceration or dog bite shut with cyanoacrylate glue in camp, trapping anaerobic bacteria deep beneath the skin.
Z10-P22:verify Confirm wound was irrigated with potable water, covered cleanly without improvised closure, and scheduled for prompt clinical review.
Z10-P22:stop Gaping wounds, exposed fat/tendon/bone, heavy contamination, facial cuts, or bite wounds require timely professional medical closure and tetanus/antibiotic review.
Z10-P23:action1 Inspect every healing field wound at least once daily for spreading redness, increasing warmth, worsening throbbing pain, swelling, foul odor, or yellow/green pus drainage.
Z10-P23:action2 Outline the outer edge of any skin redness lightly with a pen and note the time so you can see objectively whether redness is expanding outward over subsequent hours.
Z10-P23:action3 Treat red streaks traveling up a limb, fever, chills, shaking, rapid breathing, or new confusion as urgent systemic infection emergencies requiring immediate evacuation and clinical antibiotics.
Z10-P23:failure Waiting three days on a multi-day trip while redness climbs past the ankle and fever begins, assuming basic ointment will cure a deep infection.
Z10-P23:verify Confirm wound appearance, pen-border progress, and presence or absence of fever/chills are logged daily.
Z10-P23:stop Expanding redness past marked lines, pus, joint stiffness, red streaks, fever, or confusion mandate immediate exit to medical care.
Z10-P27:stop If blood or body fluids splash into a caregiver's eyes, mouth, or broken skin, flush immediately with clean potable water and seek prompt clinical post-exposure evaluation.
Z10-P28:action2 Keep intact fluid-filled blisters unbroken whenever possible because intact roof skin is the body's best sterile dressing; if a blister tears open on its own, rinse gently with clean potable water, leave loose skin flat if clean, and cover with sterile non-stick dressing.
Z10-P28:failure Ignoring a burning heel hot spot for five miles until raw torn skin fills with trail mud and becomes infected.
Z10-P28:verify Confirm feet are inspected dry at every camp stop and no spreading redness, pus, or worsening limp is developing.
Z10-P28:stop Spreading redness, warmth, pus, inability to walk normally, or any foot breakdown in a diabetic traveler requires halting the trip and seeking clinical evaluation.
Z10-P34:failure Attempting to rinse deeply or push an exposed tibia back under the skin in camp, driving dirt deep into the bone marrow.
Z10-P51:action3 Escalate to prompt clinical evaluation for widespread blistering, severe facial swelling, fever, chills, nausea, confusion, or signs of blister infection (pus, spreading red streaks).
Z10-P57:action1 Move promptly away from the nest or swarm zone to prevent multiple stings; if a honeybee stinger remains in skin, scrape it off promptly sideways with a flat edge (card/fingernail) or pull gently without squeezing a visible venom sac.
Z10-P57:action2 Wash the sting area gently with soap and safe water, remove rings near finger stings early before swelling builds, and apply a cool clean damp cloth for comfort.
Z10-P57:verify Confirm stinger removed, rings off, local site cleaned, and zero distant hives or breathing symptoms over monitoring window.
Z10-P58:action3 Wash the bite site and hands thoroughly with soap and safe water, note the date and location on your body, and seek medical evaluation promptly if a rash (expanding bull's-eye or other rash), fever, chills, body aches, or joint swelling appears within 30 days.
Z10-P59:action2 Control active bleeding with clean direct pressure, cover loosely with a sterile dressing without sealing dirty puncture wounds shut with glue, and document animal species, behavior, and location (or owner vaccination contact if domestic).
Z10-P62:action1 Wash the bite site gently with soap and safe water, apply a clean cool damp cloth (not bare ice) for local discomfort, elevate the limb if comfortable, and keep the person resting calmly.
Z10-P64:action1 If exposed to suspected poison ivy, oak, or sumac, rinse skin thoroughly as soon as possible with COOL running water and mild soap (avoiding hot water initially, and scrubbing gently under fingernails) to wash away sticky urushiol oil before it binds.
Z10-P64:action2 Isolate and wash contaminated clothing, shoelaces, tools, and pet fur carefully—urushiol oil remains active on fabric and gear for months and spreads easily to faces and eyes, whereas rash blister fluid itself does NOT spread the rash.
Z10-P64:verify Confirm exposed skin, fingernails, and tools were washed thoroughly with cool soap/water and zero vines enter any fire.
Z10-P64:stop Any facial/eye swelling, widespread blistering, breathing difficulty after smoke exposure, or signs of secondary skin infection require prompt clinical care.
Z10-P71:action1 For a knocked-out permanent adult tooth, pick it up ONLY by the white biting crown—NEVER touch or scrub the delicate root—rinse briefly with clean water/saline ONLY if dirty, and store submerged in cold milk or sterile saline (do NOT store dry or scrub) while heading immediately to a dentist/ED.
Z10-P71:action2 Control gum socket bleeding by having an alert patient bite firmly on clean folded damp gauze, and save any broken tooth fragments cleanly without gluing anything back in the mouth.
Z10-P71:action3 Treat toothache accompanied by expanding cheek/jaw/neck swelling, fever, difficulty swallowing, or eye-area swelling as an urgent spreading deep-infection emergency requiring immediate clinical care (never wait days in camp).
Z10-P71:failure Scrubbing the root of a knocked-out permanent tooth with soap and wrapping it dry in tissue paper, or ignoring jaw swelling and fever that threaten the airway.
Z10-P71:verify Confirm tooth handled by crown only in moist milk/saline, bleeding controlled with gauze, and any facial swelling/fever triggers urgent exit.
Z10-P71:stop Spreading facial/neck swelling, fever, trouble swallowing/breathing, or severe uncontrolled oral bleeding requires immediate 911/emergency department care.
Z10-P72:action1 NEVER insert tweezers, sticks, cotton swabs, or improvised probes deep into an ear canal or nostril to dig out a foreign object—blind probing commonly ruptures eardrums or pushes objects deeper into the airway.
Z10-P72:action2 For painful elevation-change ear pressure (barotrauma), slow descent/ascent, yawn, or swallow gently—never force hard blowing if severe sharp pain occurs; do NOT put random liquids or oils into an ear that has fluid, blood, or suspected eardrum rupture.
Z10-P72:action3 Seek prompt clinical evaluation for any embedded ear/nose object, blood or clear fluid draining from an ear after head trauma (immediate 911 red flag), severe worsening ear pain with fever, or sudden hearing loss/vertigo.
Z10-P72:failure Digging at a pebble or tick inside a child's ear canal with pocketknife tweezers, tearing the eardrum.
Z10-P72:verify Confirm zero deep probing occurred, no unapproved drops entered a draining ear, and head-trauma ear drainage triggers immediate 911.
Z10-P77:action2 Recognize hard non-improvisable boundaries: thin shoelaces/cord fail as tourniquets, dirty cloth or untreated water contaminates open wounds, household glues/needles cause deep infection, and improvised pole litters collapse under heavy loads.
Z15-P28:action3 If accidental skin contact occurs, wash immediately and thoroughly with soap and confirmed safe potable water, keep any open cuts covered cleanly, and seek prompt medical evaluation for any floodwater-exposed wound or tetanus update.
Z15-P28:failure Letting kids splash barefoot in ankle-deep neighborhood street floodwater near a storm drain and submerged electric transformer box.
Z15-P28:verify Confirm zero recreational wading, zero bare-skin floodwater contact, immediate soap/safe-water washing if splashed, and cuts escalated clinically.
Z16-P45:action2 Open Z10-P20 for clean minor cuts and abrasions with potable water and protect against dirt; Z10-P31 for maintain spinal motion restriction after high-force falls or impacts; Z10-P32 for immobilize suspected limb fractures in the position found.
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. General minor wound advice cannot validate deep wounds, closure, antibiotics or every water source.

Z10-P24:action2 Never apply ice, snow, butter, cooking oil, toothpaste, or unapproved ointments to a fresh burn—ice deepens tissue damage and greasy substances trap heat and bacteria.

Z10-P25:action1 Call 911 immediately for ANY burn that is large (larger than the patient's palm on high-risk zones or extensive body area), deep (waxy white, brown, charred, or painless), or involves the face, eyes, hands, feet, groin, major joints, or completely encircles a limb/chest.
Z10-P25:action2 Treat singed nose hairs, soot around the mouth/nose, hoarse voice, coughing, or breathing difficulty after fire/smoke exposure as a potential airway-swelling emergency requiring immediate EMS.

Z10-P25:failure Dousing a large torso burn repeatedly in cold lake water until the patient develops severe hypothermia, or ignoring hoarse voice after a stove flare-up.

Z10-P26:action1 Stay back from energized equipment, floodwater or downed lines. Call 911 and approach only after qualified personnel or the dispatcher confirm the area is safe.
Z10-P26:failure Grabbing a person still touching an energized generator cord, or pouring a tiny cup of water onto dry caustic lime powder so it activates and spreads across skin.
Z10-P26:verify Confirm power or chemical source is isolated, rescuers avoided contamination, and exact chemical identity or voltage context is logged for EMS.
Z10-P26:stop Any electrical contact, loss of consciousness, chest pain, or chemical eye/airway exposure requires immediate emergency medical evaluation.
Z10-P51:action1 Move out of direct sun immediately, apply cool damp clean cloths gently to tender skin, wear loose soft sun-blocking fabric over the area, and rehydrate steadily with safe potable water.
Z10-P51:action2 Leave intact sunburn blisters unbroken and avoid petroleum jelly, butter, or topical benzocaine/home remedies that trap heat or trigger allergic skin reactions.
Z10-P51:action3 Escalate to prompt clinical evaluation for widespread blistering, severe facial swelling, fever, chills, nausea, confusion, or signs of blister infection (pus, spreading red streaks).
Z10-P51:failure Continuing full-sun paddling with raw blistering shoulders until fever, dehydration, and secondary skin infection develop.
Z10-P51:verify Confirm UV exposure is blocked, hydration is maintained, intact blisters are protected, and systemic fever/chills are absent.
Z10-P51:stop Extensive blistering, fever/chills, dizziness, or signs of heat exhaustion/stroke require stopping travel and seeking clinical care.
Z10-P54:action3 Activate 911 immediately, start trained/dispatcher-guided CPR and AED use on anyone not breathing normally, and arrange clinical evaluation for ALL struck persons (checking burns, hearing/eye injury, and spinal precautions).
Z10-P57:action2 Wash the sting area gently with soap and safe water, remove rings near finger stings early before swelling builds, and apply a cool clean damp cloth for comfort.
Z13-P11:action3 Never lift cracked or leaking battery cases without acid-resistant protection; treat conceptual battery-bank schematics strictly as hazard-awareness guides rather than DIY electrical wiring designs.
Z15-P36:action1 Return ONLY after fire officials lift evacuation closures; walk carefully wearing thick leather boots, gloves, and N95 masks because gray ash heaps conceal **smoldering underground root embers and hot ash pits** capable of melting soles and causing deep burns weeks after flames pass.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z10-P14:action1 Do NOT move a non-ambulatory patient with suspected neck, spine, pelvis, femur, or internal injury unless immediate life-threatening scene danger (rising floodwater, fire, rockfall, or airway threat) forces a short urgent move.
Z10-P32:action1 Expose the injured area gently to check for open wounds or deformity, remove rings/watches early before swelling tightens, and support the limb steadily in the exact position found—do NOT attempt to snap or force visibly deformed bones straight.
Z10-P32:action2 Pad all bony prominences and natural hollows generously, secure a splint wide enough to immobilize the joint ABOVE and the joint BELOW the suspected fracture (or bones above/below an injured joint), and tie snug—never tight enough to choke circulation.
Z10-P32:action3 Check warmth, color, sensation, and gentle toe/finger movement beyond the splint immediately after tying, and arrange clinical X-ray evaluation.
Z10-P32:failure Tying narrow paracord directly over the fracture site without padding or attempting to yank an angulated forearm straight in camp.
Z10-P32:verify Confirm padding cushions all gaps, ties sit above/below the break (not over it), and circulation/sensation beyond the splint remain intact.
Z10-P32:stop Cold pale/blue fingers or toes, numbness, open bone, or severe uncontrollable pain requires loosening tight ties immediately and activating urgent EMS.
Z10-P33:action1 Before applying any splint or wrap—and again immediately after securing it—compare the injured hand or foot against the uninjured side for skin warmth/pink color (Circulation), light-touch feeling (Sensation), and gentle finger/toe wiggle (Movement).
Z10-P33:action2 Leave fingertips or toes visibly exposed at the end of every splint or wrap so you can recheck CSM every 15 to 30 minutes as swelling progresses.
Z10-P33:action3 If fingers or toes turn cold, pale, bluish, numb, tingling, or intensely throbbing under a wrap, loosen the ties immediately and recheck within minutes.
Z10-P33:failure Wrapping a swollen ankle tightly inside an opaque boot and never checking cold numb toes over a three-hour hike out.
Z10-P33:verify Confirm baseline and repeated timed CSM checks (warm/pink, normal touch, intact wiggle) are recorded on the patient log.
Z10-P33:stop Persistent loss of warmth, color, or sensation even after loosening wraps is a limb-threatening emergency requiring urgent EMS transport.
Z10-P34:action1 Call 911 for a suspected open fracture. Report the injury, severe bleeding and any change in alertness or limb color.
Z10-P34:action2 Use emergency bleeding-control guidance for life-threatening blood loss. Keep pressure off protruding bone itself and do not push bone back into the wound.
Z10-P34:action3 Protect the wound with a clean dressing. Follow dispatch on moving or supporting the limb, and monitor breathing, alertness and circulation while waiting for help.
Z10-P34:failure Attempting to rinse deeply or push an exposed tibia back under the skin in camp, driving dirt deep into the bone marrow.
Z10-P34:verify Confirm bleeding is controlled gently around edges, sterile cover protects exposed tissue, distal CSM is checked, and EMS is inbound.
Z10-P34:stop Heavy bleeding uncontrolled by gentle pressure, cold pale extremity, or shock signs trigger immediate maximum-priority trauma escalation.
Z10-P35:action1 Activate 911/SAR immediately for suspected pelvic or femur fracture—both can bleed rapidly into deep internal compartments and trigger fatal hemorrhagic shock without visible external blood.
Z10-P35:action2 Keep the person completely flat and still where found, do NOT rock or squeeze the pelvis repeatedly to "test stability," and place soft padding gently beside the legs and hips for comfort without rolling the patient.
Z10-P35:failure Trying to help a hiker with severe hip/pelvis pain stand up and hop to a vehicle, disrupting a fragile internal pelvic clot.
Z10-P35:verify Confirm the patient remained flat and still, zero pelvic-rocking tests were performed, warmth is maintained, and SAR knows urgent trauma carry is needed.
Z10-P36:action1 Halt travel promptly, inspect the joint for deformity, severe bone-edge tenderness, or numbness, and protect the joint with rest, gentle comfortable compression wrap (never tight), and elevation when resting.
Z10-P36:action2 Remember that severe sprains and hairline/undisplaced fractures feel identical in the field—only a clinical X-ray can rule out a fracture; never force a traveler to walk on a joint that buckles or cannot bear weight.
Z10-P36:action3 Check distal warmth, color, and toe/finger sensation repeatedly after wrapping, and plan an assisted exit or SAR call if the terrain or pain prevents safe weight-bearing.
Z10-P36:failure Assuming a massively swollen ankle is "just a sprain" and marching five downhill miles on an undisplaced fibula fracture.
Z10-P36:verify Confirm CSM remains intact below any wrap, bony-edge tenderness was noted, and exit mode matches actual safe mobility.
Z10-P36:stop Visible deformity, bone-point pain, numbness, cold toes, or inability to take four controlled weight-bearing steps requires immobilization and non-weight-bearing evacuation.
Z10-P37:action1 Immobilize a suspected dislocated shoulder, elbow, kneecap, hip, or finger gently in the position of greatest comfort using padded slings or pillows—do NOT yank or attempt lay joint reduction in the field.
Z10-P37:action2 Check distal circulation, sensation, and movement (CSM) immediately and repeatedly; knee and hip dislocations carry especially high artery-injury risk requiring urgent EMS transport.
Z10-P37:action3 Keep the patient warm, withhold food/water if surgical sedation may be needed at the hospital, and arrange prompt clinical orthopedic evaluation.
Z10-P37:failure Having untrained bystanders tug forcefully on a dislocated arm or knee, trapping an artery or fracturing the joint rim.
Z10-P37:verify Confirm the joint is cushioned comfortably as found, distal CSM is logged, and clinical evacuation is underway.
Z10-P37:stop Any pale, cold, pulseless, or numb extremity beyond a dislocated joint is a limb-threatening emergency requiring immediate 911 activation.
Z10-P77:action1 Recognize safe lay improvisations when commercial supplies run out: clean folded cloth for direct bleeding pressure, rolled jackets and foam pads for cushioned limb splinting, and dry insulated sleeping bags/tarps for hypothermia wraps.
Z10-P77:verify Confirm cleanest dry cloth used for pressure, generous padding under improvised splints, and zero unsafe improvised closure or thin-cord tourniquets.
Z16-P45:action2 Open Z10-P20 for clean minor cuts and abrasions with potable water and protect against dirt; Z10-P31 for maintain spinal motion restriction after high-force falls or impacts; Z10-P32 for immobilize suspected limb fractures in the position found.
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. General fracture reference does not validate traction, splint types, reduction, CSM cadence or evacuation movement.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z10-P22:action2 Never stitch wounds with improvised sewing needles, staple skin, or seal dirty, jagged, puncture, or animal-bite wounds shut with household superglue—trapping bacteria inside an airtight wound causes severe deep abscess and sepsis.
Z10-P22:failure Sealing a muddy trail laceration or dog bite shut with cyanoacrylate glue in camp, trapping anaerobic bacteria deep beneath the skin.
Z10-P22:stop Gaping wounds, exposed fat/tendon/bone, heavy contamination, facial cuts, or bite wounds require timely professional medical closure and tetanus/antibiotic review.
Z10-P59:action1 Move safely away from the animal (do NOT try to trap or touch a wild or aggressive animal), then wash the bite immediately and thoroughly with soap and copious running potable water for several minutes to flush saliva and bacteria out.
Z10-P59:action2 Control active bleeding with clean direct pressure, cover loosely with a sterile dressing without sealing dirty puncture wounds shut with glue, and document animal species, behavior, and location (or owner vaccination contact if domestic).
Z10-P59:action3 Obtain prompt medical evaluation for EVERY skin-breaking mammal bite—clinicians assess infection risk (especially deep cat/hand bites), tetanus currency, and urgent rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP).
Z10-P59:failure Washing a raccoon scratch lightly with a wet wipe and skipping medical follow-up because the scratch looks small.
Z10-P59:verify Confirm prolonged soap-and-potable-water wash completed, bleeding controlled, animal details noted, and clinical evaluation scheduled promptly.
Z10-P59:stop Deep bleeding bites, bites to face/hands/joints, or contact with wild rabies-vector species require immediate same-day emergency medical care.
Z10-P60:action1 Understand that rabies is nearly always fatal once symptoms begin, yet completely preventable with timely clinical post-exposure treatment—and tiny bat bites often leave NO visible mark or wake a sleeping person.
Z10-P60:action2 If a bat is found in a room with a sleeping person, unattended child, or anyone who cannot reliably rule out contact—or if any direct skin contact occurs—wash any contact site with soap and water and contact your local health department or doctor promptly.
Z10-P60:action3 Never handle a bat with bare hands; if public health advises safe capture for testing, avoid crushing the head and do not risk being bitten—if the bat flies away or cannot be tested, clinical rabies risk assessment still applies immediately.
Z10-P60:failure Shooing a bat out of a cabin bedroom where children were sleeping and assuming "nobody saw a bite, so no doctor is needed."
Z10-P60:verify Confirm zero bare-hand contact occurred and medical/public-health consultation is initiated promptly for any uncertain sleeping-room exposure.
Z10-P60:stop Any confirmed bat bite/scratch or uncertain exposure during sleep requires prompt clinical consultation—never wait for symptoms.
Z16-P27:action2 Open Z10-P59 for clean mammal bites thoroughly and arrange prompt infection and rabies review; Z10-P60 for treat indoor bat encounters as potential rabies exposures requiring public-health review; Z07-P22 for rabies, Bite and Claw Trauma Risks with Distressed Wildlife.
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. Wash and seek evaluation, with rabies risk controlled by species, exposure and local public health. Bat encounter is a separate question.

Z07-P21:stop Stop approaching immediately; seek urgent medical care and report to public health if any wild mammal bite or saliva-scratch exposure occurs.

Z07-P22:action3 If any bite, scratch, or saliva exposure occurs, wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water immediately and seek urgent medical evaluation for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis and tetanus.

Z10-P16:action3 Offer small sips of safe potable water ONLY if the patient is fully alert, swallowing normally, and has no suspected shock, abdominal injury, or imminent surgery red flags.
Z10-P49:action1 Stop all exertion immediately at the first heat-exhaustion signs, move the person into shade or air conditioning, loosen heavy clothing/packs, and lay them down slightly elevated feet if dizzy.
Z10-P49:action2 Cool actively by applying cool wet cloths or misting cool water over skin while fanning air across the body, and offer small steady sips of cool safe water or labeled oral rehydration solution ONLY while fully alert and not vomiting.
Z10-P51:action1 Move out of direct sun immediately, apply cool damp clean cloths gently to tender skin, wear loose soft sun-blocking fabric over the area, and rehydrate steadily with safe potable water.

Z10-P65:action1 For alert patients able to swallow, offer frequent tiny sips (a spoonful or small sip every few minutes) of confirmed potable water or commercial labeled oral rehydration solution—gulping large volumes rapidly often triggers renewed vomiting.
Z10-P65:action3 Evacuate promptly for medical care if vomiting prevents keeping fluids down over hours, stools contain blood or black tar, high fever develops, urine stops or turns very dark, or dizziness/confusion appear.

Z10-P65:verify Confirm fluids are confirmed potable, sips stay down steadily, urine output/color is tracked, and hand hygiene isolates the group.

Z10-P69:action1 Recognize that infants and young children lose body heat much faster (high surface-area-to-mass ratio), dehydrate rapidly during vomiting/diarrhea, and deteriorate abruptly from shock or heat illness after looking "fine" minutes earlier.
Z10-P69:verify Confirm extra warmth/water checks are scheduled frequently and any head bump on blood thinners or pediatric lethargy triggers prompt medical review.
Z10-P69:stop Unusual quietness/lethargy in a child, minimal wet diapers/urine, or ANY head injury in an older adult taking anticoagulants mandates prompt clinical evaluation.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z10-P01:action2 Activate 911 or emergency dispatch early whenever life-threatening signs appear—distinguishing immediate lay stabilization (pressure, airway positioning, warmth) from dispatcher-guided actions and hospital clinical interventions.
Z10-P01:action3 Act strictly within your actual training and carried supplies; never attempt invasive procedures, prescribe medication dosages, or diagnose internal conditions in the field.
Z10-P01:failure Rushing into an active rockfall or ice-edge hazard without checking the scene, or attempting improvised medical procedures outside lay training.
Z10-P01:stop Stop any intervention that exceeds lay training or puts rescuers in unmitigated danger; prioritize scene safety and rapid EMS handoff.
Z10-P04:action2 Lock the windlass securely, write the exact application time on the tourniquet strap and patient log, and leave the tourniquet uncovered and clearly visible for arriving EMS crews.
Z10-P05:verify Confirm the patient is insulated underneath and overhead, external bleeding is checked, breathing is monitored, and zero oral fluids are given.
Z10-P06:action1 Write down the exact injury/onset time, mechanism of harm, allergies, current medications, and baseline mental status (alert, confused, responds to voice, or unresponsive) right after initial stabilization.
Z10-P06:action2 Re-check and log breathing effort, skin color/warmth, bleeding dressing saturation, pain changes, and mental clarity at steady intervals—roughly every 15 minutes for unstable patients or every 30 to 60 minutes if stable.
Z10-P06:action3 Hand the written time-stamped sheet directly to EMS or SAR clinicians on arrival rather than relying on memory under stress.
Z10-P06:failure Relying on verbal memory across a two-hour carryout and forgetting when a tourniquet was applied or when confusion first started.
Z10-P06:verify Confirm times, baseline symptoms, interventions, and trend direction (improving, steady, or worsening) are legible on paper.
Z10-P06:stop Downward trend in responsiveness, rising breathing effort, spreading swelling, or new neurological signs requires immediate emergency escalation regardless of earlier stability.
Z10-P07:action2 Report the number of patients, age/sex if known, mechanism of injury, current responsiveness, breathing status, severe bleeding, and immediate weather or terrain hazards.
Z10-P07:stop If cellular or radio contact fails completely at the scene, keep one caregiver with the patient and send a paired runner with the written report only if terrain is safe.
Z10-P11:action2 Ask if the patient carries their own prescribed rescue inhaler or epinephrine auto-injector; assist only with their own labeled device per its instructions—never share another person's prescription medication.
Z10-P11:failure Forcing an asthmatic or short-of-breath hiker to "walk it off" uphill or sharing someone else's unprescribed inhaler.
Z10-P11:verify Confirm breathing rate, speech length (full sentences vs single words), skin/lip color, and time of any own-prescription use are logged.
Z10-P12:action1 Stop all activity immediately, seat or lay the person comfortably at rest in shelter, and log the exact minute symptoms started (critical for hospital stroke treatment windows).
Z10-P12:action3 Call 911 immediately and follow dispatcher instructions; do NOT let the patient drive, walk out strenuously, or take unprescribed medications unless a 911 dispatcher or clinician specifically directs it.
Z10-P12:verify Confirm exact symptom-onset time is written down, exertion has stopped, and emergency transport is inbound.
Z10-P13:action1 Consider walking out ONLY when the patient is fully alert, stable across repeated checks, able to bear weight safely without worsening the injury, and daylight/weather allow a conservative exit.
Z10-P13:action3 Weigh nightfall, steep slippery terrain, and rescuer exhaustion honestly—two exhausted companions trying to drag an injured hiker down steep trails frequently trigger secondary falls.
Z10-P13:stop Any deterioration in patient stability, darkness, storm onset, or rescuer fatigue halts movement immediately in favor of warm shelter and SAR activation.
Z10-P14:action2 Recognize that improvised pole-and-jacket litters require six to eight fresh rotating carriers on uneven trails and often collapse, drop the patient, or exhaust small parties within a few hundred yards.
Z10-P14:verify Confirm scene is stable, patient is insulated in place, and SAR dispatch knows the patient is non-ambulatory and requires a litter team.
Z10-P16:action2 Protect the patient's shelter from wind and rain, maintain scheduled mental-status and breathing checks through the night, and keep caregivers fed, hydrated, and rotating rest shifts so no one collapses from exhaustion.
Z10-P16:verify Confirm ground insulation, dry outer barrier, scheduled caregiver watch shifts, and ongoing timed patient notes are active.
Z10-P16:stop Rapid deterioration in warmth, alertness, or breathing overnight triggers immediate re-contact with dispatch/beacon activation if not already deployed.
Z10-P19:action3 Keep the patient completely still, horizontal and insulated from cold ground, withhold all food and fluids (NPO), and monitor alertness and breathing continuously.
Z10-P19:verify Confirm mechanism of injury, abdominal/bruising signs, vital trends, and urgent evacuation request are documented clearly.
Z10-P23:action1 Inspect every healing field wound at least once daily for spreading redness, increasing warmth, worsening throbbing pain, swelling, foul odor, or yellow/green pus drainage.
Z10-P23:action2 Outline the outer edge of any skin redness lightly with a pen and note the time so you can see objectively whether redness is expanding outward over subsequent hours.
Z10-P23:verify Confirm wound appearance, pen-border progress, and presence or absence of fever/chills are logged daily.
Z10-P27:action1 Put on clean disposable nitrile gloves (or clean plastic-bag barriers if gloves are absent) before touching blood, open wounds, vomit, or body fluids, and wash hands thoroughly before and after patient care.
Z10-P27:action2 Remove soiled gloves carefully from the inside out without snapping droplets onto skin or eyes, seal blood- or waste-soaked items in double leak-proof bags for proper pack-out/disposal, and wash hands immediately afterward.
Z10-P29:action2 Keep a responsible companion observing the person continuously for worsening symptoms over the next several hours, logging mental clarity, speech, and headache trends on paper.
Z10-P29:verify Confirm hazardous activity stopped immediately, a buddy is watching continuously, and baseline orientation questions are recorded with times.
Z10-P30:verify Confirm exact time of impact, responsiveness level, and any red-flag progression are transmitted clearly to EMS/SAR.
Z10-P31:verify Confirm the head and spine remained unmoved, sensation/movement in extremities was noted, and EMS knows spinal precautions are active.
Z10-P33:action1 Before applying any splint or wrap—and again immediately after securing it—compare the injured hand or foot against the uninjured side for skin warmth/pink color (Circulation), light-touch feeling (Sensation), and gentle finger/toe wiggle (Movement).
Z10-P33:action2 Leave fingertips or toes visibly exposed at the end of every splint or wrap so you can recheck CSM every 15 to 30 minutes as swelling progresses.
Z10-P33:verify Confirm baseline and repeated timed CSM checks (warm/pink, normal touch, intact wiggle) are recorded on the patient log.
Z10-P35:action3 Insulate heavily against cold ground, keep strictly NPO, monitor mental status and breathing continuously, and await trained EMS/SAR extraction teams.
Z10-P37:verify Confirm the joint is cushioned comfortably as found, distal CSM is logged, and clinical evacuation is underway.
Z10-P40:action3 Position the patient comfortably (often slightly upright for chest pain or knees gently bent for abdominal pain), insulate from cold ground, and withhold food, water, and painkillers that mask deterioration.
Z10-P40:failure Sealing an open chest wound tightly on all four sides with duct tape without venting, or giving heavy pain pills for worsening lower-right abdominal pain and waiting overnight.
Z10-P40:verify Confirm breathing effort, abdominal rigidity/pain trend, and NPO status are logged clearly for incoming EMS.
Z10-P41:verify Confirm wind/wet exposure is stopped, dry layers and ground pad are in place, and mental clarity is improving across timed checks.
Z10-P44:failure Sending a child or paddler home to nap after a brief near-drowning episode without medical assessment while persistent coughing worsens.
Z10-P44:verify Confirm breathing rate, cough severity, mental clarity, and medical evaluation plan are documented and communicated.
Z10-P49:verify Confirm active cooling is working, nausea/dizziness improve within 30 minutes, and mental status remains completely sharp.
Z10-P50:verify Confirm 911 is activated, continuous active cooling is underway, airway is protected, and zero oral fluids are forced into an altered patient.
Z10-P52:verify Confirm ascent halted immediately, buddy monitoring is continuous, and a safe lower-elevation descent path is identified.
Z10-P53:action3 Keep the patient warm, minimize their physical exertion (carry their pack, support balance closely, or await SAR evacuation if steep/night terrain makes moving unsafe), and leave prescription altitude medications strictly to clinicians or the patient's own prescribed regimen.
Z10-P55:verify Confirm 911 is dispatched, exact auto-injector time is recorded, and breathing/alertness are tracked continuously.
Z10-P56:action3 Keep the patient resting calmly with continuous buddy monitoring during exit, keeping their spare prescribed auto-injector immediately accessible rather than buried in a pack.
Z10-P56:verify Confirm exact trigger, dose time, symptom resolution timeline, and direct evacuation route to a hospital are active.
Z10-P59:verify Confirm prolonged soap-and-potable-water wash completed, bleeding controlled, animal details noted, and clinical evaluation scheduled promptly.
Z10-P61:action2 Remove rings, watches, bracelets, and tight clothing near the bitten limb immediately before rapid swelling begins, keep the limb comfortably supported at roughly heart level (or per dispatcher/toxicology guidance), and mark the leading edge of swelling with time.
Z10-P61:verify Confirm rings/tight items removed, patient resting calm and still, swelling edge marked with time, and urgent hospital transport active.
Z10-P66:action1 Before departure, ask willing companions privately to share critical emergency needs (asthma inhaler location, epinephrine location, diabetes fast-acting glucose, seizure plan, or cardiac medications) and keep a written summary accessible.
Z10-P66:action2 During a flare-up, stop exertion immediately, provide calm shelter, and assist ONLY with the person's OWN prescribed labeled rescue device or documented personal action plan—never adjust prescription dosages or share another person's medication.
Z10-P66:action3 Activate 911/EMS early whenever a chronic condition fails to respond promptly to the person's own rescue plan, requires repeated rescue doses, or causes breathing distress, chest pain, or altered alertness.
Z10-P66:failure Discovering mid-trip that a companion's rescue inhaler or epinephrine is buried at the bottom of a locked car at the trailhead.
Z10-P66:verify Confirm personal rescue devices are carried on the person (protected from freezing/heat) and trip leaders know where they are stored.
Z10-P67:failure Trying to pry open a seizing person's jaw with a stick or failing to time the seizure duration for arriving EMS.
Z10-P67:verify Confirm exact seizure duration recorded, surroundings cleared, post-seizure side-lying airway check performed, and 911 rules applied.
Z10-P68:action1 Watch for rapid low-blood-sugar (hypoglycemia) onset during heavy outdoor exertion or skipped meals—sweating, trembling, sudden weakness, irritability, or dizziness—and stop activity immediately.
Z10-P69:action3 Lower your stop-and-evacuate threshold dramatically for children and older adults—turn back early, insulate proactively before shivering starts, and contact EMS/clinicians promptly rather than watching and waiting overnight.
Z10-P69:verify Confirm extra warmth/water checks are scheduled frequently and any head bump on blood thinners or pediatric lethargy triggers prompt medical review.
Z10-P71:action1 For a knocked-out permanent adult tooth, pick it up ONLY by the white biting crown—NEVER touch or scrub the delicate root—rinse briefly with clean water/saline ONLY if dirty, and store submerged in cold milk or sterile saline (do NOT store dry or scrub) while heading immediately to a dentist/ED.
Z10-P75:action1 Pack supplies you actually know how to use cleanly under stress—prioritizing scene barriers (nitrile gloves), hemorrhage control (sterile gauze, pressure bandage, plus commercial tourniquet if trained), wound cleaning/dressings, blister padding, tweezers, and a waterproof patient log card.
Z10-P75:action2 Omit surgical scalpels, suture kits, unprescribed prescription drugs, or invasive tools you are NOT clinically licensed and trained to use—untrained gear adds weight and tempts dangerous improvisation.
Z10-P75:action3 Inspect the entire kit before every season and after every outing to replace used items, verify intact sterile wrappers, discard expired personal medications per instructions, and protect contents in dry waterproof bags.
Z10-P75:failure Carrying a dusty five-year-old kit with dried-out tape, cracked gloves, and complex gadgets no one in the party knows how to operate.
Z10-P75:verify Confirm every item is unexpired, dry-packed, familiar to the carrier, and matched to group size and trip length.
Z10-P75:stop Do not launch remote multi-day travel with an uninspected kit or missing essential personal rescue medications.
Z10-P76:action1 Carry essential personal medications in their original pharmacy-labeled containers (plus an extra multi-day reserve split across a companion's pack if appropriate) so EMS clinicians can verify exact drug names and strengths instantly.
Z10-P76:action3 Keep a waterproof written list of all medications, dosages, prescribing clinics, and allergies inside your wallet and first-aid kit so rescuers have accurate records even if you become unresponsive.
Z10-P76:verify Confirm original pharmacy labels, spare backup days, temperature-buffer storage, and written medication/allergy list are packed.
Z10-P76:stop Frozen, cloudy/discolored (check drug label), damaged, or expired emergency medications must be replaced before relying on them in remote areas.
Z10-P77:action2 Recognize hard non-improvisable boundaries: thin shoelaces/cord fail as tourniquets, dirty cloth or untreated water contaminates open wounds, household glues/needles cause deep infection, and improvised pole litters collapse under heavy loads.
Z10-P77:action3 Treat ANY improvised stabilization as a temporary bridge strictly meant to keep the patient stable until professional EMS/SAR supplies and clinicians take over.
Z10-P77:failure Relying on improvised wilderness tricks when carrying basic commercial gauze, nitrile gloves, and a commercial tourniquet (with training) weighs ounces.
Z10-P78:action1 Recognize that lay field exams cannot diagnose internal bleeding, hairline fractures, concussions vs brain bleeds, appendicitis, or cardiac events—use functional red flags (alertness, breathing, bleeding, mobility, trend direction) to drive evacuation decisions instead of guessing diagnoses.
Z10-P78:action2 Do NOT prescribe or calculate medication dosages for companions, administer another person's prescription drugs, or perform invasive field procedures (cutting wounds, lancing deep abscesses, field suturing, or airway incisions).
Z10-P78:action3 Remember that wilderness first-aid reference cards support memory AFTER hands-on certified training—they NEVER substitute for formal CPR, Stop the Bleed, WFA/WFR courses, or live 911/clinical medical direction.
Z10-P78:failure Acting as an amateur physician in camp—guessing a "harmless stomach virus" and withholding evacuation until an appendix ruptures or shock sets in.
Z10-P78:verify Confirm decisions rest on objective functional trends and red flags rather than speculative field diagnoses.
Z10-P78:stop Uncertainty paired with worsening pain, fever, abnormal breathing, or declining alertness ALWAYS resolves in favor of evacuation and clinical evaluation.
Z10-P79:action3 Verify current hands-on first-aid/CPR certifications within the group and review who carries emergency comms, the group kit, and any voluntarily shared personal emergency action plans.
Z10-P79:verify Confirm written trip plan is lodged with a reliable contact, bailout routes are mapped, and group kits/medications are checked before leaving trailhead.
Z10-P80:action1 Treat every Z10 page as an editorial review draft on `publication: HOLD` with ZERO qualified human clinical approvals until wilderness-medicine physicians, trauma/EMS directors, toxicologists, and infectious-disease reviewers sign off formally.
Z10-P80:action3 Direct every reader toward accredited hands-on CPR/AED, Stop the Bleed, and Wilderness First Aid/First Responder training—printed text alone never confers clinical competency.
Z10-P80:failure Distributing unreviewed AI-assisted medical drafts as "field-validated clinical instructions" without qualified physician and EMS sign-off.
Z10-P80:verify Confirm `publication: HOLD` banner, specialist hold H11 visibility, and zero unauthorized dosages or invasive procedures across all 80 Z10 cards.
Z10-P80:stop Do NOT authorize public distribution or field clinical reliance until qualified human clinical sign-off is formally recorded in the custody ledger.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z10-P28:action1 Stop immediately at the very first warm stinging "hot spot" on a heel or toe—air and dry the foot, change into dry socks, remove grit from boots, and place smooth friction-reducing tape or donut padding around the spot.
Z10-P28:action2 Keep intact fluid-filled blisters unbroken whenever possible because intact roof skin is the body's best sterile dressing; if a blister tears open on its own, rinse gently with clean potable water, leave loose skin flat if clean, and cover with sterile non-stick dressing.
Z10-P28:action3 Treat ANY foot wound, blister, or skin crack in a person with diabetes, neuropathy, or poor circulation as a high-risk medical issue requiring strict protection and early clinical inspection.
Z10-P28:failure Ignoring a burning heel hot spot for five miles until raw torn skin fills with trail mud and becomes infected.
Z10-P28:verify Confirm feet are inspected dry at every camp stop and no spreading redness, pus, or worsening limp is developing.
Z10-P28:stop Spreading redness, warmth, pus, inability to walk normally, or any foot breakdown in a diabetic traveler requires halting the trip and seeking clinical evaluation.
Z10-P47:action1 Recognize that immersion/trench foot develops from prolonged wet cold WITHOUT freezing—feet turn cold, pale, wrinkled, numb, or tingling, then swell, throb, redden, and blister painfully upon warming.
Z10-P47:action3 If trench foot signs appear, remove wet boots/socks immediately, dry feet gently without rubbing or soaking in hot water, keep feet clean, warm, dry, and elevated in shelter, and arrange non-weight-bearing evacuation for clinical care.
Z10-P47:stop Persistent numbness, swelling, purple/pale mottling, or painful blistering halts hiking and requires medical evaluation.
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. Blister-specific clinical evidence and tissue handling need a direct locator. Do not describe the roof as sterile.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z10-P16:action1 Place maximum ground insulation beneath an immobile patient first—an injured person generates minimal body heat and loses warmth rapidly into cold soil or snow even in mild seasons.
Z10-P16:failure Giving all sleeping pads to caregivers while the injured patient lies on a thin raincoat overnight and slips into hypothermia before dawn.
Z10-P41:action2 Move out of wind and wet exposure into shelter, insulate underneath with a thick pad, replace wet garments with dry wool/synthetic layers and hat, and wrap in a dry sleeping bag.
Z10-P41:action3 If the person is completely alert, oriented, and swallowing normally, offer warm (not scalding) sweet drinks and quick calories—never alcohol or tobacco—and keep monitoring until shivering stops and warmth stabilizes.
Z10-P41:stop Slurred speech, confusion, drowsiness, or shivering that stops while the person remains cold indicates moderate-to-severe hypothermia requiring immediate 911 evacuation.
Z10-P42:action1 Activate 911/SAR immediately and treat the patient as critically fragile—keep them HORIZONTAL and handle them extremely gently (no vigorous rubbing, rough standing, or sudden jostling, which can trigger lethal heart arrhythmias in a cold heart).
Z10-P42:action2 Protect from all further heat loss by cutting away wet clothing gently if inside shelter, placing thick insulation underneath and all around the body (hypothermia wrap), and covering the head and neck.
Z10-P42:action3 Keep insulation in place and use protected trunk warming within your training. Withhold oral fluids if alertness is impaired. If the person does not respond or breathe normally, activate 911 and follow dispatcher advice without inserting a fixed lay waiting period.
Z10-P42:failure Forcing a confused, non-shivering hypothermic victim to stand up and walk, or dunking their limbs in hot water.
Z10-P42:verify Confirm patient stays horizontal, wrapped against ground/wind loss, zero oral fluids given while altered, and urgent EMS transport is active.
Z10-P42:stop Unresponsiveness with absent normal breathing triggers immediate dispatcher-guided CPR and continuous evacuation until hospital rewarming.
Z10-P43:action1 Call 911 after significant cold immersion, breathing trouble or altered alertness. Once the person is safely out of the water, shelter them from wind, handle them gently and follow the dispatcher on position and movement.
Z10-P43:action2 Remove soaked clothing gently (cutting it off if movement causes strain), pat skin dry without vigorous rubbing, insulate heavily underneath and around the torso and head, and monitor breathing and mental clarity continuously.
Z10-P43:action3 Watch closely for delayed deterioration ("circum-rescue collapse" or continued core cooling) and potential water aspiration even if the person initially insists they feel fine.
Z10-P43:failure Letting someone who fell through lake ice walk a mile back to a cabin in wet clothes because they initially feel adrenaline-warm.
Z10-P43:verify Confirm survivor is horizontal, dry-wrapped out of wind, monitored continuously, and medically evaluated by EMS.
Z10-P43:stop Any shivering cessation, confusion, coughing/breathing labor, or faintness escalates immediately to emergency resuscitation readiness and urgent transport.
Z16-P05:action2 Open Z10-P43 for stabilize cold-water immersion survivors and guard against post-rescue collapse; Z13-P18 for consolidate household heat into one safe insulated interior room.
Z16-P05:stop Call for urgent help during significant cold exposure with altered alertness. Suspected frostbite has a separate protection and refreezing boundary.
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. CDC supports warming and urgent care. Fixed lay CPR delays and universal core positions are outside the source.

Z10-P45:action2 Recognize true frostbite cues: waxy white, grayish, or mottled skin, numbness ("wooden" loss of feeling), and firm or hard-frozen underlying tissue—remembering field inspection cannot reliably determine final tissue depth.
Z10-P45:action3 Stop exposed travel immediately upon finding numb or waxy skin, shield from wind, remove rings/watches/tight boots before swelling begins, and never rub frozen skin with snow or bare hands.
Z10-P45:failure Ignoring numb toes inside damp boots for hours or rubbing white waxy cheeks with snow, which mechanically shreds frozen skin cells.
Z10-P45:verify Confirm buddy face/hand checks occurred, jewelry/tight items are removed, and wind exposure has stopped.
Z10-P45:stop Numb waxy or hard-frozen skin requires immediate trip abort, protection from trauma/refreezing, and clinical frostbite evaluation.
Z10-P46:action1 Keep frozen tissue protected from crushing, friction, and impact—do NOT actively thaw frostbitten feet or hands in the field if ANY chance of refreezing exists before reaching definitive clinical care, because a thaw-refreeze cycle causes devastating tissue necrosis.
Z10-P46:action2 Never hold numb frostbitten tissue near campfires, stoves, car heaters, or exhaust pipes—loss of sensation allows severe deep thermal burns without pain warning.
Z10-P46:action3 When refreezing remains possible, protect the frozen area and prioritize evacuation. Ask qualified medical support before controlled water rewarming. Use the WMS protocol only when its water temperature, protection and no-refreezing conditions can be met.
Z10-P46:failure Thawing frozen toes over a camp stove, then putting cold wet boots back on to hike out so the thawed tissue refreezes solid.
Z10-P46:verify Confirm the evacuation plan avoids refreezing and that the tissue is protected from friction, pressure and direct heat.
Z10-P46:stop Frozen extremities require immediate evacuation to clinical care; walking on thawed, swollen, blistered feet risks massive tissue destruction.
Z10-P47:action3 If trench foot signs appear, remove wet boots/socks immediately, dry feet gently without rubbing or soaking in hot water, keep feet clean, warm, dry, and elevated in shelter, and arrange non-weight-bearing evacuation for clinical care.
Z10-P80:action2 Preserve strict traceability between every consequential medical assertion and its primary authoritative source (ACS Stop the Bleed, ARC, NIH MedlinePlus, CDC, WMS, Poison Control), updating protocols whenever clinical guidelines revise.
Z16-P05:stop Call for urgent help during significant cold exposure with altered alertness. Suspected frostbite has a separate protection and refreezing boundary.
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. WMS no-refreezing and protection boundary aligns with clinical framework. Temperature and evacuation details need clinician review.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z13-P02:action1 Contact your electric utility BEFORE storm season to enroll voluntarily in any available medical-priority restoration registry—while remembering registries do NOT guarantee uninterrupted power or instant repair during widespread ice storms.
Z13-P02:action2 Calculate exact device wattage and runtime needs with the medical equipment supplier to stage UL-listed battery backups, spare oxygen cylinders, or pre-arranged hospital/shelter relocation before storms arrive.
Z13-P02:verify Confirm medical device runtime calculations, backup batteries tested charged, and pre-agreed relocation trigger logged on paper.
Z13-P04:action1 Switch immediately to battery LED flashlights or lanterns—never candles—check whether neighbors also lost power, and report the outage to your utility via phone or outage line.
Z13-P04:action2 Record the exact power-loss clock time on paper, keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed to preserve cold air, and verify battery-backed CO and smoke alarms are operating.
Z13-P04:action3 Turn off or unplug sensitive electronics and high-draw heating/cooling appliances (leaving one single interior lamp switched on as a restoration indicator) to prevent overload or voltage-spike damage when power returns.
Z13-P04:verify Confirm outage time is logged, candles are absent, fridge/freezer doors remain closed, and sensitive loads are unplugged.
Z13-P05:action1 Unplug computers, medical chargers, televisions, refrigerators/freezers (if unstable flickering brownouts persist), and space heaters that could turn on unattended when power suddenly returns.
Z13-P05:action2 Leave one low-wattage interior LED lamp switched on so you notice immediately when utility service returns, then wait several minutes for voltage to stabilize before reconnecting appliances one at a time.
Z13-P05:action3 Treat dim glowing lights, rhythmic flickering, humming motors, or hot outlets during partial restoration as hazardous brownout/open-neutral electrical faults—shut off affected breakers or main switch if safe and report to your utility/electrician immediately.
Z13-P05:failure Leaving a portable electric space heater switched ON during an outage so it ignites nearby blankets when power restores overnight.
Z13-P05:verify Confirm unattended heat appliances are unplugged, one indicator lamp is set, and loads reconnect gradually only after stable restoration.
Z13-P05:stop Burning electrical odor, sparking outlets, or persistent half-voltage flickering requires switching off power if safe, exiting, and calling the utility or fire service.
Z13-P09:action1 Check both continuous wattage AND startup surge wattage on every device label before plugging in—portable battery stations work cleanly indoors with zero exhaust for phones, LED lights, NOAA radios, CPAP machines, Wi-Fi routers, and intermittent modern refrigerators.
Z13-P13:action1 Use LED flashlights, hands-free headlamps, and battery-powered LED lanterns exclusively during outages—open-flame candles are a leading cause of fatal outage house fires, especially around children, pets, drapes, and fatigued occupants.
Z13-P13:action3 Run LED lanterns on low-output modes to multiply battery life tenfold across multi-day blackouts, and store spare batteries cool and dry with annual expiration checks.
Z13-P14:action3 Recognize that vehicle 12V outlets and small plug-in inverters are intended strictly for phones, radios, and low-watt battery banks—not household appliances—and avoid running down the starter battery with the engine off.
Z13-P17:action1 Keep at least 3 feet of dry, unobstructed clearance in front of the main electrical panel at all times, and NEVER touch a breaker box while standing on wet concrete, in basement floodwater, or with wet hands.
Z13-P17:action2 If a single branch breaker trips once after overloading an outlet, unplug excess loads and reset it cleanly ONCE—if a breaker trips again immediately, smells burnt, feels hot, buzzes, crackles, or sparks, LEAVE IT OFF and call a licensed electrician.
Z13-P17:action3 Treat ANY floodwater that reached basement outlets, furnaces, or the main electrical panel as a severe electrocution hazard requiring the electric utility or licensed electrician to shut off and inspect before anyone enters.
Z13-P66:action2 Plan for multi-story building dependencies: elevators fail immediately (never use elevators during storms/fires—know both enclosed stairwell exits), municipal upper-floor water booster pumps can fail during outages, and hallways rely on short-duration emergency lights.
Z13-P68:action1 When the indicator lamp stays steadily lit (not flickering or dim) for 10 to 15 minutes, reconnect essential appliances ONE AT A TIME—starting with heating/cooling controls and refrigeration before high-draw laundry, ovens, or EV chargers—to prevent simultaneous startup surge trips.
Z13-P68:action2 Inspect the house immediately upon power return: verify no stove burners, irons, or space heaters were left switched ON, verify refrigerators/freezers resume normal cooling, and check appliance thermometers against official USDA/FoodSafety.gov keep/discard charts before eating chilled food.
Z13-P68:action3 Confirm sump pumps, septic lift pumps, and water softeners cycle normally without tripping breakers, and verify CO/smoke alarms return to normal green/standby status.
Z13-P68:failure Flipping every breaker and heavy appliance on simultaneously during unstable brownout restoration, tripping panels and eating warmed food without checking temperatures.
Z13-P68:verify Confirm voltage steady, zero unintended heat appliances running, chilled food checked by thermometer, and pumps/alarms operating cleanly.
Z13-P68:stop Flickering partial power, burning odors, tripping breakers, or failed heating/refrigeration restart require switching affected circuits OFF and calling utility or licensed trades.
Z13-P70:action1 Preserve `Z13-R03` explicitly as a labeled `Reconstruction draft` tied to the unrecovered Home Resilience primer while keeping all 69 newly authored Z13 cards bound to current FEMA, CPSC, NFPA, EPA, CDC, and Minnesota Department of Health primary sources.
Z15-P09:action1 Complete errands EARLY on Winter Storm Watch days: top off vehicle fuel tanks, fill critical prescription refills, stage stored drinking water and no-cook pantry foods, fully charge all phones/power banks/medical batteries, and bring a snow shovel and ice-melt/sand inside near the door.
Z15-P25:stop Rising water approaching basement electrical panels or lower exits requires moving upward early—never waiting in basements to "save boxes."
Z15-P27:action2 Test sump pumps and battery backups, clear storm drains/gutters safely, elevate or unplug lower-level appliances if dry, and follow official municipal guidance on sandbagging or utility shutoffs ONLY while access roads remain completely dry and open.
Z15-P28:stop Downed wires near floodwater, fuel sheens, fast current, or open wounds prohibit entering the water completely.
Z15-P29:action2 Keep main electricity OFF until a licensed electrician/utility verifies wet panels, outlets, and submerged appliances are safe, do NOT drink municipal tap or private well water until utility/certified-lab clearance issues, and photograph all damage thoroughly for insurance/FEMA BEFORE stripping debris.
Z15-P29:failure Flipping the basement breaker back ON to run a wet shop-vac in a damp flooded basement before an electrician inspects submerged outlets.
Z15-P42:action1 Map the cascading chain BEFORE storms hit: when regional power drops, **gas-station fuel pumps stop**, **ATMs and credit-card terminals go offline**, **cell-tower backup batteries drain within hours to a day**, **elevators and residential well/septic pumps stop**, and **municipal water pressure may drop** triggering Boil Water notices.
Z15-P43:action1 Establish a calm daily blackout rhythm right away: switch to low-mode LED lighting (zero candles), log power-off times and guard refrigerator/freezer doors, unplug surge-sensitive electronics/heaters, and conserve smartphone power strictly for brief SMS check-ins and 911.
Z15-P54:failure Relying solely on a 300-pound powered wheelchair with no manual backup or pre-arranged lift-van network during an apartment power outage and flood evacuation.
Z15-P57:action1 Organize prolonged emergencies intentionally into THREE operational phases, beginning with **Days 1–3 (Stabilize)**: secure life safety, CO/smoke alarms, shelter warmth/cooling, fridge/freezer outage triage, family check-ins, and zero indoor combustion.
Z15-P57:action3 Transition cleanly into **Days 15–30 (Sustain & Recover):** Maintain health/morale routines, monitor reserve replenishment triggers with 48-hour buffers, coordinate mutual aid and county/FEMA assistance claims, and execute safe phased utility restoration as infrastructure returns.

Z13-P19:action1 Maintain at least a full 3-foot kid-free and pet-free clearance zone around EVERY space heater, wood stove, fireplace, or baseboard heater—keeping bedding, curtains, rugs, firewood stacks, cardboard, and drying laundry completely outside that perimeter.

Z13-P20:action1 NEVER turn on a gas or electric kitchen oven or stovetop burners to heat a living space—gas ovens generate silent lethal carbon monoxide and burn hazards, while open oven doors cause severe fire and child-scald injuries.
Z13-P20:verify Confirm zero ovens, ranges, grills, or camp stoves are used for space heating and household evacuation warming options are ready.
Z13-P21:action1 Verify FIRST that local fire codes and rental/condo rules legally allow unvented fuel heaters—never assume an outdoor garage/construction torpedo heater or camp heater is indoor-rated.
Z13-P21:action2 Operate a strictly indoor-rated heater ONLY per its exact manufacturer manual: maintain required open fresh-air ventilation (cracked window per manual), keep 3-foot combustible clearance, use ONLY the exact specified fuel (e.g., 1-K clear kerosene; NEVER gasoline), and never bypass safety tip-over or ODS sensors.
Z13-P21:action3 NEVER sleep with an unvented fuel-burning heater running, ALWAYS refuel outdoors after full cooldown, and keep working battery CO alarms active in the room and hallway.
Z13-P21:failure Running an outdoor construction propane heater inside a closed basement or accidentally filling a kerosene heater with gasoline.
Z13-P21:verify Confirm legal code compliance, exact indoor-rated model manual followed, fresh-air vent open, CO alarms active, and unit shut off before sleep.
Z13-P21:stop If a CO alarm sounds or poisoning is suspected, get everyone outside immediately and call 911. Do not stop to turn off the heater or wait for symptoms.
Z13-P22:action1 Have every wood stove, flue pipe, and chimney inspected and cleaned annually by a qualified chimney professional BEFORE winter heating season to remove flammable creosote buildup and animal nests.
Z13-P22:action3 Maintain manufacturer floor-pad and 3-foot wall/combustible clearances, keep stove doors latched or fireplace screens tightly closed, and treat conceptual wood-heat schematics strictly as safety reminders—NOT DIY flue installation guides.
Z13-P30:action3 NEVER use a propane blowtorch, kerosene/propane heater, charcoal stove, or open flame to thaw pipes—open flames ignite concealed wood framing and insulation silently inside wall cavities.
Z13-P60:action1 Store gasoline, kerosene, and ALL pressurized propane cylinders (both 20-lb tanks and 1-lb green cylinders) STRICTLY OUTSIDE living spaces—NEVER inside basements, bedrooms, closets, or near water-heater/furnace pilot flames (heavier-than-air fuel vapors creep along floors and explode upon reaching ignition sparks).
Z13-P60:failure Storing three five-gallon plastic cans of gasoline and two spare 20-lb propane tanks in a basement mechanical room next to a gas furnace.
Z13-P61:action1 Schedule qualified HVAC furnace servicing and certified wood-stove/chimney sweeping in early autumn, change furnace air filters, and clear brush/leaves away from exterior PVC intake/exhaust vents and snow-plow markers around wellheads.
Z13-P61:stop Cracked heat exchangers, damaged chimney liners, leaking fuel lines, or electrical panel faults found in autumn must be repaired by licensed trades before winter use.
Z13-P69:action3 Remember that local Minnesota and municipal building/fire codes vary by city, county, and rental lease—always verify permits and manufacturer manuals rather than improvising home systems from diagrams.
Z13-P70:action2 Treat every Z13 electrical, heating, water-heater, well, and septic diagram strictly as a conceptual safety boundary—NEVER as an engineered installation drawing, wiring schematic, or substitute for local building codes and manufacturer manuals.

Z13-P10:action1 Buy and use ONLY independently safety-listed (UL/ETL/NRTL) battery packs and their exact manufacturer-specified chargers—damaged, off-brand, or mismatched chargers cause internal short circuits and violent thermal runaway fires.

Z13-P11:action1 Recognize that charging flooded lead-acid batteries releases explosive hydrogen gas—never charge unsealed lead-acid batteries inside sealed closets, bedrooms, or near furnace pilot lights, water-heater flames, or spark-producing switches.

Z13-P13:verify Confirm zero open-flame candles in outage kits, working LEDs staged on each floor, and fresh spare batteries inspected.
Z13-P13:stop If a candle or open flame is ever knocked over or catches fabric, evacuate immediately and call 911 if fire exceeds safe extinguisher scope.
Z13-P16:action2 Route cords smoothly without pinching them inside closed windows/doors, coiling tightly under heavy load (which traps heat), running under rugs, or letting plug junctions rest in snowmelt or puddles.
Z13-P16:action3 Inspect plugs, insulation, and grounding prongs before use—feel cords periodically during operation; ANY warm/soft jacket, scorched prong, or tingling shock sensation demands immediate unplugging and retirement.
Z13-P17:action1 Keep at least 3 feet of dry, unobstructed clearance in front of the main electrical panel at all times, and NEVER touch a breaker box while standing on wet concrete, in basement floodwater, or with wet hands.
Z13-P17:action2 If a single branch breaker trips once after overloading an outlet, unplug excess loads and reset it cleanly ONCE—if a breaker trips again immediately, smells burnt, feels hot, buzzes, crackles, or sparks, LEAVE IT OFF and call a licensed electrician.

Z13-P19:action1 Maintain at least a full 3-foot kid-free and pet-free clearance zone around EVERY space heater, wood stove, fireplace, or baseboard heater—keeping bedding, curtains, rugs, firewood stacks, cardboard, and drying laundry completely outside that perimeter.
Z13-P19:action2 Plug portable electric space heaters DIRECTLY into a solid wall receptacle (NEVER into extension cords or power strips, which melt and ignite), place them on flat hard floors, and turn them completely OFF whenever leaving the room or going to sleep.

Z13-P19:failure Plugging a 1,500-watt electric space heater into a thin extension cord next to a sofa throw blanket overnight.

Z13-P22:stop Loud roaring/rumbling sound in the flue, glowing red stovepipe, dense indoor smoke, or exterior chimney sparks require evacuating everyone immediately and calling 911.
Z13-P23:action1 Scoop cooled ashes strictly with a metal shovel into a dedicated lidded METAL container—NEVER into cardboard boxes, paper bags, plastic buckets, or household vacuums (hidden embers ignite days later).
Z13-P23:action2 Carry the tightly lidded metal ash can immediately OUTDOORS onto bare dirt, snow, gravel, or concrete at least 10+ feet away from wood decks, porches, siding, fences, and garages—never leave an ash bucket sitting on a wooden porch "just for tonight."
Z13-P23:failure Leaving a metal pail of "cold" wood-stove ash on a wooden back deck overnight where insulated coals heat the metal bottom and ignite the decking.
Z13-P30:action3 NEVER use a propane blowtorch, kerosene/propane heater, charcoal stove, or open flame to thaw pipes—open flames ignite concealed wood framing and insulation silently inside wall cavities.
Z13-P30:failure Aiming a handheld propane torch into a basement joist bay to thaw a frozen copper pipe, igniting hidden dust and dry framing inside the wall.
Z13-P56:action1 Install working smoke alarms inside every bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every floor (including basements), AND working carbon monoxide alarms on every level and outside all sleeping areas strictly per manufacturer placement instructions.
Z13-P56:action2 Press the TEST button on every smoke and CO alarm monthly, replace removable backup batteries at least annually (or use sealed 10-year lithium-battery units), and vacuum dust gently from sensor vents.
Z13-P56:verify Confirm alarms present on every floor and outside bedrooms, monthly test logged, and every unit is within its manufacturer lifespan.
Z13-P57:action1 Keep a UL-listed Class ABC extinguisher mounted near the kitchen exit and heating/utility zones (checking monthly that the gauge needle sits cleanly in the green zone and the pin/nozzle are intact)—NEVER throw water onto a burning kitchen grease pan or energized electrical fire (water explodes burning grease upward!).
Z13-P57:action2 Evacuate everyone FIRST and call 911; consider using an extinguisher ONLY if the fire is tiny and confined (wastebasket size), your back is squarely toward an unobstructed exit door, smoke is NOT filling the room, and you know PASS (Pull pin, Aim at base, Squeeze handle, Sweep side to side).
Z13-P57:action3 If the fire does NOT go out immediately with one extinguisher, grows past waist height, or emits thick dark smoke, DROP the extinguisher, close doors behind you if safe to slow spread, get outside, and stay outside.

Z13-P60:action1 Store gasoline, kerosene, and ALL pressurized propane cylinders (both 20-lb tanks and 1-lb green cylinders) STRICTLY OUTSIDE living spaces—NEVER inside basements, bedrooms, closets, or near water-heater/furnace pilot flames (heavier-than-air fuel vapors creep along floors and explode upon reaching ignition sparks).
Z13-P60:action2 Use ONLY approved, tightly sealed, properly color-coded safety fuel containers within local residential fire-code volume limits, kept upright in a cool shaded ventilated outdoor shed or exterior storage cabinet out of children's reach.

Z13-P60:stop For a strong fuel odor, active leak or hissing cylinder, leave the area. Avoid switches, engines and flames. Call the fire service or supplier from a safe location. Do not move a leaking cylinder yourself.
Z13-P63:action1 Evacuate immediately and call 911/utility from outside for ANY gas-leak cue (rotten-egg odor, hissing pipes), electrical-fire cue (burning plastic/fish odor, hot/buzzing breaker panel, sparking outlets, flickering partial voltage), or carbon monoxide alarm.
Z13-P63:failure Ignoring a faint fishy burnt-plastic smell near a bedroom outlet or walking under a downed storm power line to check a fence.
Z13-P63:verify Confirm household members can name the four instant-evacuation utility cues (gas odor, CO alarm, burning/arcing electrical, downed lines).
Z13-P66:action2 Plan for multi-story building dependencies: elevators fail immediately (never use elevators during storms/fires—know both enclosed stairwell exits), municipal upper-floor water booster pumps can fail during outages, and hallways rely on short-duration emergency lights.
Z13-P66:stop Building fire/CO alarms, stairwell smoke, or freezing upper-floor rooms without heat require immediate evacuation via stairs and calling 911/management.
Z13-P68:stop Flickering partial power, burning odors, tripping breakers, or failed heating/refrigeration restart require switching affected circuits OFF and calling utility or licensed trades.
Z15-P27:action1 Move vital documents, irreplaceable photos, medications, electronics, and hazardous basement chemicals (paints, fuels, pesticides—so floodwaters do NOT turn into toxic chemical soup!) up to upper floors well before flood crests arrive.
Z15-P43:action1 Establish a calm daily blackout rhythm right away: switch to low-mode LED lighting (zero candles), log power-off times and guard refrigerator/freezer doors, unplug surge-sensitive electronics/heaters, and conserve smartphone power strictly for brief SMS check-ins and 911.
Z15-P47:action3 Never hoard gasoline in unapproved jugs, glass bottles, or inside car trunks/living quarters during storm panics—spilled fuel vapors ignite explosively from static sparks or rear-end collisions.
Z15-P47:verify Confirm household vehicles routinely refuel at half-tank, small cash bills staged safely, and zero fuel stored inside vehicle cabins/homes.
