exact_operational_assertions:
Z01-P01:action3 If travel has stopped, use available shelter and insulation. Tell everyone where to wait and who is trying to make contact.
Z01-P03:action3 If you cannot determine a safe route, stay together in a findable location, shelter from weather and prepare to signal when responders are nearby.
Z01-P09:action3 If no message can get through, avoid uncertain travel just to find signal. Prepare to be located using known landmarks, shelter and available signals.
Z01-P19:action2 Establish immediate exposure control—wind barrier, dry ground insulation and dry rest layers—before spending effort on secondary tasks.
Z01-P19:failure Pushing into darkness until exhausted, neglecting ground insulation until shivering begins, or draining phone batteries on futile searches for signal.
Z01-P19:verify Every occupant has wind/ground protection, reachable exit lighting, a rationed water plan and a scheduled communication or signaling window.
Z01-P21:action2 If no urgent red flags are present, rest in shelter, address footwear, hydration, nutrition and pack load redistribution, and reassess honestly.
Z02-P02:action1 Choose the sheltered side of an existing stable barrier. Check that you remain clear of runoff and falling material.
Z02-P02:action2 Keep the exit easy to reach. Put on dry layers and protect yourself from the ground while conditions allow.
Z02-P02:action3 Reassess as wind direction or drifting changes. Seek a safer shelter if the barrier no longer works.
Z02-P02:verify Group members can move out without climbing over a barrier. Clothing and bedding are staying dry.
Z02-P03:action1 Select ground away from runoff and above standing water. Keep dry gear out of splash and wet snow.
Z02-P03:action2 Place dry insulation between body and ground. Add dry layers above and keep protection available for wind and precipitation.
Z02-P03:action3 Check for gaps under the body and wet material after settling. Replace wet insulation or move if the site is deteriorating.
Z02-P03:verify The body is separated from cold ground and the bedding stays dry where the person rests.
Z02-P04:action2 Assemble the shelter according to its instructions. Keep exits and equipment access clear and avoid putting wet gear on dry bedding.
Z02-P04:action3 Inspect all attachment points and observe how the shelter responds to wind. Adjust within manufacturer limits or relocate to suitable shelter.
Z02-P04:stop If wind, runoff or structural movement exceeds what you can manage safely, leave for more suitable cover.
Z02-P07:action2 Before a stop, find wind protection and add the reserved dry layer. Separate wet items from dry insulation.
Z02-P07:verify The rest layer is dry and easy to reach, and the group can stop without standing in exposed wind.
Z02-P09:action1 From a safe position look for new runoff, pooling, drift at exits or displacement of the shelter and its anchors.
Z02-P09:action2 Keep exits free of gear or snow. Follow the shelter's operating instructions for its vents and supports. Keep combustion outside.
Z02-P09:action3 If you cannot restore safe conditions without remaining in danger, leave to a known safer location while the route is available.
Z02-P09:verify An occupant can identify and use the exit and the sleep area stays dry.
Z02-P10:action2 Install the shelter and ground protection as instructed. Keep bedding away from standing water and wet gear.
Z02-P12:action2 Use available dry insulation and make the vehicle visible without exposing yourself to traffic or the storm.
Z02-P13:action3 Treat lightweight tarps and emergency bivies as limited weather barriers that require skillful site selection and dry ground insulation rather than all-weather enclosures.
Z02-P15:action1 Recognize that cooler, denser air flows downhill at dusk and settles in closed basins, valley bottoms and marsh margins—often producing lower temperatures and heavier frost than nearby mid-slopes.
Z02-P15:action3 Keep extra dry insulation accessible because rapid radiative cooling after sunset can push cool humid hollows toward hypothermia conditions above freezing.
Z02-P15:stop Relocate to higher dry ground or add insulation promptly if valley fog, pooling chill or sudden frost threatens sleeping gear dryness.
Z02-P18:action3 Avoid pitching an open tarp mouth directly into oncoming wind—open fronts act like parachutes that tear tie-outs and strip away trapped calm air.
Z02-P18:stop If shifting gusts push against an exposed broad wall and threaten pole or anchor failure, re-orient before dark or move to a more sheltered site.
Z02-P20:action3 Treat improvised natural windbreaks as a last-resort exposure measure when no manufactured shelter or safe refuge exists—never as an equivalent substitute for rated shelter.
Z02-P20:failure Spending hours building a shaky branch hut while a trailhead vehicle or ranger shelter sits safely twenty minutes back along a verified road.
Z02-P23:action1 Block conduction into cold ground or snow first using dry uncompressed insulation beneath the body; air and ground drain heat rapidly through compressed fabric.
Z02-P23:action2 Block convection with a windbreak or windproof shell, and limit evaporation by shedding damp cotton, venting sweat during work and keeping rain off insulation.
Z02-P23:action3 Recognize that radiation still escapes to clear night skies and cold walls; overhead cover and dry lofted layers slow radiative cooling without sealing away fresh breathing air.
Z02-P23:failure Wrapping in a windproof jacket while lying directly on frozen soil, or piling on thick wool while standing exposed in driving wind.
Z02-P23:verify Point to the exact barrier addressing ground contact, moving air, wetness and sky exposure in your current setup.
Z02-P24:action1 Keep manufacturer-designed high and low vents open—even in cold weather—so warm moist breath escapes upward rather than condensing onto fabric and dripping onto bedding.
Z02-P24:action2 Guy out the rainfly cleanly so a continuous air gap separates the wet outer fly from the breathable inner tent wall; fabric touching fabric wicks water straight inside.
Z02-P24:failure Zipping every tent vent completely shut in cold air to stay warm, turning the shelter interior into a dripping condensation chamber that wets sleeping loft.
Z02-P25:action3 Recognize that a waterproof groundsheet stops liquid seepage only—it provides almost no thermal insulation from cold ground, so an insulating pad is still mandatory inside.
Z02-P26:action1 Combine a closed-cell foam pad underneath an insulated inflatable pad in cold conditions to increase ground separation and shield the air pad from punctures.
Z02-P26:action3 Keep underbody insulation centered beneath shoulders, hips and torso—not just the head—using folded dry spare clothing or a dry pack under feet if a short pad is used.
Z02-P26:failure Relying on a single uninsulated air mattress on frozen ground, where convective air movement inside the pad drains core warmth all night.
Z02-P26:verify Lie briefly in full sleep position to confirm no shoulder, hip or knee presses directly against cold ground or deflated chambers.
Z02-P26:stop If an inflatable pad fails in freezing weather and no dry foam or backup ground insulation keeps the sleeper warm, switch to dry natural/clothing buffers and reassess exit or rescue.
Z02-P27:action2 Change into dry sleep-only base layers and dry socks before entering the bag, and avoid tucking your nose and mouth inside the bag—exhaled breath condenses inside the loft overnight.
Z02-P27:action3 Keep the foot box and outer shell clear of damp tent walls and give sleeping bags time to loft fully after unpacking; compressed down or wet fibers lose thermal resistance rapidly.
Z02-P27:failure Breathing inside a cinched sleeping bag hood all night or stuffing a damp jacket into the foot box, saturating down insulation by morning.
Z02-P28:action1 Use an emergency reflective sheet primarily as a windproof outer shell or lean-to reflector over existing dry insulating layers and a ground barrier—thin foil alone conducts cold straight from the ground.
Z02-P28:failure Climbing inside a sealed plastic emergency bag in damp clothes directly on frozen earth, waking soaked in trapped sweat and chilled by ground conduction.
Z02-P28:verify Confirm dry insulation lies beneath and inside the reflective layer, breathing space is clear and edges are protected from tearing.
Z02-P29:action2 Shake snow and droplets off outer shells before entering shelter and isolate wet boots, rain jackets and wet gloves in a vestibule or waterproof bag apart from dry bedding.
Z02-P29:action3 Change out of damp daytime base layers only after entering wind-protected shelter with dry replacement garments immediately in hand.
Z02-P33:action3 Recognize that improvised deadfall frames and field-cut poles have unknown wood grain, rot and joint friction—never assign them unvalidated snow-load or wind-load capacities.
Z02-P34:stop Do not rely on a shelter with split pole ferrules, failed floor waterproofing or broken door zippers for wet or cold overnight travel.
Z02-P35:stop Anchor strength varies wildly with soil moisture and snow crystal state—no universal pullout rating is implied; relocate to protected refuge if anchors creep in rising wind.
Z02-P38:action1 Select an immovable natural barrier—such as a terrain rise, solid rock outcrop or firmly embedded low log—after confirming zero overhead dead limbs, rolling rocks or runoff channels.
Z02-P38:action2 Position your dry insulated bed tightly on the calmer leeward side while keeping an open, unobstructed exit path clear of stacked sticks or snow banks.
Z02-P38:action3 Resist stacking heavy dead branches overhead to create a roof; a low open windbreak paired with dry insulation avoids overhead collapse hazards and saves critical energy.
Z02-P38:failure Wedging beneath an unstable tilted root-ball or piling heavy rotten limbs across a log where wind or snow can collapse them onto the sleeper.
Z02-P38:verify Confirm the natural barrier cannot roll or shift, zero load hangs overhead and you can stand and exit freely.
Z02-P38:stop If wind shifts around the barrier, blowing snow buries the bed or exposure worsens, relocate to a safer refuge or summon emergency help.
Z02-P39:action2 Recognize that deadfall ridgepoles and side ribs have unpredictable internal rot, knots and joint slippage; fallen-branch framing carries ZERO validated snow-load or wind-load rating.
Z02-P39:action3 Recognize that wet leaves, damp moss or melting snow piled onto an improvised frame soak bedding rapidly and add sudden roof weight that can collapse onto an occupied sleeping area.
Z02-P39:failure Sleeping beneath a heavy debris roof built from brittle deadwood during wet snowfall or rising wind.
Z02-P39:verify Confirm you can explain why a low windbreak plus dry ground insulation beats an untested overhead roof when wood soundness or weather loading is uncertain.
Z02-P40:action1 Treat an open lean-to strictly as a directional windbreak clear of overhead hazards and runoff, keeping an unobstructed exit at all times.
Z02-P40:verify Confirm exposure control relies on dry insulation and wind protection first, with zero flame or hot embers threatening fabric, wood or breathing air.
Z02-P41:verify Confirm avalanche terrain is excluded, dry layers stay protected from sweat and no occupant sleeps beneath an unverified snow roof.
Z02-P42:verify Confirm that without qualified training and suitable snowpack, the group chooses existing refuge, rated winter tent or surface windbreak and rescue signaling instead.
Z02-P43:action2 Reject improvised stone-roofed cavities and boulder crevices where shifting rock loads, cold-air pooling and trapped groundwater seepage create severe crush and hypothermia hazards.
Z02-P43:stop Abort any excavation or cavity occupation immediately; relocate to stable above-ground shelter, dry insulation and verified exit routes.
Z02-P44:action3 Add dedicated underbody insulation (underquilt or properly positioned pad) because compressed sleeping-bag loft beneath a suspended hammock loses heat rapidly to moving air underneath.
Z02-P44:verify Confirm site legality, live sound anchor trees, clear overhead canopy, low safe hang height over clear ground and full underbody insulation.
Z02-P45:action3 Keep upper vents and doorway tracks cleared as snow falls so drifting cannot seal fresh airflow or jam frozen zippers shut.
Z02-P45:stop If wet snow loads faster than you can safely clear it, poles bend sharply or fabric tears, exit immediately while routes remain passable and move to substantial shelter.
Z02-P47:stop If main structural hubs fail, multiple poles snap or weather exceeds your temporarily stabilized shelter, end the overnight stay and relocate to safer refuge.
Z02-P50:action3 Separate heat and light completely from combustion inside sleeping spaces: use battery LED headlamps for light and dry layers plus ground pads for warmth.
Z02-P51:action1 Rely primarily on dry layered clothing, blankets and blocked wind inside the vehicle—shelter protection does NOT require continuous engine idling.
Z02-P53:action1 Keep shelter doorways completely free of stacked packs, tangled guylines, loose boots and gear piles so anyone can reach and unzip the exit by touch in total darkness.
Z03-P03:action1 Move to an identifiable safe sheltered spot. Get out of wind and off the cold ground.
Z03-P03:action2 Put on available dry insulation. Keep wet outer gear from soaking your dry layers.
Z03-P03:verify The group has protection below and around the body and someone knows how help will be requested.
Z03-P05:action2 Use dry layers and ground insulation for warmth in sleeping areas. Keep the exit clear.
Z03-P36:stop If two disciplined attempts fail because fuel is soaked or wind is too strong, stop trying to build a fire and commit immediately to dry insulation and shelter.
Z03-P42:action1 Reduce heat loss first by getting out of wind, insulating underneath from cold ground and changing into dry wool or synthetic layers with a hat and mittens.
Z03-P42:action2 Support internal metabolic heat with easy-to-eat high-calorie foods and safe hydration while pacing light gentle movement without working up a chill-inducing sweat.
Z03-P42:action3 If using commercial air-activated chemical warmers, follow package directions and keep a cloth layer between warmers and bare or numb skin to prevent contact burns.
Z03-P42:failure Trying desperately to build an illegal or wet wood fire for two hours instead of eating calories, putting on dry spare insulation and climbing onto a foam pad.
Z03-P42:verify Confirm wind block, dry underbody pad, dry head/hand/core layers and no-cook calories are active without needing combustion.
Z04-P55:action1 Halt strenuous travel in shade or wind protection to slow fluid loss through sweat and respiration while assessing remaining safe water and exit distance.
Z08-P35:action1 Scan overhead canopies for leaning dead trees and hung-up widowmaker limbs before inspecting any downed wood below.
Z08-P35:failure Pulling on standing dead snags or relying on punky ground-contact logs causes fatal overhead limb falls and collapsed supports.
Z08-P35:verify Overhead hazard scan is clear and inspected deadfall shows solid uncrumbled dry fibers.
Z08-P35:stop Stop immediately and move clear of leaning snags, hung branches, and wind-swaying dead trees.
Z09-P32:action3 Reserve natural-material improvised windbreaks strictly for genuine unequipped survival emergencies—and even then choose dead downed material on safe ground without cutting live timber needlessly.
Z09-P38:action3 Keep a thin closed-cell foam pad or dry spare clothing plan ready in cold weather so a slow overnight leak never leaves the sleeper lying directly on frozen ground.
Z09-P38:failure Trying to stick a cold patch onto a wet soapy sleeping pad at midnight without cleaning valve grit first.
Z09-P38:stop If a baffle ruptures internally or a seam splits beyond patch width in freezing temperatures, rely on closed-cell foam/dry natural insulation below and shorten the trip.
Z09-P41:action2 Evaluate the consequence of a second failure: a patched jacket pocket is trivial, whereas a splinted tent pole ahead of a forecast windstorm or a leaking pad before a 10°F night threatens life safety.
Z10-P05:action2 Call 911 immediately, control any external bleeding, lay the person flat on an insulating ground pad (unless breathing distress or spinal concern dictates otherwise), and wrap them against wind and ground cold.
Z10-P05:failure Leaving a pale, shivering trauma patient sitting upright on cold bare ground or encouraging them to drink sugary fluids while awaiting EMS.
Z10-P10:verify Confirm the chest rises smoothly, the mouth angles slightly downward to drain, and ground insulation is beneath the torso.
Z10-P13:stop Any deterioration in patient stability, darkness, storm onset, or rescuer fatigue halts movement immediately in favor of warm shelter and SAR activation.
Z10-P14:action3 Prioritize building warm windproof ground-insulated shelter around the patient in place while activating professional SAR litter teams equipped with rigid stretchers and rigging.
Z10-P16:action1 Place maximum ground insulation beneath an immobile patient first—an injured person generates minimal body heat and loses warmth rapidly into cold soil or snow even in mild seasons.
Z10-P16:action2 Protect the patient's shelter from wind and rain, maintain scheduled mental-status and breathing checks through the night, and keep caregivers fed, hydrated, and rotating rest shifts so no one collapses from exhaustion.
Z10-P16:failure Giving all sleeping pads to caregivers while the injured patient lies on a thin raincoat overnight and slips into hypothermia before dawn.
Z10-P16:verify Confirm ground insulation, dry outer barrier, scheduled caregiver watch shifts, and ongoing timed patient notes are active.
Z10-P19:action3 Keep the patient completely still, horizontal and insulated from cold ground, withhold all food and fluids (NPO), and monitor alertness and breathing continuously.
Z10-P24:action3 Cover the cooled burn loosely with clean non-stick sterile gauze, keep intact burn blisters unbroken as a natural sterile barrier, and keep the patient warm overall to prevent hypothermia.
Z10-P35:action3 Insulate heavily against cold ground, keep strictly NPO, monitor mental status and breathing continuously, and await trained EMS/SAR extraction teams.
Z10-P40:action3 Position the patient comfortably (often slightly upright for chest pain or knees gently bent for abdominal pain), insulate from cold ground, and withhold food, water, and painkillers that mask deterioration.
Z10-P41:action2 Move out of wind and wet exposure into shelter, insulate underneath with a thick pad, replace wet garments with dry wool/synthetic layers and hat, and wrap in a dry sleeping bag.
Z10-P42:action2 Protect from all further heat loss by cutting away wet clothing gently if inside shelter, placing thick insulation underneath and all around the body (hypothermia wrap), and covering the head and neck.
Z10-P77:action1 Recognize safe lay improvisations when commercial supplies run out: clean folded cloth for direct bleeding pressure, rolled jackets and foam pads for cushioned limb splinting, and dry insulated sleeping bags/tarps for hypothermia wraps.
Z11-R09:stop If uncertainty persists after calm map comparison or visibility/daylight drops, stop moving, shelter in place and contact rescue with your last verified point.
Z11-P11:action2 Keep the entire group tightly together within arm's reach or voice range, add wind/cold protection and verify whether a short unmistakable backtrack to recent shelter exists.
Z11-P11:verify Confirm everyone is accounted for, sheltered from wind and holding on verified stable land until visibility returns safely.
Z11-P11:stop Zero visibility with no unmistakable safe handrail or nearby refuge requires halting on stable ground, sheltering and alerting contacts or rescue.
Z11-P16:action1 Choose a sheltered spot adjacent to a clear natural opening (meadow, clearing edge or open ridge) where bright contrasting colors or cleared snow/ground letters stand out from overhead without exposing the group to wind or avalanche.
Z11-P16:verify Confirm bright contrast is visible from above/nearby trails, whistle and light are immediately in hand and the group stays sheltered together.
Z11-P18:action3 If the remaining trail is unverified, technical, icy or too far for group stamina, STOP with at least 45–60 minutes of usable daylight left to pick a safe dry site, set shelter and prepare insulation calmly.
Z11-P18:verify Confirm remaining daylight minutes, headlamp battery state and an explicit group decision to either finish cleanly or stop early and stabilize.
Z11-P18:stop Never continue cross-country off-trail navigation after dark over uncertain terrain; stop early on safe ground and wait for daylight.
Z11-P20:action1 STOP immediately on stable dry land away from ice, wind corridors and overhead snags—sit on pack or foam pad, put on dry insulation and eat/drink safe reserves to protect clear judgment.
Z11-P20:action3 PLAN conservatively: stay put, build a windbreak/dry bed and display high-contrast signals unless an unmistakable, short, verified land route leads to immediate safe shelter.
Z11-P20:verify Confirm the group is off ice, out of wind, wearing dry insulation, accounted for and either contacting rescue or displaying clear signals.
Z11-P48:stop Never guess cross-country shortcuts out of position uncertainty; if relocation fails after one calm check, stay put, shelter and contact rescue.
Z11-P49:action3 Shift full attention decisively to selecting a safe dry site, wind/ground protection, hydration, warmth and scheduled communication rather than half-heartedly inching forward.
Z11-P49:failure Stumbling half a mile further in freezing rain after dusk trying to shave twenty minutes off tomorrow's hike, triggering an injury or hypothermia rescue.
Z11-P50:action1 **S — Stop:** Sit down physically on a pack or dry spot, take slow controlled breaths, put on a warm layer and take a small drink of safe water to calm adrenaline before making a single decision.
Z11-P50:action3 **P — Plan:** Choose one conservative, defensible action—usually staying put, securing shelter/insulation and setting signals—and revisit it calmly as conditions evolve.
Z11-P50:verify Confirm everyone has physically paused, calmed breathing, added warmth if chilled and agreed on one written or spoken next step.
Z11-P52:action3 Whenever the site is safe (or can be made sheltered) and the exit route is uncertain, stay put together—stationary people conserve warmth, avoid injury and are found vastly faster by rescuers.
Z11-P55:action1 Assign clear rotating tasks suited to each person's ability: shelter/insulation upkeep, scheduled audio/light signaling watch, medical/warmth buddy checks and water/battery conservation log.
Z11-P55:action2 Set realistic expectations honestly—remote ground or air rescue can take many hours depending on weather, darkness and terrain—and prevent panic by keeping everyone warm, hydrated and occupied with calm routine checks.
Z11-P55:action3 Keep one awake listener/watcher during active search windows (especially when aircraft or vehicle lights are nearby) while others rest warmly inside dry layers.
Z11-P55:verify Confirm everyone has an explicit role, dry warmth protection, rationed water/power plan and continuous readiness to answer searchers.
Z11-P68:action3 When uncertainty or hazard strikes: execute STOP immediately, prioritize shelter/insulation before wandering, lead any emergency call with exact location/format and stay visible until rescue arrives.
Z12-P01:action3 Move early into sound upland timber or substantial shelter before blowing snow erases landmarks and wind chill spikes.

Z12-P05:action3 Move an alert mildly chilled person out of wind onto dry ground insulation with dry layers and monitor closely; for ANY confusion, slurred speech, severe drowsiness or unresponsiveness, call 911 immediately, handle gently, protect core heat and give NO oral food or drink to impaired patients.
Z12-P09:action2 If stranded in a blizzard with no immediately visible safe building, STAY WITH THE VEHICLE, call 911/contact with mile marker or road name, tie a bright cloth to the mirror/antenna when wind permits and rely on dry layers first.

Z12-P12:failure Skipping dinner and water because it feels too cold to cook outside, then shivering awake all night with depleted energy and dehydration.

Z12-P34:action1 Expect massive diurnal temperature swings of 30°F–50°F+ after sunset in dry high deserts—dry air and clear skies radiate daytime warmth straight to space within hours of dusk.
Z12-P34:action2 Pack a lightweight warm insulating layer, wind shell and ground barrier even when trailhead afternoon temperatures feel hot, especially if any risk of delay or overnight stranding exists.
Z12-P34:stop Shivering, clumsy hands or chilled damp clothes at dusk require stopping in wind-sheltered ground insulation early rather than pushing tired into cold darkness.

Z13-P18:action2 Pitch a small fabric tent or blanket canopy over mattresses/sleeping pads inside the room to trap body heat safely WITHOUT any fuel-burning heat inside, dressing everyone in dry layered wool/synthetic clothing, hats, and warm socks.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z02-P15:action1 Recognize that cooler, denser air flows downhill at dusk and settles in closed basins, valley bottoms and marsh margins—often producing lower temperatures and heavier frost than nearby mid-slopes.
Z02-P15:action2 Prefer a gently elevated, sheltered bench slightly above the valley floor—avoiding both the cold damp hollow below and the high wind-swept ridge crest above.
Z02-P15:failure Camping beside a misty creek bottom for convenience and waking soaked with heavy condensation in temperatures far colder than the forecast.
Z02-P15:verify Confirm the selected camp sits above obvious cold-air hollows and out of exposed hilltop wind corridors.
Z02-P18:action1 Observe cloud motion, tree sway, snow drift tails and forecast frontal passages to identify both current wind direction and expected overnight wind shifts.
Z02-P18:action2 Aim the lowest, narrowest or most reinforced side of the shelter into the expected wind and place the door on the leeward or crosswind side to limit blowing rain and drifting snow.
Z02-P18:failure Facing a tent door into an approaching cold front because the sunset view faces west, flooding the vestibule and packing snow across the zipper.
Z02-P18:verify Confirm the windward profile is low and guyed cleanly while the doorway opens into calmer leeward air with a clear exit.
Z02-P23:action2 Block convection with a windbreak or windproof shell, and limit evaporation by shedding damp cotton, venting sweat during work and keeping rain off insulation.
Z02-P23:action3 Recognize that radiation still escapes to clear night skies and cold walls; overhead cover and dry lofted layers slow radiative cooling without sealing away fresh breathing air.
Z02-P23:failure Wrapping in a windproof jacket while lying directly on frozen soil, or piling on thick wool while standing exposed in driving wind.
Z02-P23:verify Point to the exact barrier addressing ground contact, moving air, wetness and sky exposure in your current setup.
Z02-P28:action1 Use an emergency reflective sheet primarily as a windproof outer shell or lean-to reflector over existing dry insulating layers and a ground barrier—thin foil alone conducts cold straight from the ground.
Z02-P32:action1 Use a symmetrical A-frame pitch for overhead rain protection with open end ventilation; drop edges closer to the ground when blowing rain enters from the sides.
Z02-P32:action2 Use an open lean-to pitch only for mild windbreak or shade when rain will not swirl under the high open front; expect wind shifts to expose the interior.
Z02-P32:action3 Use a low-profile storm pitch (half-pyramid or low windward wedge) with windward edge near the ground and leeward vent when gusts rise, accepting reduced headroom and keeping exits reachable.
Z02-P38:action2 Position your dry insulated bed tightly on the calmer leeward side while keeping an open, unobstructed exit path clear of stacked sticks or snow banks.
Z02-P44:action3 Add dedicated underbody insulation (underquilt or properly positioned pad) because compressed sleeping-bag loft beneath a suspended hammock loses heat rapidly to moving air underneath.
Z02-P44:failure Hanging from a dead brittle snag in breezy woods, or sleeping in a hammock at 45°F with only a sleeping bag and waking hypothermic from convective cooling underneath.
Z02-P49:action1 Recognize that wind-driven snow drifts rapidly in the lee of shelters and vehicles, quietly burying lower vents, zippers and doors even after snowfall stops.
Z04-P48:action1 Prefer wide-mouth hard bottles over narrow-neck bottles or thin hydration bite-valves and tubes, which freeze shut quickly in subfreezing wind.
Z04-P48:action2 Carry water inside insulated sleeves or near the center of your pack wrapped in spare layers, storing wide-mouth bottles upside down so ice forms away from the threads first.
Z04-P48:failure Relying on an exposed shoulder-strap hose that freezes solid in the first mile, leaving liters of water inaccessible until camp.
Z10-P45:action1 Watch buddies' cheeks, nose, and ears frequently—early frostnip shows pale/red cold skin with stinging or tingling that remains soft and pliable and responds promptly to shelter and gentle skin-to-skin warmth (such as tucking bare fingers into your own armpit).
Z10-P45:verify Confirm buddy face/hand checks occurred, jewelry/tight items are removed, and wind exposure has stopped.
Z11-P40:failure Leaving wind shells packed at the bottom of a bag in a calm valley trailhead, then hitting 45-mph freezing gusts at an exposed pass.
Z11-P40:verify Stage windproof outer layers and reassess tree/wave exposure before entering open passes, ridges or large-lake shorelines.
Z12-P01:action1 Scan downwind across open fields and lake edges for lifting snow plumes—strong winds can erase trails and create near-zero visibility without a single new snowflake falling.
Z12-P01:action3 Move early into sound upland timber or substantial shelter before blowing snow erases landmarks and wind chill spikes.
Z12-P01:failure Stepping onto an open snow-swept corridor because snowfall ended, then losing all landmark contrast in blowing drift ten minutes later.
Z12-P01:verify Confirm current visibility distance, wind direction and immediate wind-protected timber or building refuge before crossing open winter terrain.
Z12-P02:action1 Understand wind chill accurately: wind strips away the body's thin warm boundary layer, speeding skin cooling and frostbite onset dramatically (while NOT lowering the freezing temperature of inanimate gear below air temperature).
Z12-P02:action2 Cover cheeks, nose, ears, wrists and fingers cleanly with windproof loose-fitting layers before stepping into bitter headwinds—use goggles in extreme wind chill to protect eyes and bridge of nose.
Z12-P02:action3 Run frequent buddy checks on each other's faces for pale waxy patches or loss of feeling, because numb skin stops hurting right as freezing begins.
Z12-P02:failure Walking into a 25-mph subzero headwind with exposed cheeks and tight thin gloves until fingers and nose freeze silently.
Z12-P02:verify Confirm zero bare skin gaps at hood, cuff and neck seals and pair companions for mutual face checks every 15–20 minutes.
Z12-P02:stop Numbness, hard/waxy patches or severe biting cold wind-chill warnings require immediate retreat to warm wind-blocked shelter and clinical frostbite screening.
Z12-P03:action1 Start slightly cool ("be bold, start cold") and open collar/pit vents or strip an insulating mid-layer BEFORE heavy exertion starts sweating into your base fabric.
Z12-P03:action3 At every rest stop, immediately zip vents closed, move out of wind and pull a dedicated dry insulated layer over your shell before body heat drops.
Z12-P04:action2 Prefer insulated mittens over five-finger gloves in severe cold (fingers share warmth together), wearing thin liner gloves underneath so bare skin never touches freezing metal tools or stove parts.
Z12-P04:failure Jamming extra socks into tight boots until toes go numb, or removing mittens bare-handed in subzero wind to adjust metal bindings.
Z12-P08:action3 Keep eyewear fog-free by venting face masks cleanly downward away from lenses rather than removing eye protection in intense glare.
Z12-P11:action2 Anticipate mechanical cold brittleness: plastic pack buckles snap under sharp impact, frozen zippers jam on ice glaze, hydration hoses freeze solid and liquid white gas causes instant frostbite if spilled on bare skin.
Z12-P34:action1 Expect massive diurnal temperature swings of 30°F–50°F+ after sunset in dry high deserts—dry air and clear skies radiate daytime warmth straight to space within hours of dusk.
Z12-P37:action1 Expect air temperatures to drop roughly 3°F–5°F for every 1,000 feet of elevation gain (plus severe wind chill on open passes)—a 75°F valley trailhead routinely meets 40°F sleet and freezing gusts at an alpine pass.
Z12-P53:action2 Avoid pitching inside low willow/alder swales where cold damp mist pools overnight, biting insects swarm heavily and standing water rises through tent floors.
Z12-P60:action3 Expect coastal marine fog to roll inland rapidly, erasing headland landmarks and chilling damp skin—stage compass, tide table and windproof dry shell at the top of your pack.
Z12-P72:action1 Reassess clothing, footing and shelter margins EVERY time you cross a major transition—such as climbing above treeline into snow, dropping from a windy pass into a fog-filled valley or watching warm rain turn into wet heavy snow.
Z12-P72:action2 Put on waterproof shells and warm gloves EARLY at the first sign of sleet or dropping wind chill while hands still have full dexterity to work zippers and straps cleanly.
Z15-P11:action1 Restrict outdoor exposure strictly to brief essential tasks during Extreme Cold Warnings—wind chill below minus 30°F freezes exposed cheeks, nose tips, and bare fingers in minutes, while metal door handles and bare fuel nozzles cause instant contact frostbite.
Z15-P11:action2 Cover 100% of exposed skin before stepping outside (windproof shell, insulated mittens over gloves, face mask/balaclava, goggles, warm hat, dry wool socks), buddy-check faces frequently, and bring pets indoors into heated shelter.
Z15-P11:action3 Watch vulnerable plumbing pipes, check that car batteries crank before urgent trips, check on elderly/solo neighbors by phone or safe daytime knock, and never let anyone venture out alone in extreme cold without a check-in time.
Z15-P11:failure Stepping outside bare-handed in minus 35°F wind chill to shovel snow or pump gas for "just five minutes," freezing fingertips white and numb.
Z15-P11:verify Confirm zero exposed skin during brief outdoor tasks, pets sheltered warm, exterior-wall sink cabinets open, and vulnerable neighbors checked.
Z15-P11:stop Tingling/numb white skin, shivering/clumsiness, or outdoor work that can wait until midday warmth halts exposure immediately.

Z02-P31:action1 Recognize that freestanding dome tents hold basic shape without stakes for positioning on rock or hard pads, yet still MUST be staked and guyed against wind lift.
Z02-P31:action2 Recognize that tunnel and non-freestanding trekking-pole tents rely completely on opposing stake tension and guyline alignment to stand; one failed end stake can flatten the whole frame.
Z02-P31:action3 Follow the manufacturer's exact pole-sleeve, clip and guy-out sequence rather than substituting missing poles or skipping guy points in breezy weather.
Z02-P31:failure Leaving a freestanding dome tent unstaked while stepping away, letting a sudden gust tumble or tear the shelter across camp.

Z02-P32:action2 Use an open lean-to pitch only for mild windbreak or shade when rain will not swirl under the high open front; expect wind shifts to expose the interior.
Z02-P32:action3 Use a low-profile storm pitch (half-pyramid or low windward wedge) with windward edge near the ground and leeward vent when gusts rise, accepting reduced headroom and keeping exits reachable.
Z02-P32:failure Pitching a flat high tarp in heavy rain, allowing water to pool in the center until fabric tears or tie-outs pull free.
Z02-P32:stop Tarps offer no lightning protection and limited defense against severe squalls, heavy snow or extreme wind; relocate to rated or substantial shelter when storms intensify.
Z02-P33:action1 Identify three separate paths: gravity loads the roof supports, wind acts on fabric and frame, and guyline tension transfers to anchors. The actual path depends on the shelter design.
Z02-P33:failure Attaching a heavy tarp mid-panel with a pebble knot or leaning snow-laden branches onto a cracked deadwood ridgepole.
Z02-P33:verify Confirm every load-bearing junction—pole ferrule, corner seam, guyline knot and ground stake—shows even tension without kinks, splits or loose play.
Z02-P33:stop If supports shift, split or deform or the shelter tears, leave the hazard area. Keep people out until a competent assessment.
Z02-P35:action1 Check substrate firmness before pitching; slim wire pegs pull straight out of soft mud, loose sand, thick leaf duff and dry snow under modest wind gusts.
Z02-P35:action3 Inspect for movement after setup and weather changes. A gentle hand check can reveal a loose stake but cannot establish capacity in gusts.
Z02-P35:failure Expecting standard aluminum wire pegs pushed into wet forest duff or melting spring snow to hold a tarp through a night squall.
Z02-P35:verify Confirm every primary corner and windward guyline sits in firm substrate and resists steady hand tension without creeping.
Z02-P35:stop Anchor strength varies wildly with soil moisture and snow crystal state—no universal pullout rating is implied; relocate to protected refuge if anchors creep in rising wind.
Z02-P36:action1 Attach guylines strictly to manufacturer-reinforced seam loops and pole-crossing tabs—never pinch unreinforced fabric panels that tear under gust loads.
Z02-P36:action2 Set guyline angles cleanly outward along seam load lines and equalize tension across opposing sides so no single windward corner takes the full shock load.
Z02-P36:failure Guying out only one windward corner tightly while leaving pole-midpoints unguyed, snapping a flexed tent pole during a cross-gust.
Z02-P36:verify Walk around the shelter checking that all windward guylines share even tension, stay clear of exit paths and keep rainfly separated from inner walls.
Z02-P36:stop If gusts cause fabric seams to stretch noticeably or lines repeatedly slacken, lower exposure or move immediately to substantial shelter.
Z02-P37:action2 Recognize that disposable polyethylene sheeting tears rapidly along small punctures, traps heavy condensation and offers low wind resistance compared to ripstop fabrics.
Z02-P37:stop Retire UV-brittle, tearing or delaminated shelter fabric before storms; never patch over failed structural seams to push a shelter into severe weather.
Z02-P39:failure Sleeping beneath a heavy debris roof built from brittle deadwood during wet snowfall or rising wind.
Z02-P39:stop Keep people out from under improvised roofs of unknown capacity. Sagging, movement or added wet debris are further reasons to leave the area immediately.
Z02-P44:stop Never hang from dead trees, fragile saplings, railings or unrated structures; switch to ground shelter or substantial refuge during high winds or lightning.
Z02-P46:action1 Watch and listen for flapping panels, rhythmic pole slapping, creeping ground stakes, elongated needle holes along seams and slackening guylines as gusts increase.
Z02-P46:action2 Re-tension guylines, add secondary anchors or lower windward tarp edges ONLY while conditions outside remain safe and clear of falling limbs.
Z02-P46:action3 Reassess surrounding trees immediately whenever wind picks up—sound shelters cannot protect occupants from falling trunks or snapped overhead branches.

Z02-P47:action3 Recognize that field splints and tape patches are temporary stabilization aids—they do NOT restore full storm strength to a fractured frame.
Z02-P47:stop If main structural hubs fail, multiple poles snap or weather exceeds your temporarily stabilized shelter, end the overnight stay and relocate to safer refuge.
Z09-P10:failure Using slick UV-faded polypropylene twine with a sloppy knot on a storm-exposed ridge tarp, or assuming camp paracord equals certified climbing rope.
Z09-P13:failure Running a tight synthetic guyline directly across a sharp granite edge in high wind, sawing through the sheath within an hour.
Z09-P14:failure Tying a capsized slip loop by pulling the working end wrong, or leaving a tiny untied tail on slick nylon cord that works free in gusty wind.
Z09-P16:action3 Lock any clove hitch exposed to shifting gusts with two half hitches on the standing part so the binding cannot unwind overnight.

Z02-P26:action2 Inspect inflatable valves and seams before bedtime and avoid over-pressurizing or dragging air pads over pine cones, gravel or sharp frozen twigs.
Z02-P26:failure Relying on a single uninsulated air mattress on frozen ground, where convective air movement inside the pad drains core warmth all night.
Z02-P27:action1 Pack sleeping bags inside a sealed waterproof liner during travel so rain, river splashes or leaking water bottles cannot reach the insulation.
Z02-P27:action3 Keep the foot box and outer shell clear of damp tent walls and give sleeping bags time to loft fully after unpacking; compressed down or wet fibers lose thermal resistance rapidly.
Z02-P27:verify Confirm the bag stays inside dry storage during transit, lofts evenly at camp and remains clear of damp tent fabric and exhaled moisture.
Z02-P31:action1 Recognize that freestanding dome tents hold basic shape without stakes for positioning on rock or hard pads, yet still MUST be staked and guyed against wind lift.
Z02-P31:action2 Recognize that tunnel and non-freestanding trekking-pole tents rely completely on opposing stake tension and guyline alignment to stand; one failed end stake can flatten the whole frame.
Z02-P31:action3 Follow the manufacturer's exact pole-sleeve, clip and guy-out sequence rather than substituting missing poles or skipping guy points in breezy weather.
Z02-P31:failure Leaving a freestanding dome tent unstaked while stepping away, letting a sudden gust tumble or tear the shelter across camp.
Z02-P31:verify Confirm all pole tips seat fully in grommets, guylines tension evenly per instructions and the shelter stays firmly anchored when tested gently by hand.
Z02-P31:stop Do not use a three-season geometry in severe storms, heavy wet snow or high winds outside its manufacturer limits; relocate to substantial shelter.
Z02-P32:action1 Use a symmetrical A-frame pitch for overhead rain protection with open end ventilation; drop edges closer to the ground when blowing rain enters from the sides.
Z02-P32:failure Pitching a flat high tarp in heavy rain, allowing water to pool in the center until fabric tears or tie-outs pull free.
Z02-P32:verify Confirm taut sloped runoff planes with zero water-pooling sags, clear exit clearance and reliable ground-splash setback.
Z02-P33:action2 Check joints, anchors and line routing against the shelter instructions. A taut panel cannot establish load capacity.
Z02-P33:verify Confirm every load-bearing junction—pole ferrule, corner seam, guyline knot and ground stake—shows even tension without kinks, splits or loose play.
Z02-P34:action1 Pitch or lay out the shelter in daylight to inspect pole ferrules for hairline splits, check internal shock-cord elasticity and confirm all rainfly buckles and tie-outs are intact.
Z02-P34:action2 Check interior waterproof coatings and seam tape for stickiness, flaking, mildew odor or pinholes, and slide every door zipper gently to verify clean teeth alignment.
Z02-P34:action3 Pack a compatible pole repair splint, fabric patch tape and spare guyline cord matched to the shelter before departure.
Z02-P34:failure Discovering peeling polyurethane floor coating and snapped pole shock-cord at dusk during a cold downpour.
Z02-P34:verify Confirm complete component count (body, fly, poles, stakes, guys, repair kit) and smooth zipper/pole operation prior to packing.
Z02-P34:stop Do not rely on a shelter with split pole ferrules, failed floor waterproofing or broken door zippers for wet or cold overnight travel.
Z02-P35:action1 Check substrate firmness before pitching; slim wire pegs pull straight out of soft mud, loose sand, thick leaf duff and dry snow under modest wind gusts.
Z02-P35:action2 Use shelter-maker instructions for anchor type, placement and orientation. Saturated, soft or changing ground requires a different site when anchors cannot be secured. Follow site rules for any disturbance.
Z02-P35:action3 Inspect for movement after setup and weather changes. A gentle hand check can reveal a loose stake but cannot establish capacity in gusts.
Z02-P35:failure Expecting standard aluminum wire pegs pushed into wet forest duff or melting spring snow to hold a tarp through a night squall.
Z02-P35:verify Confirm every primary corner and windward guyline sits in firm substrate and resists steady hand tension without creeping.
Z02-P36:action1 Attach guylines strictly to manufacturer-reinforced seam loops and pole-crossing tabs—never pinch unreinforced fabric panels that tear under gust loads.
Z02-P36:action2 Set guyline angles cleanly outward along seam load lines and equalize tension across opposing sides so no single windward corner takes the full shock load.
Z02-P36:action3 Use high-visibility cordage or mark lines clearly at walking routes so companions do not trip in the dark, snapping stakes or ripping seams.
Z02-P36:failure Guying out only one windward corner tightly while leaving pole-midpoints unguyed, snapping a flexed tent pole during a cross-gust.
Z02-P36:verify Walk around the shelter checking that all windward guylines share even tension, stay clear of exit paths and keep rainfly separated from inner walls.
Z02-P37:action1 Recognize that silicone- or polyurethane-coated nylon sags when wet and requires re-tensioning in rain, whereas polyester stretches less when wet but varies by denier and coating quality.
Z02-P37:failure Pitching a nylon rainfly tightly in dry afternoon air without re-checking wet sag at night, letting wet fabric droop onto sleeping bags, or sparking a synthetic tarp near a stove.
Z02-P37:verify Identify your shelter's primary fabric class, check wet-tension adjustment access and confirm zero flame or spark sources operate nearby.
Z02-P37:stop Retire UV-brittle, tearing or delaminated shelter fabric before storms; never patch over failed structural seams to push a shelter into severe weather.
Z02-P44:action2 Use wide tree-friendly webbing straps on sound, sufficiently thick live trees—never hang over sharp rocks, steep drop-offs or high above the ground where a strap slip causes serious fall injury.
Z02-P44:action3 Add dedicated underbody insulation (underquilt or properly positioned pad) because compressed sleeping-bag loft beneath a suspended hammock loses heat rapidly to moving air underneath.
Z02-P45:action1 Monitor roof shape periodically during steady snowfall—heavy wet snow adds rapid load that bows fiberglass or aluminum poles and collapses flat roof panels long before morning.
Z02-P45:action2 Tap gently from inside or brush snow off the outer fly carefully from outside before heavy buildup forms, clearing snow piles away from perimeter walls so the tent is not pinched inward.
Z02-P45:failure Sleeping through six hours of heavy wet snow in a flat-roofed three-season tent until poles snap onto sleeping occupants.
Z02-P45:verify Confirm poles retain smooth design curvature, walls stand clear of packed snowdrifts and exits open smoothly without binding.
Z02-P46:action1 Watch and listen for flapping panels, rhythmic pole slapping, creeping ground stakes, elongated needle holes along seams and slackening guylines as gusts increase.
Z02-P46:action2 Re-tension guylines, add secondary anchors or lower windward tarp edges ONLY while conditions outside remain safe and clear of falling limbs.
Z02-P46:failure Ignoring loud rainfly flapping and pulled windward stakes until a gust shreds the fly and bends the main pole at 2 a.m.
Z02-P47:action1 If a tent pole cracks or splits, relieve fabric tension first, slide the manufacturer splint sleeve centered over the break and tape ends snugly—wear eye/hand caution around splintered carbon or fiberglass.
Z02-P47:action2 If a door zipper jams on draft-flap fabric, stop pulling aggressively; back the slider slowly while easing trapped fabric clear, and keep a secondary exit or toggle closure usable.
Z02-P47:action3 Recognize that field splints and tape patches are temporary stabilization aids—they do NOT restore full storm strength to a fractured frame.
Z02-P47:failure Yanking a snagged rainfly zipper until the slider rips off the track in freezing rain, or leaving a jagged broken pole punching through the canopy.
Z02-P47:verify Confirm splinted pole joints hold smoothly without puncturing fabric and that at least one exit opens reliably from inside in the dark.
Z02-P47:stop If main structural hubs fail, multiple poles snap or weather exceeds your temporarily stabilized shelter, end the overnight stay and relocate to safer refuge.
Z02-P48:action1 Check floor corners, seam tape and underside feel during steady rain—cold wet pooling under body pressure indicates groundwater seepage, hydrostatic failure or a protruding groundsheet funneling water.
Z02-P48:action2 Inspect the outside perimeter with a light from a safe stance to see whether new runoff rivulets are flowing toward the tent pad or pooling beside the entrance.
Z02-P48:verify Confirm dry floor corners, zero active runoff channels crossing the pad and dry insulation elevated off damp spots.
Z02-P53:stop Rearrange gear immediately whenever doorway access is narrowed or zippers bind—never sleep inside a shelter with a blocked or jammed exit.
Z09-P10:action1 Recognize that nylon stretches slightly when wet and absorbs modest shock cleanly, whereas polyester stretches less when wet (often preferred for taut tarp ridgelines).
Z09-P17:action1 Use a midshipman's hitch (an improved friction grip over the classic taut-line hitch) around a stake when you need one-handed slide adjustment to take up wet-nylon sag.
Z09-P17:action3 Apply moderate controlled tension—over-cranking a trucker's hitch can rip tarp tie-out seams, bend poles or pull stakes right out of damp soil.
Z09-P17:failure Pulling a ridgeline bar-tight with excessive mechanical leverage on a lightweight nylon tarp, tearing the corner stitching in the first gust.
Z09-P30:failure Trying to tape or wedge a split fiberglass tent pole or cracked hatchet handle and assuming it is restored to full storm or chopping strength.
Z09-P34:action1 Audit every critical gear item you carry—shelter poles, fabric coating (silicone vs polyurethane), inflatable pad, pack hip-belt buckle, boots and stove—and pack the exact compatible patch or spare part.
Z09-P34:action2 Recognize adhesive limits: standard duct tape peels right off silicone-coated (silnylon) tarps and wet cold fabrics—pack coating-matched tenacious/silicone repair tape where needed.
Z09-P34:failure Packing only a roll of household duct tape on a cold wet trip with a silnylon tarp and inflatable sleeping pad, where the tape slides straight off wet silicone fabric.
Z09-P34:stop Do not rely on a field repair kit to compensate for already-failing primary shelter, footwear or water-treatment gear prior to departure.
Z09-P35:action1 Dry and wipe dirt, grease or moisture completely off the torn fabric area—adhesive fails rapidly on damp, dusty or cold greasy fabric.
Z09-P35:action3 Keep high-stress seam rips or corner tie-out failures lightly loaded—adhesive tape stops drafts and small drips cleanly but cannot match sewn structural reinforcement in gales.
Z09-P35:failure Sticking a ragged square strip of damp tape onto a wet tent wall in driving rain without backing both sides or easing guyline tension.
Z09-P35:verify Confirm clean dry bond, rounded patch edges, eased seam tension and dry interior below the patch during rain.
Z09-P38:action1 Inflate the pad firmly, check the valve seal first for grit or loose threads, then listen closely or wipe a thin film of clean water/soap suds across seams and fabric to spot tiny bubbles at pinholes—dry thoroughly before patching.
Z09-P38:action2 Mark the pinhole, clean and dry the surface completely, apply the manufacturer-compatible rounded patch with firm even pressure and allow full cure time before leaning body weight on it.
Z09-P38:action3 Keep a thin closed-cell foam pad or dry spare clothing plan ready in cold weather so a slow overnight leak never leaves the sleeper lying directly on frozen ground.
Z09-P38:failure Trying to stick a cold patch onto a wet soapy sleeping pad at midnight without cleaning valve grit first.
Z09-P38:verify Re-inflate after curing and press gently for several minutes to confirm the pad holds firm pressure without hissing.
Z09-P41:action1 Treat EVERY field patch, pole splint, taped boot sole or knotted strap as a degraded temporary fix with lower strength and shorter service life than intact factory gear.
Z09-P41:failure Pushing two days deeper into remote mountains after splinting a snapped main tent pole and taping a delaminating boot sole.
Z12-P60:action2 Rinse salt and sand out of tent zippers, fishing/camp hardware and metal blades with clean freshwater promptly after coastal exposure, drying and lightly oiling metal parts.
Z12-P60:failure Pitching a tent directly in blowing dune sand with open zippers and leaving an un-oiled carbon knife exposed to night sea mist until rusted shut.
Z12-P70:action2 Audit fabrics, fasteners and metals: wet marshes drive trench foot and soak down loft; coastal salt spray pits carbon steel and windblown sand jams zippers and stove jets; UV desert sun degrades nylon and plastics rapidly.
Z12-P70:stop Never commit to an extreme environment with untested or single-point-failure gear unsuited to the forecast temperature, humidity, elevation or salinity.
Z12-P72:action3 Recognize that wet snow transitioning to subfreezing dusk turns slushy trails into solid glare ice and freezes wet boots and tent zippers rock-hard overnight.

Z02-P16:action1 Check official regional avalanche forecasts before travel and treat slopes roughly 30 to 45 degrees—and terrain directly beneath them—as avalanche hazard zones.
Z02-P16:action2 Look far upslope above flat valley bottoms and meadows; large slides travel well beyond steep ground into seemingly gentle runout paths and gullies.
Z02-P16:action3 Avoid overhanging wind-sculpted snow cornices along ridge crests and stay clear of steep snow-loaded gullies or recent debris piles when stopping or camping.
Z02-P16:failure Pitching a winter tent on a flat valley floor directly under an unassessed steep snow slope or overhanging cornice.
Z02-P16:verify Confirm the site sits clear of steep upper slopes, overhead cornices and connected gully runout paths using both terrain inspection and map contours.
Z02-P16:stop Without formal avalanche training, rescue gear and favorable current forecasts, exclude all avalanche slopes and runout zones completely.
Z02-P41:action2 Exclude avalanche slopes, cornices, stream channels and unstable granular snow; snow depth alone NEVER proves roof strength or block cohesion.
Z02-P41:action3 Avoid roofed excavations in this guide. Use stable surface shelter and insulation or an established refuge. Tools or training alone do not establish roof capacity at a specific site.
Z02-P41:failure Digging a roofed snow trench with bare gloves in sugary unconsolidated snow, soaking clothing with sweat and risking sudden slab collapse.
Z02-P41:verify Confirm avalanche terrain is excluded, dry layers stay protected from sweat and no occupant sleeps beneath an unverified snow roof.
Z02-P41:stop Leave if an excavation shows movement, drift affects exit, or exposure worsens. Get to safer ground without entering runout terrain and seek help.
Z02-P42:action1 Treat snow caves and quinzhees as structural systems requiring specialized training, proper snow sintering evaluation and supervised practice—never as a no-gear emergency shortcut.
Z02-P42:action3 Avoid avalanche runouts, unstable snow and cornices. Treat this as hazard recognition; do not enter, excavate or test an overhead snow cavity using the diagram.
Z02-P42:stop Exit immediately to fresh air and safer shelter if collapse, an obstructed exit or poor air is suspected. Seek emergency help for symptoms of CO exposure or serious cold illness.
Z11-P52:action1 Ask Question 1 — **Is this exact spot immediately dangerous?** Active flash flood, wildfire, avalanche runout, falling timber, tidal cutoff or toxic fumes require moving immediately to the nearest safer clear ground.
Z12-P41:action1 Check the official regional avalanche forecast daily before winter mountain travel—remembering most human-triggered avalanches release on slopes between roughly 30 and 45 degrees (and steep wind-loaded convex rolls).
Z12-P41:action2 Look high above seemingly flat valley trails and meadows: large slides travel far down gullies and across flat valley runout zones, and wind-sculpted overhanging snow cornices fracture far back behind ridge crests.
Z12-P41:action3 Stick strictly to low-angle terrain (below 30 degrees) completely disconnected from steep slopes above unless every party member holds certified avalanche training, carries a beacon/shovel/probe and follows verified forecast guidance.
Z12-P41:failure Skiing or snowshoeing happily along a flat snowy creek gully directly beneath steep wind-loaded 38-degree canyon walls.
Z12-P41:verify Confirm both your current slope angle AND all terrain connected overhead sit safely outside avalanche start zones and runouts.
Z12-P41:stop High/Considerable avalanche danger ratings, steep snow slopes or lack of formal avalanche training and rescue gear require staying strictly in flat disconnected terrain.
Z12-P42:action1 Treat five classic red flags as immediate alarms of unstable snow: (1) recent avalanche debris on nearby slopes, (2) shooting cracks racing outward from skis/boots, (3) loud hollow "whumpfing" collapses underfoot.
Z12-P42:action2 Watch for the other two major red flags: (4) rapid heavy new snowfall, rain-on-snow or strong drifting winds loading leeward slopes, and (5) rapid daytime warming or wet rollerballs/pinwheels rolling down steep faces.
Z12-P42:action3 Recognize that a single "whumpf" on a flat meadow proves a weak layer just collapsed underneath—if connected to a steeper slope above, it can trigger a slide remotely from below.
Z12-P42:failure Hearing a hollow whumpf and seeing cracks shoot out from snowshoes, then shrugging and stepping onto the steeper slope ahead.
Z12-P42:verify Pause immediately upon seeing ANY red flag and re-verify that your route stays completely disconnected from steep overhead snow.
Z12-P42:stop Any observed avalanche red flag triggers immediate retreat onto low-angle disconnected terrain—never "test" a suspicious slope by jumping on it.
Z12-P74:action2 Set (3) **Terrain/Hazard limit** (avalanche red flags, unverified ice, quaking bog, burn-scar storm, sneaker surf), and (4) **Human limit** (any signs of hypothermia, frostbite, heat stroke, HAPE/HACE, cold shock or group separation).
Z12-P75:action1 Recognize that high-consequence environmental procedures—including ice self-rescue, shore witness rescue, cold-water immersion care, avalanche avoidance, high-altitude HAPE/HACE recognition and maritime distress—carry fatal risk if misapplied and remain strictly on **publication: HOLD**.
Z12-P75:action3 Pursue formal hands-on certified training (wilderness first aid, avalanche Level 1, coastal/maritime boating safety, swiftwater/ice rescue) from qualified human instructors before entering extreme environments.
Z12-P75:failure Treating an unapproved draft encyclopedia card as a substitute for certified avalanche, boating, desert or wilderness medical training.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z02-P18:failure Facing a tent door into an approaching cold front because the sunset view faces west, flooding the vestibule and packing snow across the zipper.
Z02-P20:stop Never leave a safe building or stranded winter vehicle into blinding visibility or severe storm hazards just to try a different shelter.
Z02-P24:action1 Keep manufacturer-designed high and low vents open—even in cold weather—so warm moist breath escapes upward rather than condensing onto fabric and dripping onto bedding.
Z02-P24:failure Zipping every tent vent completely shut in cold air to stay warm, turning the shelter interior into a dripping condensation chamber that wets sleeping loft.
Z02-P24:verify Confirm upper/lower vents remain clear, rainfly stands off the inner canopy and sleeping bags stay clear of damp wall edges.
Z02-P41:action1 Prefer existing stable buildings, safe vehicles or rated tents over digging snow when exposure, wind or fatigue is rising—digging burns heavy energy and causes dangerous sweating.
Z02-P41:action3 Avoid roofed excavations in this guide. Use stable surface shelter and insulation or an established refuge. Tools or training alone do not establish roof capacity at a specific site.
Z02-P41:failure Digging a roofed snow trench with bare gloves in sugary unconsolidated snow, soaking clothing with sweat and risking sudden slab collapse.
Z02-P41:stop Leave if an excavation shows movement, drift affects exit, or exposure worsens. Get to safer ground without entering runout terrain and seek help.
Z02-P42:action1 Treat snow caves and quinzhees as structural systems requiring specialized training, proper snow sintering evaluation and supervised practice—never as a no-gear emergency shortcut.
Z02-P42:action2 Recognize four acute hazards inside snow enclosures: unverified ceiling collapse (especially during warming or rain-on-snow), blocked ventilation holes, snow-drifted exits and rapid lethal CO from any stove or candle.
Z02-P42:action3 Avoid avalanche runouts, unstable snow and cornices. Treat this as hazard recognition; do not enter, excavate or test an overhead snow cavity using the diagram.
Z02-P42:failure Attempting an unsupervised quinzhee in wet warming snow or lighting a small camp stove inside a snow cave to warm the air.
Z02-P45:action1 Monitor roof shape periodically during steady snowfall—heavy wet snow adds rapid load that bows fiberglass or aluminum poles and collapses flat roof panels long before morning.
Z02-P45:action2 Tap gently from inside or brush snow off the outer fly carefully from outside before heavy buildup forms, clearing snow piles away from perimeter walls so the tent is not pinched inward.
Z02-P45:action3 Keep upper vents and doorway tracks cleared as snow falls so drifting cannot seal fresh airflow or jam frozen zippers shut.
Z02-P45:failure Sleeping through six hours of heavy wet snow in a flat-roofed three-season tent until poles snap onto sleeping occupants.
Z02-P45:verify Confirm poles retain smooth design curvature, walls stand clear of packed snowdrifts and exits open smoothly without binding.
Z02-P45:stop If wet snow loads faster than you can safely clear it, poles bend sharply or fabric tears, exit immediately while routes remain passable and move to substantial shelter.
Z02-P49:action1 Recognize that wind-driven snow drifts rapidly in the lee of shelters and vehicles, quietly burying lower vents, zippers and doors even after snowfall stops.
Z02-P49:action2 Schedule periodic awake checks during overnight storms to clear drifted snow from doorways, high vents and—for vehicles—exhaust areas, ensuring unobstructed breathing air and egress.
Z02-P49:action3 Keep a small scoop or snow clearing tool reachable inside the shelter entrance so occupants are never trapped behind a wind-packed drift slab.
Z02-P49:failure Waking to a wind-packed snow wall blocking the sole tent door and sealing perimeter vents airtight.
Z02-P49:verify Confirm both air vents and primary doorway open cleanly to outside air and a clearing tool stays staged just inside the exit.
Z02-P49:stop If drifting snow continuously seals the shelter or interior air feels stale and humid, vacate to substantial shelter when safely reachable or call for rescue assistance.
Z02-P51:action1 Rely primarily on dry layered clothing, blankets and blocked wind inside the vehicle—shelter protection does NOT require continuous engine idling.
Z02-P51:action2 Before ever briefly running the engine for heat, physically verify the tailpipe and underside around the exhaust are completely clear of snowdrifts and ice—drifting snow can re-block an exhaust pipe quickly.
Z02-P51:failure Falling asleep with an idling car while blowing snow packs around the rear bumper and channels odorless carbon monoxide into the cabin.
Z02-P51:verify Confirm tailpipe clearance visually before any brief engine run, stay awake while running and keep everyone alert for headache or dizziness.
Z02-P52:action1 Keep shelter air pathways unobstructed by gear, snow or improvised plastic seals; verify battery-backed CO alarms work on every level and outside sleeping areas in cabins and homes.
Z02-P53:action1 Keep shelter doorways completely free of stacked packs, tangled guylines, loose boots and gear piles so anyone can reach and unzip the exit by touch in total darkness.
Z02-P53:failure Blocking a tent's only door with wet packs and tangled cords while burying the headlamp at the bottom of a sleeping bag.
Z02-P53:stop Rearrange gear immediately whenever doorway access is narrowed or zippers bind—never sleep inside a shelter with a blocked or jammed exit.
Z11-P40:action2 Watch large lakes (such as Lake Superior and large Upper Midwest basins) where cold air crossing warmer open water generates sudden localized lake-effect snow squalls that erase visibility within minutes.
Z11-P45:action1 Plan winter routes around drastically shorter daylight (often dark before 4:30–5:00 p.m. in northern latitudes) and much slower pace when breaking fresh snow or wearing snowshoes.
Z11-P45:stop Turn back immediately if snow-breaking effort drops pace below your daylight return margin or if trail markers disappear in drifting snow.
Z12-P01:action1 Scan downwind across open fields and lake edges for lifting snow plumes—strong winds can erase trails and create near-zero visibility without a single new snowflake falling.
Z12-P01:action2 Inspect terrain edges for snow-hidden creek channels, slush overflow and drifted drop-offs rather than assuming a smooth white surface means firm ground.
Z12-P01:failure Stepping onto an open snow-swept corridor because snowfall ended, then losing all landmark contrast in blowing drift ten minutes later.
Z12-P07:action1 Recognize that wading knee-deep without flotation ("post-holing") burns massive energy, spikes sweating and can cut travel speed below one mile per hour—carry snowshoes or skis whenever snow depth warrants.
Z12-P09:action1 Pack winter survival layers INSIDE the passenger cabin (not locked in an unreachable iced trunk) before winter travel, keeping fuel tanks at least half full during cold snaps.
Z12-P09:action3 Keep the exhaust tailpipe completely cleared of drifting snow before any brief awake engine run; NEVER run a vehicle in a drifted snowbank or garage and shut off immediately if exhaust odor or dizziness occurs.
Z12-P09:failure Abandoning a stalled car in a rural blizzard to walk "just a mile" to town, or sleeping with the engine idling while blowing snow plugs the tailpipe.
Z12-P09:verify Confirm winter cabin kit is accessible, phone/contacts are notified and tailpipe clearance is physically checked before any brief engine use.
Z12-P10:action1 Delay travel and stay inside substantial shelter during freezing rain—heavy glaze ice coats roads, steps and tree canopies rapidly, snapping thick live branches and power lines without warning.
Z12-P10:action3 Recognize that freezing rain wets clothing fast at 31°F–33°F—prime rapid hypothermia conditions—requiring waterproof outer protection and traction cleats if short essential movement cannot wait.
Z12-P10:failure Hiking beneath ice-crusted hardwoods after a freezing-rain storm to admire the scenery while limbs crack overhead and icy trails cause head falls.
Z12-P10:verify Confirm travel is postponed until glaze melts or clears, overhead trees/wires are avoided and indoor backup warmth stays strictly CO-free.
Z12-P10:stop Snapping ice-loaded branches, downed power lines, unwalkable glare ice or wet shivering chills require staying inside substantial shelter immediately.
Z12-P42:action2 Watch for the other two major red flags: (4) rapid heavy new snowfall, rain-on-snow or strong drifting winds loading leeward slopes, and (5) rapid daytime warming or wet rollerballs/pinwheels rolling down steep faces.
Z12-P71:action1 Prepare for **both wet rain AND freezing cold on the same day** during spring and autumn—35°F–45°F sleet and freezing rain are prime hypothermia conditions because travelers pack too lightly for "almost summer" or "not yet winter."
Z12-P72:action3 Recognize that wet snow transitioning to subfreezing dusk turns slushy trails into solid glare ice and freezes wet boots and tent zippers rock-hard overnight.
Z12-P72:stop Rain turning to heavy wet snow, sudden freezing gusts or glazing trail surfaces without winter traction/shelter demands descending to lower sheltered terrain immediately.
Z13-P14:action2 During snowstorms, physically inspect and clear snowdrifts away from the ENTIRE tailpipe and underbody BEFORE starting the engine, and keep a downwind window slightly cracked while remaining awake.
Z13-P24:action1 Locate ALL exterior sidewall exhaust and combustion-air intake pipes around your home foundation in autumn—high-efficiency white PVC vents often exit just 1 to 3 feet above grade and disappear rapidly beneath Upper Midwest snowdrifts.
Z13-P24:action2 After every heavy snowfall, blizzard, or high-wind drifting event, walk the exterior perimeter and clear snow and hanging icicles away from every furnace, water-heater, and dryer vent gently without cracking cold plastic pipes.
Z13-P24:failure Assuming a modern basement gas furnace is "sealed and automatic" while a waist-deep snowdrift plugs its exterior sidewall exhaust pipe.
Z16-P31:action2 Open Z02-P05 for leave a drainage channel early; Z02-P11 for look up before stopping below trees; Z02-P49 for prevent drifting snow from sealing shelter exits and high vents overnight.
