Z09-P01:action1 Match tool design to the actual material and cut—use saws for cross-cutting deadwood, small knives for fine shaping and proper levers or shovels for prying and digging.
Z09-P01:stop If the right tool is missing or the task exceeds safe camp-tool limits, choose an alternate low-risk method rather than improvising unsafe blade or impact substitutes.
Z09-P02:action1 Check wooden or composite handles for hairline splits, rot, wobble or loose head wedges; never swing an axe or hammer with a moving head.
Z09-P02:action2 Test folding-knife and folding-saw locking mechanisms slowly with fingers completely clear of the closing arc to confirm zero blade play or slip.
Z09-P02:action3 Inspect metal edges and striking faces for cracks, chips, heavy rust or mushroomed rims that can snap or throw metal shards under load.
Z09-P02:failure Opening a gritty folding knife without checking whether the liner lock engaged, causing the blade to snap shut on fingers during a push cut.
Z09-P02:verify Confirm tight head seating, sound uncracked handle, positive lock engagement and clean intact blade edge before starting work.
Z09-P02:stop Immediately tag out and retire any tool with a loose head, cracked handle, unreliable lock or mushroomed striking poll—never patch a broken axe handle with tape.
Z09-P03:action2 Orient every cutting stroke away from your thighs, torso, knee arteries and supporting hand—always predict where the blade will travel if the wood splits suddenly or the edge slips.
Z09-P03:failure Carving a stick braced against your thigh or chopping branches while a companion walks behind your backswing.
Z09-P03:verify Confirm zero people or gear inside the work radius, clear follow-through path and solid level stance before the first cut.
Z09-P04:action2 Cut with the grain rather than forcing blades straight into hard tight knots, which deflect edges sideways and chip thin steel bevels.
Z09-P04:failure Trying to carve a load-bearing lever or split through a gnarly resinous knot with a thin pocket knife, snapping the blade tip or deflecting it into the hand.
Z09-P04:stop Reject brittle, rotted or heavily knotted wood rather than forcing a blade through resistance; never cut live trees for routine camp craft.
Z09-P05:action1 Choose a sturdy modest fixed-blade knife when repeated wood prep or wet/cold gloved handling makes pivot grit and folding-lock failure a concern.
Z09-P05:action2 Choose a locking folding knife strictly for light slicing, cord cutting and food/repair tasks—recognizing that pivot pins and locks are mechanical weak points under sideways twist or batoning.
Z09-P05:failure Baton-hammering a folding pocket knife through thick oak or prying stubborn stove parts with a thin knife tip instead of pliers.
Z09-P05:verify Confirm the carried blade or multi-tool fits the actual tasks planned, opens safely and stores in a secure sheath or pouch.
Z09-P05:stop Never rely on a non-locking slip-joint blade for heavy push cuts or wet gloved work; stop and change tools whenever a blade flexes or binds.
Z09-P06:action3 Reserve hatchets and short axes for trained operators working on a low solid chopping block; short-handled hatchets easily deflect into knees or shins when swung at mid-air sticks.
Z09-P06:failure Trying to hack springy wrist-thick dead branches with a short hatchet held in one hand while steadying the stick with the other hand inches away.
Z09-P07:action3 Recognize that very hard steel and subfreezing temperatures increase brittleness under lateral prying or heavy impact shocks.
Z09-P07:failure Using a thin kitchen or fillet blade to split frozen hardwood, snapping the blade cleanly in half toward the user's hand.
Z09-P07:stop Stop cutting if an edge chips, cracks or bends noticeably; retire damaged steel rather than forcing a compromised blade deeper into tough material.
Z09-P08:action1 Recognize that hardened knife blades and thin screwdriver shanks are engineered for cutting or torque—NOT sideways bending—and can snap explosively under prying leverage.
Z09-P08:action2 Use a solid hardwood lever, flat metal tent-stake puller, multi-tool pliers or purpose-made pry bar for lifting, separating or digging stubborn items.
Z09-P08:action3 Protect eyes and hands from sudden release whenever pulling frozen ground stakes or freeing stuck latches.
Z09-P08:failure Jamming a folding knife tip under a frozen metal container lid or twisting a blade sideways inside a split log to lever it apart.
Z09-P08:verify Confirm the tool chosen is designed for bending or pulling loads before applying lateral force.
Z09-P08:stop Stop immediately the instant any knife blade flexes laterally or binds tightly in wood—withdraw straight back and switch to a wooden wedge or lever.
Z09-P09:action1 Keep every fixed blade, axe head and saw blade fully sheathed or folded locked whenever walking, climbing over logs or setting the tool down between cuts.
Z09-P09:failure Laying an open knife on forest leaves beside a pack where a companion kneels onto the blade, or walking with an uncovered hatchet over icy roots.
Z09-P22:action1 Sit or stand stably with elbows braced or workpiece resting against a solid wooden block, directing EVERY blade edge strictly away from fingers, forearms, thighs and companions.
Z09-P22:action2 Use short controlled thumb-assisted push cuts or chest-lever grips (holding wrists locked and opening shoulders rather than jerking arms) to take thin shavings instead of muscling deep gouges.
Z09-P22:action3 Keep your supporting hand strictly behind the cutting bevel—never hold a short stick with fingertips ahead of a pushing blade.
Z09-P22:failure Sitting with knees together and carving straight downward between the thighs, where a slip hits the femoral artery.
Z09-P22:verify Before every cut, trace the exact path the blade will travel if the wood splits suddenly and confirm zero body parts lie in that path.
Z09-P22:stop Stop carving immediately if hands grow cold, wet, numb or fatigued; sheath the knife before standing or adjusting grip.
Z09-P23:action2 Carve a shallow tapered tip and clean cord-retention notch using away-from-body cuts over a stable wood block—avoid paper-thin tips that snap in rocky soil.
Z09-P23:failure Cutting green living saplings to make tent pegs in a protected park, or whittling a thin sharp spike unsupported in mid-air.
Z09-P24:action1 Score or make shallow stop-cuts with a saw first to define exact notch boundaries before paring out waste wood—stop-cuts prevent fibers from splitting down the entire workpiece.
Z09-P24:action2 Pare gradually from both sides toward the center stop-cut in thin controlled chips rather than prying chunks out sideways with the knife tip.
Z09-P24:failure Trying to dig out a deep notch in one heavy downward pry, splitting the stick in half and driving the blade into the supporting palm.
Z09-P24:verify Confirm flat mating surfaces, zero split cracks extending past the notch and safe body-clear cutting posture throughout.
Z09-P24:stop Switch to simple lashed overlap joints whenever cold hands, knotty wood or tool wear make precise notching unsafe.
Z09-P27:action2 If a knife is not specifically rated by its maker for impact use, do not strike it. No improvised blade or club configuration is validated here.
Z09-P27:action3 Never baton a folding knife, serrated thin blade or oversized knotty log—excess impact shears pivot pins, snaps tangs and bounces blades unpredictably.
Z09-P27:failure Hammering a pocket folder with a granite rock through a twisted oak knot, shattering the lock and cutting the holding hand.
Z09-P27:verify Confirm straight knot-free wood, flat solid base block, wooden striking baton only and zero fingers near the exit line.
Z09-P27:stop If a blade or wedge binds, stop applying force, clear the area and follow the tool maker or instructor for safe recovery.
Z09-P28:action3 Use the contact-split method for short kindling blocks: press the hatchet bit squarely into the end grain first, lift wood and hatchet together as one unit and bring both down together onto the chopping block—keeping your free hand completely away from the blade.
Z09-P28:failure Holding a short stove-length billet upright with fingers two inches from the top while swinging a hatchet down at it.
Z09-P29:action1 Never strike hardened steel against hardened steel (such as hammering an axe poll with a sledgehammer or driving a steel wedge with a hatchet back)—brittle steel can spall razor-sharp chips at bullet-like speed.
Z09-P29:action3 Inspect metal wedge heads and chisels regularly—mushroomed rolled rims fracture off violently under blows and must be properly dressed in a shop or retired from use.
Z09-P29:failure Pounding the hardened back of a camp axe with a rock or metal hammer to force it through a stubborn log, splitting the eye and throwing steel shrapnel.
Z09-P29:stop Retire any chisel, wedge or hammer displaying mushroomed edges, cracked eyes or chipped polls immediately.
Z09-P30:stop Never use field-wedged or tape-wrapped handles on swinging impact tools (axes, hammers) or load-bearing safety gear—retire damaged handles safely.
Z09-P31:action3 Use compact shovels strictly for soil, ash or snow work—never pry heavy boulders with thin stamped folding blades that buckle or snap.
Z09-P40:action1 Cut clean known-history plastic bottles carefully away from hands to form a scoop or funnel, immediately covering or smoothing sharp cut plastic rims with tape so edges do not slice fingers.
Z09-P40:action3 Never cut into pressurized containers, unknown chemical bottles or sharp jagged tin lids without proper metal shears and cut protection.
Z09-P40:failure Sawing hastily at a slippery tin can with a pocket knife, suffering a deep laceration, or using the same cut bottle scoop for raw creek water and boiled water.
Z09-P40:stop Reject sharp jagged tin edges and any container whose previous contents are unknown.
Z09-P46:action1 Secure an axe or heavy tool firmly against a stable bench or pegged wood support before filing, using a file fitted with both a handle and knuckle guard—never file loose handheld steel toward your fingers.
Z09-P46:action3 Wipe metal filings cleanly away from food areas and fingers, test sharpness safely on a small scrap of paper or dry wood—NEVER draw a thumb lengthwise along a blade edge.
Z09-P46:failure Trying to sharpen a hatchet held loosely between knees with an unguarded bare-tang file, slicing deeply into the palm.
Z09-P46:verify Confirm firm workpiece immobilization, protected fingers, preserved smooth bevel angle and clean safe testing on scrap material.
Z09-P46:stop Stop field honing if the blade shows deep structural cracks, heat-blued soft spots or large jagged chips—retire or professionally regrind damaged steel.
Z09-P47:stop Retire rusted-through hinges, bent saw plates or pitted corroded locks that will not open or latch smoothly after cleaning.
Z09-P48:action2 Check immediately below the metal eye/collar for crushed overstrike gouges, hairline checks, dry rot or gaps around the top wedge indicating a loose head that can fly off mid-swing.
Z09-P48:failure Wrapping electrical tape around a cracked axe neck or soaking a loose axe head in water overnight—which swells fibers briefly and leaves the head even looser after drying.
Z09-P48:stop Immediately remove any tool with a cracked handle or loose head from service until properly re-hung with a sound replacement handle.
Z09-P49:action1 Spot a dull or rolled edge by checking whether a blade slips off wood instead of biting smoothly or glints brightly along the very apex under light—forcing a dull blade causes sudden uncontrolled slips.
Z09-P49:failure Pressing with full shoulder weight on a dull rolled knife blade until it skids off a dry branch straight into the opposite thumb.
Z09-P49:stop Retire cracked blades, bent saw plates or deeply chipped edges rather than fighting defective cutting geometry in the field.
Z09-P50:action1 Check folding tool locks for grit buildup, incomplete lock-bar travel or wobbly pivot pins—never force a gritty stuck blade open by gripping the sharp edge with bare fingers.
Z09-P50:action2 Match screwdriver tips and hex wrenches snugly to fastener heads; loose undersized drivers cam out, stripping screw slots permanently and jabbing palms.
Z09-P50:failure Trying to turn a stuck Phillips stove screw with a pointed knife tip, snapping the blade point and mangling the screw head beyond repair.
Z09-P50:stop Retire any folding tool with an unreliable lock or cracked pivot and switch to a fixed backup or alternate gear plan.
Z09-P52:failure Trying to whittle kindling or split wood by dim dusk light with shivering numb fingers after a 12-mile hike, resulting in a severe hand laceration.
Z12-P25:action2 Never attempt to chop or smash holes in frozen lakes with makeshift rocks, sticks or unsuited camp knives, which damages tools and shocks thin ice directly beneath your boots.
Z15-P14:action2 Clear exterior furnace/water-heater PVC exhaust vents, fire hydrants near the curb, and primary exit doors FIRST before tackling full driveways—and NEVER stick hands or feet inside a clogged snowblower chute (always shut the engine completely OFF and use a wooden clearing stick!).

Z08-P36:action3 Inspect fallen bark fibers for mold, brittleness, and short staple length, noting that natural cordage strength is highly variable and never life-safety rated.
Z08-P37:action3 Recognize that dry brittle stems crack unless conditioned properly, and never use improvised plant twine for climbing, hoisting, or life-safety anchors.
Z08-P38:action2 Inspect both natural fibers and synthetic cords for UV sun-bleaching, stiff chalky texture, fuzzing abrasion, and knot-pinch flattening.
Z08-P38:action3 Dry wet cordage thoroughly in shade with airflow and retire any frayed, mildewed, or sun-brittle cord before use.
Z08-P38:verify Cordage is dry, flexible, unfrayed, and restricted strictly within non-life-safety limits.
Z08-P38:stop Stop using any cordage that smells musty, sheds powdery dust, snaps under light hand pull, or shows melted/cut strands.
Z08-P44:action1 Preserve B007A cordage concepts strictly as non-rated educational material demonstrations using lawfully obtained dead-plant fibers.
Z08-P44:action2 Inspect twisted natural fibers closely for dry brittleness, uneven thickness, and sharp abrasion points where strands shear rapidly under friction.
Z08-P44:action3 Use maintained manufactured cordage for any shelter ridgeline, pack lashing, or critical field tie-down rather than improvised bast twine.
Z08-P44:failure Trusting hand-twisted plant fibers for heavy loads or overhead tie-downs results in abrupt unannounced parting.
Z08-P44:verify Natural fiber samples remain strictly educational and non-load-bearing, with commercial cord carried for field tasks.
Z08-P44:stop Stop any attempt to use improvised plant cordage for human weight, climbing, towing, or heavy overhead suspension.
Z09-P02:action1 Check wooden or composite handles for hairline splits, rot, wobble or loose head wedges; never swing an axe or hammer with a moving head.
Z09-P02:stop Immediately tag out and retire any tool with a loose head, cracked handle, unreliable lock or mushroomed striking poll—never patch a broken axe handle with tape.
Z09-P04:action2 Cut with the grain rather than forcing blades straight into hard tight knots, which deflect edges sideways and chip thin steel bevels.
Z09-P06:action2 Recognize that bow saws handle thicker downed logs efficiently with replaceable blades, yet frame tension and blade alignment must be checked before every cut.
Z09-P07:action1 Recognize the basic trade-off: thin narrow bevels slice cordage and shavings cleanly with little effort, whereas thicker convex or stout bevels resist chipping on harder wood impacts.
Z09-P07:action2 Avoid cutting directly against rock, sand, metal cans or bone with fine wood-carving blades—hard abrasive contact rolls or chips thin steel edges immediately.
Z09-P07:action3 Recognize that very hard steel and subfreezing temperatures increase brittleness under lateral prying or heavy impact shocks.
Z09-P07:failure Using a thin kitchen or fillet blade to split frozen hardwood, snapping the blade cleanly in half toward the user's hand.
Z09-P07:verify Match blade thickness and grind to the target material and confirm a clean wood backing surface underneath cuts.
Z09-P07:stop Stop cutting if an edge chips, cracks or bends noticeably; retire damaged steel rather than forcing a compromised blade deeper into tough material.
Z09-P09:action3 Mark dark tool handles with bright cord or tape and wipe blades dry after rain or sap contact so tools stay visible in leaf litter and free of pitting rust.
Z09-P09:verify Confirm secure sheath retention, dry blade storage and a consistent visible camp tool-parking spot off the walking lane.
Z09-P25:failure Sawing straight down through the top of a sagging log until the gap clamps shut onto the blade, bending or snapping the saw teeth.
Z09-P30:action1 Use tapered wooden wedges to tighten loose non-critical utility joints gently by expanding mating contact surfaces—remembering that broken axe handles require proper replacement, not makeshift field wedges.
Z09-P30:failure Trying to tape or wedge a split fiberglass tent pole or cracked hatchet handle and assuming it is restored to full storm or chopping strength.
Z09-P30:verify Confirm tight snug fit with zero sharp protruding splinters and strict confinement to temporary or light-duty use.
Z09-P30:stop Never use field-wedged or tape-wrapped handles on swinging impact tools (axes, hammers) or load-bearing safety gear—retire damaged handles safely.
Z09-P45:action2 Recognize that real field materials—deadwood grain, wet rope, field-tied knots, soil anchors and worn gear—have wide unmeasured variability that invalidates textbook ideal ratios.
Z09-P46:action1 Secure an axe or heavy tool firmly against a stable bench or pegged wood support before filing, using a file fitted with both a handle and knuckle guard—never file loose handheld steel toward your fingers.
Z09-P46:action2 Match the factory bevel angle steadily along a flat sharpening stone or puck with smooth light strokes rather than grinding steep blunt edges or overheating steel on dry power grinders (which ruins temper).
Z09-P46:action3 Wipe metal filings cleanly away from food areas and fingers, test sharpness safely on a small scrap of paper or dry wood—NEVER draw a thumb lengthwise along a blade edge.
Z09-P46:failure Trying to sharpen a hatchet held loosely between knees with an unguarded bare-tang file, slicing deeply into the palm.
Z09-P46:verify Confirm firm workpiece immobilization, protected fingers, preserved smooth bevel angle and clean safe testing on scrap material.
Z09-P46:stop Stop field honing if the blade shows deep structural cracks, heat-blued soft spots or large jagged chips—retire or professionally regrind damaged steel.
Z09-P47:action1 Scrub sticky conifer pitch out of saw gullets and knife hinges gently with a brush and safe cleaner, keeping fingers well away from sharp saw tooth points—gummed teeth bind and snap blades.
Z09-P47:action2 Dry carbon-steel blades and multi-tool pivots thoroughly after rain, snow or damp use and wipe a paper-thin coat of clean protective oil (food-safe oil on food knives) to stop rust pitting.
Z09-P47:action3 Store leather-sheathed knives and axes clean and dry; trapped moisture inside damp leather corrodes carbon steel overnight.
Z09-P47:failure Stowing a sap-crusted wet folding saw in a sealed plastic bag for six months, discovering rusted seized pivot pins and bound teeth on the next trip.
Z09-P47:verify Confirm clean tooth gullets, smooth dry pivot action, lightly oiled corrosion-free steel and dry sheath storage.
Z09-P47:stop Retire rusted-through hinges, bent saw plates or pitted corroded locks that will not open or latch smoothly after cleaning.
Z09-P48:action1 Sight along wooden axe and hammer handles for straight parallel grain running lengthwise with the head—steep diagonal grain runout splits diagonally under normal impact stress.
Z09-P48:action2 Check immediately below the metal eye/collar for crushed overstrike gouges, hairline checks, dry rot or gaps around the top wedge indicating a loose head that can fly off mid-swing.
Z09-P48:action3 Keep sound wooden handles conditioned lightly with linseed oil and stored out of extreme dry stove heat that shrinks wood inside the head eye.
Z09-P48:failure Wrapping electrical tape around a cracked axe neck or soaking a loose axe head in water overnight—which swells fibers briefly and leaves the head even looser after drying.
Z09-P48:verify Confirm straight lengthwise wood grain, tight immovable head seating and zero neck splits or overstrike cracks.
Z09-P48:stop Immediately remove any tool with a cracked handle or loose head from service until properly re-hung with a sound replacement handle.
Z09-P49:action1 Spot a dull or rolled edge by checking whether a blade slips off wood instead of biting smoothly or glints brightly along the very apex under light—forcing a dull blade causes sudden uncontrolled slips.
Z09-P49:action2 Spot a warped or tooth-damaged saw blade when the saw persistently curves sideways in a straight cut, chatters violently or jams repeatedly even in open kerfs.
Z09-P49:action3 Pause work calmly to touch up a mildly dulled bevel safely, or swap to a spare blade/backup tool rather than muscling through tough material.
Z09-P49:failure Pressing with full shoulder weight on a dull rolled knife blade until it skids off a dry branch straight into the opposite thumb.
Z09-P49:verify Confirm smooth predictable bite at light hand pressure and straight tracking in saw cuts before continuing.
Z09-P49:stop Retire cracked blades, bent saw plates or deeply chipped edges rather than fighting defective cutting geometry in the field.
Z12-P60:action1 Keep electronics, compasses, cameras, stove jets and metal tools sealed inside airtight waterproof bags whenever wind blows fine salt spray or abrasive beach sand—sand jams zippers and stove valves while salt pits carbon steel overnight.
Z12-P60:action2 Rinse salt and sand out of tent zippers, fishing/camp hardware and metal blades with clean freshwater promptly after coastal exposure, drying and lightly oiling metal parts.
Z12-P60:failure Pitching a tent directly in blowing dune sand with open zippers and leaving an un-oiled carbon knife exposed to night sea mist until rusted shut.
Z12-P60:verify Confirm electronics/tools ride in sealed bags, zippers stay brushed clean of grit and wind/fog navigation tools stay reachable.
Z12-P70:action2 Audit fabrics, fasteners and metals: wet marshes drive trench foot and soak down loft; coastal salt spray pits carbon steel and windblown sand jams zippers and stove jets; UV desert sun degrades nylon and plastics rapidly.
Z12-P70:failure Bringing an unchanged fair-weather three-season backpacking kit into a −10°F winter plain, a 112°F desert canyon or a salty rocky coast.
Z14-P21:action2 Clean dirt off shovels, harvest knives, and pruning shears routinely, and sanitize blades between cutting diseased plants and healthy plants so sap does not transmit bacterial or viral wilts across the bed.
Z16-P25:action2 Open Z12-P60 for account for coastal salt spray, wind-driven sand, fog and rapid gear corrosion; Z12-P64 for interpret Small Craft Advisories, Gale Warnings and wind-against-tide wave steepening; Z12-P65 for stay with a swamped buoyant hull rather than attempting long cold-water swims.
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. USFS covers sharpening and handles. No universal bevel geometry or thermal threshold.

Z09-P04:action1 Inspect downed wood for straight parallel grain versus twisted knots, checking cracks and spongy insect-ridden rot—decayed wood snaps unpredictably under carving or lever loads.
Z09-P04:failure Trying to carve a load-bearing lever or split through a gnarly resinous knot with a thin pocket knife, snapping the blade tip or deflecting it into the hand.
Z09-P06:action1 Prefer a sharp folding saw or bow saw for cross-cutting dead branches up to wrist thickness—saws cut cleanly with far less calorie burn and no high-energy swing miss path.
Z09-P23:action1 Cut straight sound deadwood segments to length with a folding saw first, beveling the top rim gently so driving impacts do not splinter the end immediately.
Z09-P24:action1 Score or make shallow stop-cuts with a saw first to define exact notch boundaries before paring out waste wood—stop-cuts prevent fibers from splitting down the entire workpiece.
Z09-P24:action3 Match notch width and depth cleanly to the mating stick or hearth socket geometry so joints seat flat without rocking.
Z09-P24:verify Confirm flat mating surfaces, zero split cracks extending past the notch and safe body-clear cutting posture throughout.
Z09-P25:action1 Assess supports, slope and visible movement before touching the saw. A simple support sketch only indicates one possible load case; hidden constraints and decay can change the bind.
Z09-P25:action2 Leave cuts requiring bind relief, support changes or work on loaded timber to trained sawyers. If the kerf closes or wood moves, stop and clear the drop or roll area.
Z09-P25:action3 Keep your feet, knees and supporting hand well clear of where the cut log end will drop or roll once severed.
Z09-P25:failure Sawing straight down through the top of a sagging log until the gap clamps shut onto the blade, bending or snapping the saw teeth.
Z09-P25:verify Confirm compression versus tension side before sawing, maintain an open kerf and keep feet out of the drop zone.
Z09-P25:stop Leave large-diameter logs, complex tangled blowdowns and stressed trunks untouched—they require professional sawyers and exceed camp hand-saw limits.
Z09-P26:action1 Scan any bent, pinned or arched sapling or branch—wood bent under a fallen trunk stores massive spring energy that whips sideways or upward instantly with bone-breaking force if cut.
Z09-P26:action2 Scan overhead for hung-up dead trees (widowmakers) leaning into neighboring branches; cutting or shifting the base log can bring the entire overhead mass crashing down unpredictably.
Z09-P26:failure Sawing halfway through a bent sapling pinned under a fallen oak, releasing a violent whip-strike to the head or chest.
Z09-P26:verify Confirm every piece of deadwood you cut lies flat, unbent, unpinned and completely clear of leaning overhead timber.
Z09-P26:stop Never cut spring poles, under-tension windthrow trunks or leaning hung-up trees with camp tools—detour clear and report trail hazards to land managers.
Z09-P42:action1 Place a broad stable fulcrum block close to the load so the effort arm is much longer than the load arm—remembering ideal lever ratios trade longer handle movement for reduced hand force.
Z09-P42:action2 Test the lever pole gently first for hidden rot or bending cracks, stand to the SIDE rather than straddling the handle and keep feet completely clear of the rolling or dropping load path.
Z09-P42:action3 Chock or block a lifted object immediately with solid cribbing if you must pause—never place hands, fingers or feet underneath a suspended load held only by a wooden lever.
Z09-P42:failure Leaning full body weight onto a brittle dead pine lever while standing downhill of a heavy log that rolls straight over ankles when shifted.
Z09-P42:verify Confirm sound uncracked lever pole, broad stable fulcrum, clear downhill roll path and zero hands or feet under the lifted load.
Z09-P42:stop Never attempt to lift vehicles, pinned storm trunks or trapped people with unrated wooden poles if uncontrolled shifting could crush anyone; stabilize and call emergency rescue.
Z09-P49:action2 Spot a warped or tooth-damaged saw blade when the saw persistently curves sideways in a straight cut, chatters violently or jams repeatedly even in open kerfs.
Z16-P33:action1 Open Z09-P02 for inspect cutting edges, handles and locks before every job; Z09-P25 for saw downed wood cleanly while reading top and bottom log bind.
Z16-P33:action2 Open Z09-P26 for recognize spring poles and hung-up deadfall before making a cut; Z09-P44 for understand the force on a fixed pulley redirect; Z09-P48 for inspect wooden tool handles for grain runout, cracks and loose heads.
Z16-P71:action2 Open Z09-P25 for saw downed wood cleanly while reading top and bottom log bind; Z11-R01 for write a route plan and overdue handoff before departure; Z12-P56 for spot rip-current channels and escape by floating and swimming parallel to shore; Z15-P16 for move immediately to lowest interior tornado shelter on Tornado Warnings.

Z08-P52:action2 Never publish or estimate unverified pound, kilogram, or kilonewton capacities for wild wood spans, rock anchors, or hand-twisted cordage.
Z08-P52:action3 Use manufacturer-rated, inspected equipment installed per qualified instructions whenever human safety or heavy loads depend on a support.

Z09-P08:action2 Use a solid hardwood lever, flat metal tent-stake puller, multi-tool pliers or purpose-made pry bar for lifting, separating or digging stubborn items.
Z09-P08:stop Stop immediately the instant any knife blade flexes laterally or binds tightly in wood—withdraw straight back and switch to a wooden wedge or lever.
Z09-P12:action2 Apply the reverse-wrap lock: twist one strand clockwise away from you while wrapping the pair counterclockwise over each other—the opposing torsional tension locks the two plies together so the cord does not untwist.
Z09-P13:action1 Recognize that EVERY knot reduces straight-line rope strength because tight bends concentrate stress unevenly across outer versus inner fibers—tighter radii weaken cord more sharply.
Z09-P17:action2 Use a trucker's hitch (an inline slip loop used as a simple redirect) to cinch a ridgeline snugly between two anchors, locking the finish with a quick-release slipped half hitch so it unties easily when wet.
Z09-P17:action3 Apply moderate controlled tension—over-cranking a trucker's hitch can rip tarp tie-out seams, bend poles or pull stakes right out of damp soil.
Z09-P17:failure Pulling a ridgeline bar-tight with excessive mechanical leverage on a lightweight nylon tarp, tearing the corner stitching in the first gust.
Z09-P30:action1 Use tapered wooden wedges to tighten loose non-critical utility joints gently by expanding mating contact surfaces—remembering that broken axe handles require proper replacement, not makeshift field wedges.
Z09-P42:action1 Place a broad stable fulcrum block close to the load so the effort arm is much longer than the load arm—remembering ideal lever ratios trade longer handle movement for reduced hand force.
Z09-P42:action2 Test the lever pole gently first for hidden rot or bending cracks, stand to the SIDE rather than straddling the handle and keep feet completely clear of the rolling or dropping load path.

Z09-P42:verify Confirm sound uncracked lever pole, broad stable fulcrum, clear downhill roll path and zero hands or feet under the lifted load.
Z09-P43:action1 Recognize that a wedge and an inclined plane use the same physical principle—moving a modest force over a longer shallow ramp distance lifts or separates a heavier load gradually.
Z09-P43:action2 Drive wooden wedges incrementally with a wooden mallet while keeping blocking chocks tight behind the lift so the object cannot slam back if a wedge slips out.
Z09-P43:action3 Account for real-world surface friction: rough wood-on-wood friction absorbs substantial input force (reducing ideal mechanical advantage) yet also helps prevent sudden uncontrolled slide-back.
Z09-P43:failure Stacking narrow unstable loose stones under a ramp or hammering brittle wedges without blocking, causing a heavy load to kick sideways onto shins.
Z09-P43:verify Confirm shallow stable ramp/wedge angle, solid blocking support and clear operator footing outside the slip trajectory.
Z09-P43:stop Stop immediately if wedges begin shooting backward, supports tilt or the mass exceeds safe manual control.

Z09-P05:action3 Choose a pliers-based multi-tool when gear maintenance (zippers, stove nuts, wire, small screws, pot gripping) is the main need, knowing small fold-out blades have narrow grips and thin geometry.
Z09-P05:failure Baton-hammering a folding pocket knife through thick oak or prying stubborn stove parts with a thin knife tip instead of pliers.
Z09-P05:verify Confirm the carried blade or multi-tool fits the actual tasks planned, opens safely and stores in a secure sheath or pouch.
Z09-P08:action2 Use a solid hardwood lever, flat metal tent-stake puller, multi-tool pliers or purpose-made pry bar for lifting, separating or digging stubborn items.
Z09-P30:action2 Use tight overlapping cord wraps (whipping) or high-adhesion repair tape over splinted poles or split pack stays to transfer bending loads across a break evenly.
Z09-P30:action3 Test every field-joined assembly gently under light progressive pressure first and accept that temporary field joints lack full factory strength.
Z09-P30:failure Trying to tape or wedge a split fiberglass tent pole or cracked hatchet handle and assuming it is restored to full storm or chopping strength.
Z09-P30:verify Confirm tight snug fit with zero sharp protruding splinters and strict confinement to temporary or light-duty use.
Z09-P34:action1 Audit every critical gear item you carry—shelter poles, fabric coating (silicone vs polyurethane), inflatable pad, pack hip-belt buckle, boots and stove—and pack the exact compatible patch or spare part.
Z09-P34:action2 Recognize adhesive limits: standard duct tape peels right off silicone-coated (silnylon) tarps and wet cold fabrics—pack coating-matched tenacious/silicone repair tape where needed.
Z09-P34:action3 Keep the repair kit dry, compact and inventoried after every trip so used patches, blades or spare O-rings are replaced before the next outing.
Z09-P34:failure Packing only a roll of household duct tape on a cold wet trip with a silnylon tarp and inflatable sleeping pad, where the tape slides straight off wet silicone fabric.
Z09-P34:verify Confirm every major life-safety gear class has at least one compatible field patch, spare fastener or backup method in the repair pouch.
Z09-P34:stop Do not rely on a field repair kit to compensate for already-failing primary shelter, footwear or water-treatment gear prior to departure.
Z09-P35:action1 Dry and wipe dirt, grease or moisture completely off the torn fabric area—adhesive fails rapidly on damp, dusty or cold greasy fabric.
Z09-P35:action2 Cut patch corners into smooth rounded curves (square corners catch and peel immediately) leaving generous overlap beyond all tear ends, and press firmly from the center outward against a flat support; patch both sides on high-stress rips.
Z09-P35:action3 Keep high-stress seam rips or corner tie-out failures lightly loaded—adhesive tape stops drafts and small drips cleanly but cannot match sewn structural reinforcement in gales.
Z09-P35:failure Sticking a ragged square strip of damp tape onto a wet tent wall in driving rain without backing both sides or easing guyline tension.
Z09-P35:verify Confirm clean dry bond, rounded patch edges, eased seam tension and dry interior below the patch during rain.
Z09-P35:stop If a structural load seam or large fly panel splits open in high wind, abandon reliance on temporary tape and relocate to safer refuge.
Z09-P36:action1 Replace snapped side-release hip-belt or sternum buckles using a slotted field-repair buckle, or tie the webbing tails securely through the remaining loop with a flat water-knot or doubled cord loop so weight stays balanced on hips.
Z09-P36:action2 Lash a cracked external frame joint or popped stay cleanly with overlapping cord wraps or heavy zip ties, padding any sharp jagged metal or fiberglass end thoroughly so it cannot cut skin or pack fabric.
Z09-P36:action3 Redistribute heavy items (water, food, shelter) among healthy companions if a pack fails badly so no one hikes unbalanced on slick terrain.
Z09-P36:failure Continuing miles down steep terrain with one broken shoulder strap swinging loose and a sharp snapped stay poking through the back panel.
Z09-P36:verify Confirm padded sharp ends, balanced shoulder/hip weight distribution and secure knot or spare buckle holding under a test lift.
Z09-P36:stop If a major pack collapse prevents carrying essential shelter, warmth or water safely, redistribute group loads and shorten the route to the nearest exit.
Z09-P37:action1 Replace a snapped boot lace immediately with thin utility cord melted or knotted cleanly at the tips, checking that tension secures the heel without cutting off foot circulation—especially in cold weather.
Z09-P37:action2 If a boot sole peels loose at the toe, wrap several snug turns of high-strength tape or heavy cord around the forefoot sole-and-upper junction strictly as a short-term exit measure—recognizing tape wears down fast on sharp rock and becomes slick on snow or wet roots.
Z09-P37:failure Tightly strapping tape over a boot instep in cold weather, constricting blood flow and accelerating toe frostbite, or trusting taped soles on steep wet granite.
Z09-P37:verify Confirm secure heel fit, comfortable toe circulation, intact traction awareness and dry socks inside the repaired boot.
Z09-P37:stop Delaminated soles or severely damaged boots reduce traction sharply—abort technical climbs, steep slopes and extended travel and exit via the safest low-angle route.
Z09-P38:action1 Inflate the pad firmly, check the valve seal first for grit or loose threads, then listen closely or wipe a thin film of clean water/soap suds across seams and fabric to spot tiny bubbles at pinholes—dry thoroughly before patching.
Z09-P38:action2 Mark the pinhole, clean and dry the surface completely, apply the manufacturer-compatible rounded patch with firm even pressure and allow full cure time before leaning body weight on it.
Z09-P38:action3 Keep a thin closed-cell foam pad or dry spare clothing plan ready in cold weather so a slow overnight leak never leaves the sleeper lying directly on frozen ground.
Z09-P38:failure Trying to stick a cold patch onto a wet soapy sleeping pad at midnight without cleaning valve grit first.
Z09-P38:verify Re-inflate after curing and press gently for several minutes to confirm the pad holds firm pressure without hissing.
Z09-P38:stop If a baffle ruptures internally or a seam splits beyond patch width in freezing temperatures, rely on closed-cell foam/dry natural insulation below and shorten the trip.
Z09-P41:action1 Treat EVERY field patch, pole splint, taped boot sole or knotted strap as a degraded temporary fix with lower strength and shorter service life than intact factory gear.
Z09-P41:action2 Evaluate the consequence of a second failure: a patched jacket pocket is trivial, whereas a splinted tent pole ahead of a forecast windstorm or a leaking pad before a 10°F night threatens life safety.
Z09-P41:action3 Shorten the trip or exit via the nearest verified safe route whenever a core shelter, footwear, navigation or water system relies on a fragile temporary repair.
Z09-P41:failure Pushing two days deeper into remote mountains after splinting a snapped main tent pole and taping a delaminating boot sole.
Z09-P41:verify State what happens if the temporary repair fails tonight and confirm the group has a safe exit or non-dependent backup.
Z09-P41:stop When forecast weather or terrain difficulty exceeds what a temporarily repaired life-safety item can tolerate, abort onward travel and exit early.
Z09-P50:action3 Inspect snowshoe clevis pins, ski/pole locks and stove linkages for bent clips or backing-out screws before leaving camp.
Z09-P50:failure Trying to turn a stuck Phillips stove screw with a pointed knife tip, snapping the blade point and mangling the screw head beyond repair.
Z09-P50:verify Confirm clean positive lock seating, matched driver fit and tight pins/fasteners across critical gear before use.
Z12-P07:action3 Check snowshoe bindings, straps and ski pole baskets regularly in subzero cold where plastic straps grow brittle and snap suddenly.
Z12-P11:action2 Anticipate mechanical cold brittleness: plastic pack buckles snap under sharp impact, frozen zippers jam on ice glaze, hydration hoses freeze solid and liquid white gas causes instant frostbite if spilled on bare skin.
Z12-P70:action3 Carry at least one zero-battery, low-tech backup matched to the specific environment (paper map + compass, foam pad, storm matches/ferro or boiling pot, wide-mouth bottles) so one climate failure never cascades into rescue.
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. Official kit contents are examples, not validated repair methods or compatibility certification.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z08-P23:action3 Rely on a maintained manufactured sharpener for routine tool maintenance rather than improvising unverified wild stone hones.
Z08-P23:verify Routine edge care uses maintained manufactured tools; natural sandstone is observed without dry abrasion.
Z08-P49:action3 Store serviceable field tools dry, clean, and shaded from direct sunlight, retiring visibly degraded natural or synthetic parts before trips.
Z08-P49:verify Pre-trip inspection confirms dry, sound, uncracked wood, intact cordage, and rust-free metal fittings.
Z09-P03:action1 Clear bystanders, pets, tents and trip hazards well outside an arm-plus-tool-length swing radius (often called a blood circle) before unsheathing cutting or swinging tools.
Z09-P03:action2 Orient every cutting stroke away from your thighs, torso, knee arteries and supporting hand—always predict where the blade will travel if the wood splits suddenly or the edge slips.
Z09-P03:action3 Plant stable balanced footing on clear level ground rather than kneeling awkwardly on slick rocks, wet logs or loose gravel.
Z09-P03:failure Carving a stick braced against your thigh or chopping branches while a companion walks behind your backswing.
Z09-P03:verify Confirm zero people or gear inside the work radius, clear follow-through path and solid level stance before the first cut.
Z09-P03:stop Pause immediately whenever anyone steps inside the work zone, footing slips or visibility drops; re-sheath the tool before moving.
Z09-P06:stop Put away swinging tools immediately if footing is icy, lighting is dim or hands grow cold and clumsy; switch to a saw or no-cut deadfall gathering.
Z09-P08:action3 Protect eyes and hands from sudden release whenever pulling frozen ground stakes or freeing stuck latches.
Z09-P10:stop Reject frayed, sun-chalked, melted or unknown-history salvaged cordage for any overhead or tensioned utility load.
Z09-P11:action3 Perform a gentle controlled low-level hand-pull check away from eyes and face, accepting that field hand-pulling verifies only basic integrity for light utility—NOT any engineered load rating.
Z09-P11:failure Wrapping uninspected dry brittle grass or nicked twine under high tension where sudden snap-back whips toward eyes or collapses a loaded assembly.
Z09-P11:stop Discard cordage showing powdering fibers, audible strand popping, glaze melts or uneven weak joints; never substitute improvised fiber for life-safety gear.
Z09-P13:action2 Recognize that embedded sand grit acts like internal sandpaper inside braided rope fibers under cyclic tension, while wet nylon and sharp metal/rock edges accelerate cut-through failure.
Z09-P13:action3 Pad or route tensioned lines over smooth rounded surfaces rather than sharp rock corners, sheet-metal edges or rough dry bark grooves, and shake grit off lines before stowing.
Z09-P13:stop Retire any line with crushed flat spots, cut sheath strands or heat-glazed burn marks before applying tension.
Z09-P20:action1 Recognize that stretched nylon and synthetic ropes store massive elastic energy—if an anchor, knot or frayed section parts under heavy tension, the broken end whips straight back along the line axis at high speed.
Z09-P20:action2 Stand completely outside the line-of-fire recoil path (the snap-back bight and straight-line axis) and keep bystanders clear whenever tensioning heavy utility lines.
Z09-P20:action3 Pad rough rock edges, metal brackets and sharp bark corners where tensioned cord bends, and monitor for audible creaking or stretching fibers.
Z09-P20:failure Standing directly behind a taut nylon haul line wrapped around a sharp metal bumper or rusty hook when the line parts.
Z09-P20:verify Confirm all personnel stand laterally clear of the tension axis, contact edges are smooth or padded and load stays modest for the cord class.
Z09-P20:stop Stop pulling immediately if a rope begins glazing, creaking, unlaying strands or cutting into an anchor—release tension slowly from a safe offset position.
Z09-P21:action1 Treat paracord, hardware-store rope, tarp guylines, bungee cords and natural fibers strictly as non-life-safety utility lines—never use them to support human body weight, rappel, belay or arrest falls.
Z09-P21:action2 Recognize that life-safety ropes, harnesses and carabiners require independent standards certification (UIAA/CE/NFPA), documented fall history and formal technical training outside camp craft.
Z09-P21:action3 Never attach bungee cords with open metal hooks under heavy stretch near eye level—rebound hook strikes cause severe eye trauma.
Z09-P21:failure Trying to lower a person down a wet bluff or rescue someone from a steep ravine using hardware-store utility rope or 550 paracord.
Z09-P21:verify Confirm zero human weight or fall-arrest risk is placed on camp utility cordage, improvised knots or unrated hardware.
Z09-P22:action1 Sit or stand stably with elbows braced or workpiece resting against a solid wooden block, directing EVERY blade edge strictly away from fingers, forearms, thighs and companions.
Z09-P22:action3 Keep your supporting hand strictly behind the cutting bevel—never hold a short stick with fingertips ahead of a pushing blade.
Z09-P22:failure Sitting with knees together and carving straight downward between the thighs, where a slip hits the femoral artery.
Z09-P22:verify Before every cut, trace the exact path the blade will travel if the wood splits suddenly and confirm zero body parts lie in that path.
Z09-P25:action3 Keep your feet, knees and supporting hand well clear of where the cut log end will drop or roll once severed.
Z09-P25:verify Confirm compression versus tension side before sawing, maintain an open kerf and keep feet out of the drop zone.
Z09-P27:action1 Prefer small prepared fuel or a purpose-designed splitting tool used as directed on a stable work surface. Avoid knotty, twisted or stressed stock.
Z09-P28:action1 Place the workpiece firmly against a broad, solid low chopping block so any miss or pass-through buries cleanly into wood—never chop against bare soil, rock or elevated knee-height logs.
Z09-P28:action2 Keep your stance spread wide or kneel safely with the chopping block between the cutting arc and your legs so an over-swing strikes the block or ground safely short of shins and feet.
Z09-P28:verify Confirm tight head wedge, clear work circle, broad low chopping block and free hand strictly away from the impact zone.
Z09-P28:stop Never swing an axe or hatchet when tired, chilled, rushed or in dim twilight—sheath it and use a folding saw or hand-broken dead twigs instead.
Z09-P29:action2 Use a stout wooden club, rubber mallet or dedicated flat-faced soft hammer to drive tent stakes and plastic/wooden splitting wedges, keeping fingers clear of the strike top.
Z09-P29:verify Confirm soft-on-hard or wood-on-wood striking pairing, intact un-mushroomed faces and bystanders clear of potential chip paths.
Z09-P36:action2 Lash a cracked external frame joint or popped stay cleanly with overlapping cord wraps or heavy zip ties, padding any sharp jagged metal or fiberglass end thoroughly so it cannot cut skin or pack fabric.
Z09-P36:failure Continuing miles down steep terrain with one broken shoulder strap swinging loose and a sharp snapped stay poking through the back panel.
Z09-P37:action2 If a boot sole peels loose at the toe, wrap several snug turns of high-strength tape or heavy cord around the forefoot sole-and-upper junction strictly as a short-term exit measure—recognizing tape wears down fast on sharp rock and becomes slick on snow or wet roots.
Z09-P40:action1 Cut clean known-history plastic bottles carefully away from hands to form a scoop or funnel, immediately covering or smoothing sharp cut plastic rims with tape so edges do not slice fingers.
Z09-P40:action3 Never cut into pressurized containers, unknown chemical bottles or sharp jagged tin lids without proper metal shears and cut protection.
Z09-P40:verify Confirm clean known container history, taped smooth rims and strict raw-versus-potable segregation.
Z09-P42:action2 Test the lever pole gently first for hidden rot or bending cracks, stand to the SIDE rather than straddling the handle and keep feet completely clear of the rolling or dropping load path.
Z09-P42:action3 Chock or block a lifted object immediately with solid cribbing if you must pause—never place hands, fingers or feet underneath a suspended load held only by a wooden lever.
Z09-P42:failure Leaning full body weight onto a brittle dead pine lever while standing downhill of a heavy log that rolls straight over ankles when shifted.
Z09-P42:verify Confirm sound uncracked lever pole, broad stable fulcrum, clear downhill roll path and zero hands or feet under the lifted load.
Z09-P42:stop Never attempt to lift vehicles, pinned storm trunks or trapped people with unrated wooden poles if uncontrolled shifting could crush anyone; stabilize and call emergency rescue.
Z09-P43:action2 Drive wooden wedges incrementally with a wooden mallet while keeping blocking chocks tight behind the lift so the object cannot slam back if a wedge slips out.
Z09-P43:failure Stacking narrow unstable loose stones under a ramp or hammering brittle wedges without blocking, causing a heavy load to kick sideways onto shins.
Z09-P43:verify Confirm shallow stable ramp/wedge angle, solid blocking support and clear operator footing outside the slip trajectory.
Z09-P43:stop Stop immediately if wedges begin shooting backward, supports tilt or the mass exceeds safe manual control.
Z09-P44:stop Never stand beneath a hanging pack or food bag and never rig improvised pulleys to lift people or heavy equipment.
Z09-P45:action3 Use ONLY independently certified, manufacturer-rated equipment and qualified technical procedures whenever failure could drop a heavy load onto people or involve human suspension.
Z09-P45:failure Treating a conceptual 2:1 pulley schematic or natural-cordage plate as proof that camp paracord and deadwood can safely haul heavy loads over people.
Z09-P45:stop Whenever human life, overhead crushing risk or structural load capacity is at stake, do not improvise from conceptual diagrams—use certified gear or professional rescue.
Z09-P51:action1 Feel along tensioned utility ropes for flat mushy sections (indicating crushed internal core strands), stiff glossy melted spots (friction glazing) or fuzzy torn outer sheaths exposing white inner filaments.
Z09-P51:stop Immediately retire any utility cord with core damage, severe sheath cuts, chemical burns or brittle UV chalking.
Z09-P52:action1 Monitor yourself and companions for clumsy stiff fingers (early cold impairment), tunnel vision, rushed frustration or fading twilight before picking up any sharp or swinging tool.
Z09-P52:action2 Recognize that cutting wood or repairing gear in remote terrain carries amplified medical risk because EMS evacuation for a deep cut or severed tendon can take hours.
Z09-P52:action3 Warm hands inside shelter/layers first, put on a bright headlamp or defer non-urgent tool work completely until daylight and full dexterity return.
Z09-P52:failure Trying to whittle kindling or split wood by dim dusk light with shivering numb fingers after a 12-mile hike, resulting in a severe hand laceration.
Z09-P52:verify Confirm warm responsive fingers, clear lighting and calm unhurried focus before unsheathing any blade or saw.
Z09-P52:stop The moment hands fumble, shivering begins or light fades, sheath all sharp tools immediately and switch to zero-tool insulation, shelter and no-cook supplies.
Z09-P53:action3 For eye strikes from wood chips, metal spalls or snapped cords, do NOT rub the eye or attempt to pull embedded objects out—shield the eye gently without pressure and seek urgent medical care.
Z09-P53:failure Trying to keep working after a deep hand cut, rinsing an open wound with untreated creek water or rubbing a metal-shard eye injury.
Z13-P31:action2 Clear lower roof eaves from SOLID GROUND ONLY using a long-handled fiberglass/aluminum roof rake while staying completely clear of overhead electrical service drop wires and falling snow avalanches—NEVER climb onto an icy sloped roof or chop ice dams with axes/picks (which punctures shingles and causes fatal falls).
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. OSHA hazard reference supports PPE. Exact snapback exclusion distances and loads are equipment-specific.

initial_claim: Cordage strength drops significantly at knots, sharp bends, wet fibers, UV exposure and abrasion; inspect fibers before loading and never use unrated camp cord or improvised bindings for life-safety suspension or climbing.
current_claim: Cordage strength drops significantly at knots, sharp bends, wet fibers, UV exposure and abrasion; inspect fibers before loading and never use unrated camp cord or improvised bindings for life-safety suspension or climbing.
exact_section: Cordage, Anchors and Rigging Boundaries
applies: Non-life-safety camp lashing, tarps, haul lines and tie-downs
limits: No universal breaking strength applies to natural plant fibers or weathered salvaged rope.

Z08-P39:action2 Avoid relying on freshly fallen damp wood for tight tool-eye wedges or handles because drying shrinks the wood away from the steel head.
Z08-P39:action3 Inspect dry seasoned wood for deep splits extending across handle necks or tool eyes before any use.
Z08-P39:failure Fitting a damp green handle into an axe or hammer eye causes rapid loosening and dangerous head detachment once dry.
Z08-P39:verify Wood parts are seasoned dry and free of deep radial checks across high-stress zones.
Z08-P39:stop Stop using any wooden handle showing widening cracks, loose eye fit, or insect tunnels.
Z08-P40:action1 Trace wood grain lines along the entire length of a shaft or pole; grain exiting the side diagonally (runout) snaps suddenly under bending.
Z08-P40:failure Trusting a knotted or cross-grained pole for a shelter ridge or axe handle causes sudden splintering failure under load.
Z08-P40:verify Inspected wooden poles and handles show continuous lengthwise grain with zero deep knots or splits at load points.
Z08-P40:stop Stop using any wooden pole or handle with diagonal grain runout, cracking sounds, or loosened dead knots.
Z08-P49:action2 Check metal-to-wood joints and salt-exposed gear for rust pitting and swelling wood that splits handles.
Z08-P49:stop Stop using any tool handle, pole, or cordage exhibiting soft rot, insect frass, deep rust pitting, or brittle snapping.
Z09-P04:action3 Recognize that species identification and structural wood strength vary widely by moisture and decay; historical B007 wood notes do not certify field wood strength or species ID.
Z09-P10:action1 Recognize that nylon stretches slightly when wet and absorbs modest shock cleanly, whereas polyester stretches less when wet (often preferred for taut tarp ridgelines).
Z09-P10:action2 Recognize that polypropylene floats on water and resists rot, yet slips more easily in simple knots and degrades quickly under prolonged sunlight (UV) and friction heat.
Z09-P10:action3 Recognize that natural plant fibers (hemp, sisal, field-harvested inner bark) grip knots well when dry yet vary enormously in strength, fray under abrasion and rot when stored damp—zero universal load rating applies.
Z09-P10:failure Using slick UV-faded polypropylene twine with a sloppy knot on a storm-exposed ridge tarp, or assuming camp paracord equals certified climbing rope.
Z09-P10:verify Confirm the cordage matches wet/dry stretch and knot-holding needs and stays strictly within non-life-safety utility use.
Z09-P10:stop Reject frayed, sun-chalked, melted or unknown-history salvaged cordage for any overhead or tensioned utility load.
Z09-P11:action1 Inspect the entire length for thin pinched spots, brittle dry kinks, rot discoloration, cut strands and weak splices before tying—the narrowest damaged section governs failure.
Z09-P11:action2 Understand moving-cord wear from B007A/B008: reciprocating bowstrings suffer intense bending fatigue and surface friction at the spindle wrap, snapping far sooner than static tie-downs.
Z09-P11:action3 Perform a gentle controlled low-level hand-pull check away from eyes and face, accepting that field hand-pulling verifies only basic integrity for light utility—NOT any engineered load rating.
Z09-P11:failure Wrapping uninspected dry brittle grass or nicked twine under high tension where sudden snap-back whips toward eyes or collapses a loaded assembly.
Z09-P11:verify Confirm uniform thickness, flexible unrotted fibers and strict confinement to light non-life-safety utility or supervised training.
Z09-P11:stop Discard cordage showing powdering fibers, audible strand popping, glaze melts or uneven weak joints; never substitute improvised fiber for life-safety gear.
Z09-P12:action1 Prepare uniform, flexible fiber strands free of stiff brittle woody core fragments so strands twist smoothly without kinking or snapping.
Z09-P12:action2 Apply the reverse-wrap lock: twist one strand clockwise away from you while wrapping the pair counterclockwise over each other—the opposing torsional tension locks the two plies together so the cord does not untwist.
Z09-P12:action3 Stagger fiber splices at uneven intervals rather than joining both plies at the same spot, avoiding a single abrupt weak point in the finished cord.
Z09-P12:failure Twisting both strands and wrapping them in the same direction, causing the entire string to unravel immediately when released, or joining both splices side by side.
Z09-P12:verify Confirm the finished two-ply cord stays coiled tightly under light finger tension with evenly staggered splices and consistent diameter.
Z09-P12:stop Keep hand-twisted natural cordage strictly for light utility ties or supervised training—never trust improvised fiber for overhead heavy loads or human suspension.
Z09-P13:action1 Recognize that EVERY knot reduces straight-line rope strength because tight bends concentrate stress unevenly across outer versus inner fibers—tighter radii weaken cord more sharply.
Z09-P13:action2 Recognize that embedded sand grit acts like internal sandpaper inside braided rope fibers under cyclic tension, while wet nylon and sharp metal/rock edges accelerate cut-through failure.
Z09-P13:action3 Pad or route tensioned lines over smooth rounded surfaces rather than sharp rock corners, sheet-metal edges or rough dry bark grooves, and shake grit off lines before stowing.
Z09-P13:failure Running a tight synthetic guyline directly across a sharp granite edge in high wind, sawing through the sheath within an hour.
Z09-P13:verify Confirm knots are dressed neatly without twisted crossings, sharp contact corners are avoided or padded and lines stay clean of embedded grit.
Z09-P13:stop Retire any line with crushed flat spots, cut sheath strands or heat-glazed burn marks before applying tension.
Z09-P14:action1 Form an overhand loop in the standing part, pass the working end up through the loop, around behind the standing part and back down through the same loop parallel to its entry.
Z09-P14:action2 Dress the knot cleanly by seating the collar snugly with a generous working tail, and add a stopper knot (such as a double overhand) on the tail—standard bowlines can shake loose under cyclic slack-and-tug loads in slick synthetic cord.
Z09-P14:action3 Inspect the finished silhouette before loading: a distinct collar wraps the two parallel legs of the loop, and the working end sits cleanly inside the loop with its stopper tied.
Z09-P14:failure Tying a capsized slip loop by pulling the working end wrong, or leaving a tiny untied tail on slick nylon cord that works free in gusty wind.
Z09-P14:verify Check the collar shape, confirm the loop does not slip smaller when pulled and confirm the tail stopper knot is seated snugly.
Z09-P14:stop Never rely on an unverified or un-backed bowline for critical tensioned loads; keep utility bowlines strictly separate from life-safety climbing harnesses.
Z09-P15:action1 Tie a simple figure-eight stopper at line ends to stop cord from slipping through grommets, tarp eyelets or tensioners—its wider bend unties far easier than a jammed overhand knot.
Z09-P15:action2 Tie a figure-eight on a bight (folded double line) for a strong, easily inspected fixed utility loop that resists shaking loose under alternating wind gusts.
Z09-P15:action3 Dress all parallel strands smoothly side-by-side without crossed twists and leave a generous tail beyond the final collar.
Z09-P15:failure Using a tiny single overhand stopper that jams permanently under load or pulls straight through a wide tarp grommet.
Z09-P15:verify Visually confirm the clear figure-eight silhouette with parallel flat strands and an ample tail before applying utility tension.
Z09-P15:stop Remember that even cleanly dressed figure-eight loops in camp utility cordage are NOT certified life-safety climbing anchors.
Z09-P16:action1 Use a round turn and two half hitches when tying off a ridgeline under variable wind or load—the full wrap around the post takes the friction load cleanly while two half hitches lock the tail without binding.
Z09-P16:action2 Reserve a clove hitch primarily for starting/ending static pole lashings or quick temporary holds under steady pull—clove hitches can roll and slip open on smooth posts when tension goes slack and re-loads.
Z09-P16:action3 Lock any clove hitch exposed to shifting gusts with two half hitches on the standing part so the binding cannot unwind overnight.
Z09-P16:failure Tying an un-backed clove hitch to a smooth wet sapling or tent pole in gusty wind, watching the hitch spill loose mid-storm.
Z09-P16:verify Confirm full friction wrap seating, properly oriented half hitches forming a clean clove on the standing line and zero slack slip under hand tug.
Z09-P17:action1 Use a midshipman's hitch (an improved friction grip over the classic taut-line hitch) around a stake when you need one-handed slide adjustment to take up wet-nylon sag.
Z09-P17:action2 Use a trucker's hitch (an inline slip loop used as a simple redirect) to cinch a ridgeline snugly between two anchors, locking the finish with a quick-release slipped half hitch so it unties easily when wet.
Z09-P17:verify Confirm the adjustable hitch grips firmly without sliding back under hand pull and releases cleanly without jamming.
Z09-P17:stop Re-tie with dry high-friction wraps or add a backup half hitch if slick wet polypropylene or icy cord slips through the adjustable coils.
Z09-P18:action1 Use a sheet bend (or double sheet bend for slick/unequal cords) when joining two ropes of different diameters—form the bight in the thicker stiffer rope and tuck the thinner rope cleanly with both tails emerging on the SAME side.
Z09-P18:action2 Use a double fisherman's bend (grapevine knot) for joining two similar-diameter slick synthetic utility cords when maximum slip resistance is required, knowing it cinches very tight under heavy load.
Z09-P18:action3 Never use a square (reef) knot or granny knot to join two load-bearing lines—square knots capsize and spill rapidly when tugged unevenly or tied in unequal/slick ropes.
Z09-P18:failure Joining a thin nylon guyline to a thicker utility rope with a square knot, which flips straight open when wind jerks the line.
Z09-P18:verify Confirm matching tail orientation on sheet bends, opposing snug barrels on double fisherman's bends and generous tails on both ends.
Z09-P18:stop Reject bulky mismatched joins that must pass over rough edges or pulleys; keep all field bends strictly inside utility non-life-safety tasks.
Z09-P19:action1 Match the lashing to pole geometry: use square lashings for poles crossing tightly at right angles, diagonal lashings to pull springing crossed poles together and sheer/tripod lashings for light three-legged utility stands.
Z09-P19:action2 Pull three neat parallel wrapping turns firmly around the poles and finish with two tight frapping turns cinched BETWEEN the poles to take out all slack before locking off with a clove hitch.
Z09-P19:failure Skipping tight frapping turns between the poles, leaving a wobbly tripod that collapses when a water pot hangs from it.
Z09-P19:verify Confirm neat uncrossed wraps, tight frapping turns between poles and zero wobble under gentle test weight before hanging utility items.
Z09-P19:stop Never sleep beneath lashed deadfall roofs or treat camp lashings as engineered overhead structures; keep hot boiling pots stable and clear of legs.
Z09-P20:action1 Recognize that stretched nylon and synthetic ropes store massive elastic energy—if an anchor, knot or frayed section parts under heavy tension, the broken end whips straight back along the line axis at high speed.
Z09-P20:action2 Stand completely outside the line-of-fire recoil path (the snap-back bight and straight-line axis) and keep bystanders clear whenever tensioning heavy utility lines.
Z09-P20:action3 Pad rough rock edges, metal brackets and sharp bark corners where tensioned cord bends, and monitor for audible creaking or stretching fibers.
Z09-P20:failure Standing directly behind a taut nylon haul line wrapped around a sharp metal bumper or rusty hook when the line parts.
Z09-P20:verify Confirm all personnel stand laterally clear of the tension axis, contact edges are smooth or padded and load stays modest for the cord class.
Z09-P20:stop Stop pulling immediately if a rope begins glazing, creaking, unlaying strands or cutting into an anchor—release tension slowly from a safe offset position.
Z09-P21:action1 Treat paracord, hardware-store rope, tarp guylines, bungee cords and natural fibers strictly as non-life-safety utility lines—never use them to support human body weight, rappel, belay or arrest falls.
Z09-P21:action2 Recognize that life-safety ropes, harnesses and carabiners require independent standards certification (UIAA/CE/NFPA), documented fall history and formal technical training outside camp craft.
Z09-P21:action3 Never attach bungee cords with open metal hooks under heavy stretch near eye level—rebound hook strikes cause severe eye trauma.
Z09-P21:failure Trying to lower a person down a wet bluff or rescue someone from a steep ravine using hardware-store utility rope or 550 paracord.
Z09-P21:verify Confirm zero human weight or fall-arrest risk is placed on camp utility cordage, improvised knots or unrated hardware.
Z09-P21:stop Any situation requiring vertical rope lowering, swiftwater tethering or technical cliff rescue exceeds camp-tool scope—stabilize on safe ground and summon trained SAR.
Z09-P23:action3 Use wooden toggles (short stout sticks slipped through a bight) to lock quick-release utility hitches so wet cold knots break open instantly without untying jammed cord.
Z09-P23:stop Do not use brittle rotten deadwood for tensioned storm stakes or heavy pot hangers; substitute lawful rock weights or commercial hardware.
Z09-P24:stop Switch to simple lashed overlap joints whenever cold hands, knotty wood or tool wear make precise notching unsafe.
Z09-P30:action2 Use tight overlapping cord wraps (whipping) or high-adhesion repair tape over splinted poles or split pack stays to transfer bending loads across a break evenly.
Z09-P30:action3 Test every field-joined assembly gently under light progressive pressure first and accept that temporary field joints lack full factory strength.
Z09-P36:action1 Replace snapped side-release hip-belt or sternum buckles using a slotted field-repair buckle, or tie the webbing tails securely through the remaining loop with a flat water-knot or doubled cord loop so weight stays balanced on hips.
Z09-P44:action3 Inspect the concept unloaded. Use rated and independently reviewed equipment and systems for actual lifting. Keep people out of the load path and overhead hazard area.
Z09-P44:stop Never stand beneath a hanging pack or food bag and never rig improvised pulleys to lift people or heavy equipment.
Z09-P45:action1 Separate conceptual physics drawings (which illustrate force directions, knot topology or load-path principles) from certified engineering specifications backed by laboratory load testing and material grade control.
Z09-P45:action2 Recognize that real field materials—deadwood grain, wet rope, field-tied knots, soil anchors and worn gear—have wide unmeasured variability that invalidates textbook ideal ratios.
Z09-P45:action3 Use ONLY independently certified, manufacturer-rated equipment and qualified technical procedures whenever failure could drop a heavy load onto people or involve human suspension.
Z09-P45:failure Treating a conceptual 2:1 pulley schematic or natural-cordage plate as proof that camp paracord and deadwood can safely haul heavy loads over people.
Z09-P45:verify Check every Z09 figure caption and evidence drawer to confirm conceptual status and specialist-review boundaries before teaching or field use.
Z09-P45:stop Whenever human life, overhead crushing risk or structural load capacity is at stake, do not improvise from conceptual diagrams—use certified gear or professional rescue.
Z09-P51:action1 Feel along tensioned utility ropes for flat mushy sections (indicating crushed internal core strands), stiff glossy melted spots (friction glazing) or fuzzy torn outer sheaths exposing white inner filaments.
Z09-P51:action2 Check all critical utility knots after initial wind gusts or rain—watch for shrinking tails, distorted loops or loosening coils on slick wet cordage.
Z09-P51:action3 Cut out damaged end segments cleanly (fusing synthetic ends carefully away from dry fuels) or retire the entire rope if mid-line core damage or UV powdering appears.
Z09-P51:failure Reusing a sun-brittle, friction-glazed synthetic cord with an exposed inner core to guy out a shelter in rising wind.
Z09-P51:verify Confirm uniform round tactile feel, intact unglazed sheath and ample tail security on every active camp knot.
Z09-P51:stop Immediately retire any utility cord with core damage, severe sheath cuts, chemical burns or brittle UV chalking.
Z12-P69:action1 Pack ALL spare dry warm layers, sleeping gear, first-aid supplies and paper charts inside double-sealed roll-top dry bags, securing them cleanly inside hatches or tied neatly so loose floating ropes cannot entangle swimmers during a capsize.
Z16-P43:action1 Open Z09-P11 for evaluate salvaged and natural cordage under abrasion and tension; Z09-P12 for form a two-ply reverse-wrap cord from prepared dry fibers.

Z09-P01:action3 Leave unnecessary heavy or specialized tools out of field kits and never attempt high-risk felling or structural fabrication beyond your training and equipment.
Z09-P01:stop If the right tool is missing or the task exceeds safe camp-tool limits, choose an alternate low-risk method rather than improvising unsafe blade or impact substitutes.
Z09-P04:action1 Inspect downed wood for straight parallel grain versus twisted knots, checking cracks and spongy insect-ridden rot—decayed wood snaps unpredictably under carving or lever loads.
Z09-P04:action3 Recognize that species identification and structural wood strength vary widely by moisture and decay; historical B007 wood notes do not certify field wood strength or species ID.
Z09-P04:verify Confirm deadwood is lawfully downed, sound inside, reasonably straight-grained and free of hidden nails or embedded grit.
Z09-P04:stop Reject brittle, rotted or heavily knotted wood rather than forcing a blade through resistance; never cut live trees for routine camp craft.
Z09-P25:action2 Leave cuts requiring bind relief, support changes or work on loaded timber to trained sawyers. If the kerf closes or wood moves, stop and clear the drop or roll area.
Z09-P25:stop Leave large-diameter logs, complex tangled blowdowns and stressed trunks untouched—they require professional sawyers and exceed camp hand-saw limits.
Z09-P26:action1 Scan any bent, pinned or arched sapling or branch—wood bent under a fallen trunk stores massive spring energy that whips sideways or upward instantly with bone-breaking force if cut.
Z09-P26:action2 Scan overhead for hung-up dead trees (widowmakers) leaning into neighboring branches; cutting or shifting the base log can bring the entire overhead mass crashing down unpredictably.
Z09-P26:action3 Walk cleanly around storm tangles and gather small loose, unpinned deadwood lying flat on stable ground instead.
Z09-P26:failure Sawing halfway through a bent sapling pinned under a fallen oak, releasing a violent whip-strike to the head or chest.
Z09-P26:verify Confirm every piece of deadwood you cut lies flat, unbent, unpinned and completely clear of leaning overhead timber.
Z09-P26:stop Never cut spring poles, under-tension windthrow trunks or leaning hung-up trees with camp tools—detour clear and report trail hazards to land managers.
Z09-P33:action1 Recognize that standing dead trees (snags) often have hollow rotted cores, loose bark and brittle upper tops (widowmakers) that break backward straight onto the cutter at the first axe or saw vibration.
Z09-P33:action2 Restrict ALL camp woodworking and lawful firewood gathering strictly to manageable dead wood already lying flat on the ground.
Z09-P33:action3 Keep camp, rest stops and tool-work zones well clear of leaning dead trunks, split forks and wind-damaged canopies.
Z09-P33:failure Chopping at the base of a leaning dead birch snag for firewood, shaking loose a heavy rotten crown branch directly overhead.
Z09-P33:verify Confirm zero standing trees—dead or alive—are cut, wedged or shaken during camp operations.
Z09-P33:stop Walk well away from creaking or wind-stressed dead timber; never attempt to knock down a hung-up branch by throwing sticks or chopping its support.
audit_note: Retained the A02 substantive concern and checked current references. USFS handtool PDF is general. Overhead, felling and storm timber require specialized procedures/competence.

Z11-R03:action1 Check the map publication date, scale ratio, contour interval and symbol legend first—outdated sheets may omit washed-out bridges, closed roads or rerouted trails.
Z11-R04:action1 Read index contours and spacing to judge slope steepness: closely packed lines mean steep bluffs or cliffs, while wide spacing marks flatter benches or valleys.
Z11-R04:action2 Identify valley V-contours pointing uphill and blue streams, lakes, marshes and intermittent drainages that create wet-footing, flood or ice barriers along a route.

Z11-P12:failure Cutting straight across a flat white snowfield between two points on a map without realizing it is an unfrozen inlet or spring-fed lake bay.
Z11-P19:action1 Watch for six classic route breakdowns: (1) outdated maps hiding washed-out bridges or beaver-flooded trails, (2) snow-buried signs and false animal tracks, (3) windthrow blowdowns forcing off-trail detours around hazards.
Z11-P19:action2 Watch for the other three traps: (4) small cliffs/bogs hidden below contour intervals, (5) phone battery death or iron-rock compass deflection, and (6) shrinking daylight or fast-moving weather fronts invalidating a morning plan.
Z11-P19:verify Before departure, list the two most likely route-failure points on today's map and name the exact dry-land bailout for each.
Z11-P21:action1 Understand map scale fractions: a 1:24,000 USGS quadrangle shows fine terrain detail (1 inch ≈ 2,000 feet) ideal for off-trail or complex forest navigation, whereas 1:50,000 or 1:100,000 maps cover wider territory with fewer small contours.

Z11-P22:action2 Judge terrain steepness from line density: evenly spaced contours mark a uniform slope, widening spacing downhill marks a gentler concave slope and tightening lines downhill warn of a convex drop-off hiding cliffs below.
Z11-P22:failure Misreading a 40-foot contour interval as 10 feet and underestimating an exhausting climb by fourfold, or missing a convex cliff lip.
