exact_operational_assertions:
Z11-P37:action1 Watch for the classic warm-front cloud progression: high wispy cirrus thickening and lowering steadily into milky cirrostratus (often ringing sun/moon), then gray altostratus and finally low rain-bearing nimbostratus over 12–24 hours.
Z11-P37:action2 Watch for fast-moving cold-front cues: rapidly darkening western/northwestern cloud lines, sharp wind shifts, gusty outflow air and sudden steep temperature drops with brief heavy squalls or snow showers.
Z11-P37:action3 Treat visual sky reading strictly as an early-warning supplement to official NWS forecasts and NOAA Weather Radio—not a replacement for official watches and warnings.
Z11-P37:failure Ignoring a thickening lowering gray deck and shifting wind on a high exposed route because the morning started sunny.
Z11-P37:verify Note cloud height trend (lowering vs clearing) and wind direction shift every hour on exposed routes, comparing with the official forecast.
Z11-P37:stop Rapidly lowering dark cloud decks paired with rising gusts or cooling air trigger early retreat off ridges, lakes and open water before precipitation arrives.
Z11-P38:action1 Watch fair-weather puffy cumulus clouds starting late morning: rapid vertical bubbling into tall cauliflower towers (cumulus congestus) with dark flat bases warns that thunderstorm updrafts are building.
Z11-P38:action2 Recognize a spreading flat icy anvil top (cumulonimbus), darkening rain curtains and sudden cool gusty outflow winds as an active mature storm—lightning routinely strikes miles ahead of rainfall.
Z11-P38:verify Identify your descent route below treeline or nearest sturdy shelter whenever towering cumulus starts building vertically.
Z11-P39:action1 Understand that falling barometric pressure at a FIXED elevation (especially rapid drops over a few hours) generally signals an approaching low-pressure system, front, wind or precipitation—whereas changing elevation while hiking alters pressure readings falsely.
Z11-P39:action2 Check wind direction changes alongside cloud trends: winds backing or shifting abruptly ahead of darkening clouds warn of frontal passage and changing shelter exposure direction.
Z11-P39:action3 Cross-check local pressure and wind cues with official NOAA Weather Radio or alert updates whenever reception allows.
Z11-P39:failure Misreading a watch barometer drop during a 1,500-foot mountain climb as an incoming hurricane, or ignoring a steep overnight drop while camped at one elevation.
Z11-P39:verify Record overnight stationary barometric trend and wind direction shift before committing to exposed second-day travel.
Z11-P39:stop A steep stationary pressure drop combined with lowering clouds or rising gusts triggers shortening exposed legs and staging weather protection early.
Z11-P40:action1 Recognize that wind accelerates dramatically when funneled through narrow mountain passes, river gorges and open ridge saddles—calm air in a sheltered valley can mask dangerous gusts just 300 feet higher.
Z11-P40:action2 Watch large lakes (such as Lake Superior and large Upper Midwest basins) where cold air crossing warmer open water generates sudden localized lake-effect snow squalls that erase visibility within minutes.
Z11-P41:action1 Recognize that clear calm skies over damp valleys, wetlands or lakes cool ground air quickly after sunset, forming dense radiation fog that can blanket trails and roads within minutes.
Z11-P41:action2 Recognize that advection fog rolls rapidly inland off cold ocean or Great Lakes water when warm humid air passes over cold surfaces, cutting coastal visibility to zero suddenly.
Z11-P42:action1 Read point forecasts matched to your actual route elevation and terrain rather than a distant lowland city—temperatures drop markedly with elevation and local storm cells vary across counties.
Z11-P42:action3 Recognize that phone radar images can lag several minutes behind reality and miss low-altitude mountain/valley precipitation beams—never let a stale green radar screen override real darkening skies and thunder overhead.
Z11-P42:failure Relying on a city forecast 40 miles away and 3,000 feet lower, or standing under building thunder because a cached radar app still shows clear air.
Z11-P68:action2 On the move: keep the group together with lead/sweep accountability, match checkpoints and elapsed time regularly, monitor live sky/wind shifts and detour cleanly around water, ice or storm hazards.
Z11-P68:failure Treating map reading, weather monitoring, group pacing and rescue signaling as disconnected tasks until a compound failure hits at dusk.
Z12-P37:action1 Expect air temperatures to drop roughly 3°F–5°F for every 1,000 feet of elevation gain (plus severe wind chill on open passes)—a 75°F valley trailhead routinely meets 40°F sleet and freezing gusts at an alpine pass.
Z12-P37:verify Check the summit/pass elevation forecast (not valley town weather) and pack warm/waterproof layers plus UV protection before departing.
Z12-P38:action1 Start early (often at or before dawn) on above-treeline objectives so your party crosses high passes and starts descending WELL BEFORE midday convective cumulus clouds build into storms.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z11-P11:action1 Stop travel promptly as soon as landmarks, trail treads or depth contrast fade into whiteout or dense fog—continuing blindly leads straight off ledges or onto hidden water.
Z11-P11:action2 Keep the entire group tightly together within arm's reach or voice range, add wind/cold protection and verify whether a short unmistakable backtrack to recent shelter exists.
Z11-P11:action3 Remember that a compass needle shows direction only—it CANNOT warn you of cornices, stream drop-offs, vehicle traffic or thin lake ice hidden ten feet ahead in zero visibility.
Z11-P11:failure Pushing forward across a snow-covered clearing in blowing snow hoping to spot the next trail sign, walking straight onto a frozen marsh.
Z11-P11:verify Confirm everyone is accounted for, sheltered from wind and holding on verified stable land until visibility returns safely.
Z11-P11:stop Zero visibility with no unmistakable safe handrail or nearby refuge requires halting on stable ground, sheltering and alerting contacts or rescue.
Z11-P13:action2 Recognize that even real astronomical cues (sun arc or stars) require clear skies, accurate local time/season understanding and yield only coarse approximate orientation—not precise trail bearings.
Z11-P13:failure Following mossy tree trunks through a shaded northern spruce bog in overcast fog and walking steadily deeper away from the road.
Z11-P15:stop If electronic failure coincides with poor visibility or uncertain position on paper, stop moving, shelter and stay findable rather than wandering.
Z11-P23:stop When thick forest or fog hides major landform shapes, shorten checkpoint spacing and stay strictly on verified linear trails or handrails.
Z11-P27:failure Copying WGS84 smartphone coordinates onto a vintage 1965 NAD27 paper quadrangle in fog and mistaking the shifted dot for a safe trail crossing.
Z11-P31:stop When dense fog or brush collapses sighting distance to only a few paces and hazards surround you, halt compass travel and rely on verified handrails or stay put.
Z11-P40:action2 Watch large lakes (such as Lake Superior and large Upper Midwest basins) where cold air crossing warmer open water generates sudden localized lake-effect snow squalls that erase visibility within minutes.
Z11-P40:stop Violent pass gusts, blinding lake-effect squalls or snapping timber require immediate retreat back into sheltered lower terrain.
Z11-P41:action1 Recognize that clear calm skies over damp valleys, wetlands or lakes cool ground air quickly after sunset, forming dense radiation fog that can blanket trails and roads within minutes.
Z11-P41:action2 Recognize that advection fog rolls rapidly inland off cold ocean or Great Lakes water when warm humid air passes over cold surfaces, cutting coastal visibility to zero suddenly.
Z11-P41:action3 Finish complex crossings, water travel and exposed ridge descents before evening cooling sets in, keeping headlamps ready and group members tightly spaced if fog forms.
Z11-P41:failure Launching an evening paddle or late valley crossing under clear dusk skies just before dense fog hides the shoreline completely.
Z11-P41:verify Note evening dew point, cooling air and rising valley mist early enough to secure camp or reach the exit in clear visibility.
Z11-P41:stop When dense fog erases landmarks or opposing shore visibility, halt travel safely on firm ground or near known shelter rather than guessing direction.
Z11-P42:stop Real-time severe local cues (thunder, outflow gusts, rising water, whiteout) ALWAYS override an optimistic or delayed phone forecast.
Z11-P43:failure Blindly following a bouncing smartphone dot across a steep snowy canyon wall in thick clouds without noticing the track drifted off the actual ridge.
Z11-P45:stop Turn back immediately if snow-breaking effort drops pace below your daylight return margin or if trail markers disappear in drifting snow.
Z11-P49:action1 End onward navigation immediately whenever any hard limit hits: fading daylight without a short verified exit, whiteout/dense fog, severe weather warning, suspected hypothermia/heat illness or repeated unresolved map errors.
Z11-P49:stop Once navigation stops for weather, dark or fatigue, do not resume movement until safe visibility, weather stability and group recovery return.
Z11-P53:action3 Keep everyone within visual or clear whistle range in poor visibility, dense woods or steep climbs, and announce every brief bathroom/pack-adjust stop directly to the sweep so nobody steps off-trail unnoticed.
Z12-P01:action1 Scan downwind across open fields and lake edges for lifting snow plumes—strong winds can erase trails and create near-zero visibility without a single new snowflake falling.
Z12-P01:action2 Inspect terrain edges for snow-hidden creek channels, slush overflow and drifted drop-offs rather than assuming a smooth white surface means firm ground.
Z12-P01:action3 Move early into sound upland timber or substantial shelter before blowing snow erases landmarks and wind chill spikes.
Z12-P01:failure Stepping onto an open snow-swept corridor because snowfall ended, then losing all landmark contrast in blowing drift ten minutes later.
Z12-P01:verify Confirm current visibility distance, wind direction and immediate wind-protected timber or building refuge before crossing open winter terrain.
Z12-P01:stop When blowing snow drops visibility or erases trail contrast, halt exposed travel on stable land, shelter from wind and avoid crossing frozen water.
Z12-P16:action3 Recognize that drifting snow bridges over pressure cracks, spring holes, old angler holes and open water pockets, disguising lethal plunge hazards as flat white walking ground.
Z12-P33:action3 If caught on foot outdoors, move clear of loose blowing debris and roadways, protect eyes and airways with eyewear and cloth/particulate mask and wait low behind stable wind cover until visibility clears.
Z12-P33:stop Never attempt to drive blindly through a dense dust wall or step onto an active highway shoulder during a dust storm.
Z12-P60:action1 Keep electronics, compasses, cameras, stove jets and metal tools sealed inside airtight waterproof bags whenever wind blows fine salt spray or abrasive beach sand—sand jams zippers and stove valves while salt pits carbon steel overnight.
Z12-P60:action3 Expect coastal marine fog to roll inland rapidly, erasing headland landmarks and chilling damp skin—stage compass, tide table and windproof dry shell at the top of your pack.
Z12-P60:verify Confirm electronics/tools ride in sealed bags, zippers stay brushed clean of grit and wind/fog navigation tools stay reachable.
Z12-P60:stop When dense coastal fog and high surf combine on rocky headlands, halt shoreline travel on high dry land until visibility and tide safety return.
Z12-P68:action1 Stay completely outside marked commercial shipping channels, ferry tracks and harbor fairways whenever fog threatens—large ships cannot stop quickly, cannot see low kayaks on radar and travel silently until dangerously close.
Z12-P68:action2 Before crossing any open bay when fog may roll in, take a verified magnetic compass course to shore and keep a loud horn/whistle ready to sound navigation fog warnings per maritime rules.
Z12-P68:action3 Head immediately to the nearest safe shoreline or hug shallow non-shipping edges the moment a low white marine fog bank appears offshore—do not gamble on beating advection fog across wide open water.
Z12-P68:failure Paddling across a busy harbor entrance as coastal fog rolls in without a compass bearing, radar reflector or horn.
Z12-P68:verify Confirm compass heading to safe shore, bright visibility gear, working whistle/horn and clear separation from commercial shipping lanes.
Z12-P68:stop Dense zero-visibility sea fog ends open-water crossings immediately—land safely on nearest dry shore or hold clear of all traffic lanes and monitor VHF 16.
Z15-P12:action1 Check live state DOT road reports (such as Minnesota 511) AND NWS forecasts BEFORE leaving—Remember clear blue sky plus 35 mph wind over open farmland still generates zero-visibility ground blizzards and black-ice whiteouts.
Z15-P12:action3 Exit early into a safe open town, motel, or rest stop the moment visibility drops, wipers freeze solid, or plows pull off the road—NEVER push past closed-road gates or follow tail lights blindly into whiteouts.

exact_operational_assertions:
Z11-R09:action1 Admit position uncertainty immediately the first time an expected junction, bridge or slope fails to appear within your expected time window.
Z11-R09:action2 Stop on stable ground, record the exact last place and time you positively verified your location, and list every direction and landmark seen since that point.
Z11-R09:action3 Avoid guessing shortcuts off-trail to force a match; only backtrack along unmistakable tracks/trails if you are 100% certain of the return path, otherwise stay put and prepare to signal.
Z11-R09:failure Walking another mile down an unverified spur trail hoping a familiar sign will appear, multiplying the search area.
Z11-R09:verify Write or state aloud the last confirmed landmark, elapsed walking time since leaving it and your stay-or-backtrack decision criteria.
Z11-R09:stop If uncertainty persists after calm map comparison or visibility/daylight drops, stop moving, shelter in place and contact rescue with your last verified point.
Z11-R10:action2 Brief every participant—including youth—on the day's checkpoints, turnaround time, whistle stop signal and the strict rule to stay put if separated.
Z11-P13:action3 Rely on verified instruments (oriented paper map, metal-clear compass, verified offline GPS) paired with terrain features; when instruments and position fail together, stop and signal rather than guessing.
Z11-P13:stop If overcast skies, dead electronics and lack of a working compass leave direction unverified, stop moving, shelter and stay findable.
Z11-P16:action1 Choose a sheltered spot adjacent to a clear natural opening (meadow, clearing edge or open ridge) where bright contrasting colors or cleared snow/ground letters stand out from overhead without exposing the group to wind or avalanche.
Z11-P16:action2 Deploy high-contrast panels or bright gear securely anchored against wind, keeping a whistle worn around the neck and a headlamp ready at dusk to answer searcher calls or lights.
Z11-P16:action3 Stay at your marked position rather than walking away from signals—abandoning a signaled spot forces searchers to search empty ground.
Z11-P16:failure Hiding completely beneath dense dark evergreen canopy wearing olive/brown jackets while search aircraft or ground teams pass nearby.
Z11-P16:verify Confirm bright contrast is visible from above/nearby trails, whistle and light are immediately in hand and the group stays sheltered together.
Z11-P17:action1 Stop the remaining group together immediately, record the exact time and Point Last Seen (PLS) without trampling surrounding tracks, and blow timed whistle calls while listening quietly for replies.
Z11-P17:action2 Conduct ONLY a brief, bounded high-probability check of immediate camp hazards (nearby tents, vehicles, shoreline edges, rest areas) using paired spotters who keep voice contact—never scatter solo into woods.
Z11-P17:action3 Call 911 or park dispatch EARLY—especially for young children, older adults, medical needs or cold/dark weather—giving exact PLS, clothing colors, footwear tread, age, medical history and direction last headed.
Z11-P17:failure Delaying a 911 call for hours out of embarrassment while six untrained friends trample all footprints around the Point Last Seen and get lost themselves.
Z11-P17:verify Confirm the Point Last Seen is marked cleanly, remaining group stays accounted for and exact missing-person details have been relayed to dispatch.
Z11-P17:stop Never send solo searchers into dark, flooded, icy or unfamiliar terrain; follow arriving SAR incident-command instructions strictly.
Z11-P19:stop When field terrain contradicts the map and no verified detour appears, halt before drifting off-route and reassess from known ground.
Z11-P20:action2 THINK and OBSERVE: count the group, screen for early hypothermia (fumbling, slurred speech, confusion), check last confirmed landmark and test whether 911/text/beacon works without risky wandering.
Z11-P20:action3 PLAN conservatively: stay put, build a windbreak/dry bed and display high-contrast signals unless an unmistakable, short, verified land route leads to immediate safe shelter.
Z11-P20:failure Panicking and power-walking rapidly in freezing wind to stay warm, sweating out inner layers while moving farther away from the Point Last Seen.
Z11-P20:verify Confirm the group is off ice, out of wind, wearing dry insulation, accounted for and either contacting rescue or displaying clear signals.

Z11-P36:stop When an unexpected fork, missing bridge or dense blowdown severs map agreement, stop at the last verified point and backtrack cleanly or consult current official routes.
Z11-P44:stop If you lose the trail in flat featureless forest or swamp, STOP immediately before wandering farther—retrace visible footprints only if unmistakable, otherwise stay put and signal.
Z11-P47:action1 Watch for **"bending the map"**—mentally forcing mismatched real landmarks to fit where you WISH you were on the map (e.g., calling a creek a mapped river or ignoring a missing ridge).
Z11-P47:action2 Watch for **confirmation bias and groupthink**: accepting one confident speaker's guess without asking for two independent supporting features, or walking faster when uneasy instead of stopping to check.
Z11-P47:failure Rationalizing away three missing trail signs and an uphill slope that should be downhill until nightfall catches the party miles off-route.
Z11-P47:verify Ask one companion to argue honestly against your current position assumption—if the map cannot answer their objections cleanly, stop and relocate.
Z11-P47:stop Two unexplained map-to-ground contradictions equal position uncertainty—halt immediately and follow the STOP relocation protocol.
Z11-P48:action1 Stop on stable ground and mark your exact spot visually (drop pack in view) so you do not wander while thinking; review your last 100% confirmed checkpoint and exact elapsed travel time since leaving it.
Z11-P48:action2 Draw a mental maximum-travel radius around that last confirmed point based on realistic pace, then orient the map cleanly to check whether two unmistakable surrounding landforms or a clear backtrack match one spot inside that circle.
Z11-P48:action3 Backtrack along unmistakable fresh tracks or a clearly signed trail ONLY if you are 100% sure it leads cleanly back to your last confirmed checkpoint; otherwise hold position and prepare to signal.
Z11-P48:failure Picking a random compass direction to "cut over to the highway" from an unverified starting dot, crossing into unfamiliar drainages.
Z11-P48:verify Confirm either a positive two-feature match inside your realistic travel circle or a disciplined stay-put shelter and signaling decision.
Z11-P48:stop Never guess cross-country shortcuts out of position uncertainty; if relocation fails after one calm check, stay put, shelter and contact rescue.
Z11-P50:action1 **S — Stop:** Sit down physically on a pack or dry spot, take slow controlled breaths, put on a warm layer and take a small drink of safe water to calm adrenaline before making a single decision.
Z11-P50:action2 **T — Think & O — Observe:** Inventory immediate physical hazards (weather, ice, cliffs, daylight), group health, exact gear in packs and your last verified location without blaming anyone.
Z11-P50:action3 **P — Plan:** Choose one conservative, defensible action—usually staying put, securing shelter/insulation and setting signals—and revisit it calmly as conditions evolve.
Z11-P50:failure Reacting to sudden fear with frantic running down an unknown ravine, losing gear, exhausting calories and leaving the primary search corridor.
Z11-P50:verify Confirm everyone has physically paused, calmed breathing, added warmth if chilled and agreed on one written or spoken next step.
Z11-P51:action1 Stay in ONE compact safe area near a visible opening—every unnecessary walk around the woods lays confusing false tracks and scatters scent trails.
Z11-P51:action2 Leave clear unmistakable signs of your presence right at your waiting site (bright pack cover or jacket hung visible, large cleared ground mark or boot print preserved on soft earth/snow where safe) without littering or destroying live trees.
Z11-P51:action3 If immediate danger forces you to shift a short distance to safer ground, leave a clear durable note or directional arrow at the old spot stating time, party size and direction moved.
Z11-P51:failure Wandering half a mile away from a visible meadow after hearing a distant helicopter, hiding under dark trees with zero directional note left behind.
Z11-P51:verify Confirm your waiting site displays clear visual clues, minimizes scattered wandering tracks and records any forced move explicitly.
Z11-P51:stop Never leave an intact safe shelter to chase faint unconfirmed voices or distant engine noise over hazardous terrain—answer loudly with your whistle instead.
Z11-P52:action2 Ask Question 2 — **Do we have a 100% verified safe route, adequate daylight, visibility and group health to reach definite safety?** Only if every factor is YES should a lost party consider moving out.
Z11-P52:action3 Whenever the site is safe (or can be made sheltered) and the exit route is uncertain, stay put together—stationary people conserve warmth, avoid injury and are found vastly faster by rescuers.
Z11-P52:failure Leaving a safe stranded car or sheltered camp in a blizzard to "walk out for help" along an unverified road, succumbing to hypothermia half a mile away.
Z11-P52:verify Answer both stay-or-go questions aloud with the whole group and confirm everyone understands the chosen decision.
Z11-P52:stop Any injury preventing safe walking, worsening hypothermia/heat illness, darkness or route uncertainty locks the decision to STAY PUT and signal/call for rescue.
Z11-P54:action1 Freeze all non-essential camp movement, note exact clock time and mark the Point Last Seen (PLS) clearly without walking over nearby ground tracks.
Z11-P54:action2 Assign one calm coordinator to stay put at the PLS (in case the missing person walks back) while buddy pairs check immediate obvious areas (tent, vehicle, bathroom, shoreline edge) within shouting/whistle range for no more than 10–15 minutes.
Z11-P54:action3 Call 911 or park dispatch immediately if the brief bounded check fails—or IMMEDIATELY with zero delay if the missing person is a small child, medically vulnerable, near water/cliffs or in freezing weather.
Z11-P54:failure Everybody bolting in different directions yelling randomly while nobody stays at camp and nobody calls 911 until nightfall.
Z11-P54:verify Confirm one adult stays anchored at the PLS, clue area stays undisturbed and 911 dispatch receives accurate clothing, footwear, time and health details.
Z11-P54:stop Never launch an uncoordinated dark or off-trail search party; once 911/SAR is notified, hold remaining group together and follow responder directions.
Z11-P55:action2 Set realistic expectations honestly—remote ground or air rescue can take many hours depending on weather, darkness and terrain—and prevent panic by keeping everyone warm, hydrated and occupied with calm routine checks.
Z11-P55:action3 Keep one awake listener/watcher during active search windows (especially when aircraft or vehicle lights are nearby) while others rest warmly inside dry layers.
Z11-P55:failure Burning through all headlamp batteries and shouting hoarse in the first hour while ignoring shivering group members.
Z11-P55:verify Confirm everyone has an explicit role, dry warmth protection, rationed water/power plan and continuous readiness to answer searchers.
Z11-P58:stop Never leave a safe sheltered site or cross hazardous terrain solely to hunt for one bar of cell signal.
Z11-P60:action1 Use a pea-less whistle (standard ball-pea whistles jam when wet or frozen in winter) clipped permanently to an accessible chest strap or jacket zipper where cold stiff hands can reach it immediately.
Z11-P60:action2 Sound three sharp, loud blasts spaced evenly (a widely recognized outdoor distress pattern), then PAUSE and listen quietly for at least one full minute so you can hear faint distant replies or responder whistles.
Z11-P60:action3 Reserve shouting for close-range confirmation—shouting strains vocal cords quickly, burns energy and carries far less distance against wind or rushing water than a sharp whistle tone.
Z11-P60:failure Wearing no whistle, screaming hoarse continuously without pausing to listen for searchers' return calls, or carrying a wet frozen ball-pea whistle.
Z11-P60:verify Test the whistle briefly during pre-trip check, confirm pea-less construction and verify every group member knows the three-blast distress cadence.
Z11-P60:stop Stay stationary at your sheltered spot when trading whistle calls with approaching searchers unless responders explicitly direct you to a safe visible meeting point.
Z11-P61:action1 Lay out large geometric contrast shapes (large X, V or long straight bright tarp strips weighted securely with rocks/snow) in an open clearing adjacent to your shelter—nature rarely forms sharp straight neon shapes.
Z11-P61:action2 On bright snow, stomp out large deep letters or dark evergreen-branch lines (using dead downed branches) to maximize shadow and color contrast from overhead aircraft.
Z11-P61:action3 Use a sighting signal mirror strictly on sunny days to sweep brief flashes across distant ridges or toward searching aircraft—avoid blinding helicopter pilots continuously at close landing approach.
Z11-P61:failure Waving a small gray handkerchief from beneath tall pine branches where aerial spotters cannot distinguish motion or color.
Z11-P61:verify Confirm ground markers are large, high-contrast against the seasonal background, securely weighted against wind/rotor wash and visible from open sky.
Z11-P61:stop Secure all loose tarps, jackets and gear tightly before any rescue helicopter approaches—loose fabric sucked into rotor blades endangers the entire aircrew.
Z11-P62:action1 Conserve primary battery power during long quiet night hours—use low dim light for personal camp tasks and save high-beam sweeps or flashing bursts for when you hear vehicles, voices, whistles or approaching aircraft.
Z11-P62:action2 Flash three deliberate light pulses (or activate a dedicated strobe mode) toward open sky or clearings when responders are nearby, avoiding shining bright beams directly into the eyes of approaching drivers or low helicopter pilots.
Z11-P62:stop Never shine blinding steady beams directly into helicopter windscreens during night approach—illuminate the ground clearing beside you instead.
Z11-P63:action1 Write down six essentials BEFORE dialing or pressing send: (1) exact location or Last Known Point + coordinate format, (2) nature of emergency & number of injured/total people, (3) immediate medical red flags (responsiveness, breathing, bleeding, hypothermia/heat).
Z11-P63:action2 Add (4) surrounding access hazards (flooded roads, steep cliffs, ice, downed wires, weather), (5) shelter/water/battery status and clothing colors, and (6) confirmation whether you are staying put and your callback number.
Z11-P64:action2 Separate verified facts strictly from estimates: clearly label your last 100%-confirmed landmark and time ("passed Bear Creek Bridge at 14:10") apart from any rough guess of where you walked afterward.
Z11-P64:failure Rounding off trailing GPS decimals casually or giving a guessed lake name as a confirmed fact, misdirecting rescue teams to the wrong valley.
Z11-P64:stop If you cannot read coordinates reliably due to stress, cold or screen cracks, report plain verified landmarks and stay stationary rather than inventing numbers.
Z11-P65:action1 Secure EVERY lightweight loose object (tarps, sleeping pads, rain jackets, pack covers, trash bags) tightly inside weighted packs BEFORE any helicopter approaches—rotor downwash turns loose items into lethal debris.
Z11-P65:failure Running enthusiastically downhill toward a landing rescue helicopter with a flapping orange tarp in hand.
Z11-P65:verify Confirm all loose items are stowed/weighted, group waits together clear of snags/wires and zero movement occurs until crew direct approach.
Z11-P65:stop If approaching ground or air crews encounter an unseen hazard (downed wire, thin ice, active rockfall), signal danger clearly from safe ground without rushing into the hazard.
Z11-P67:action2 Rehearse the group's lost-person drill calmly (STOP reset, whistle stop signal, Point Last Seen marking, six-item 911 script) WITHOUT placing real emergency calls or triggering live PLB/SOS alerts.
Z11-P68:action3 When uncertainty or hazard strikes: execute STOP immediately, prioritize shelter/insulation before wandering, lead any emergency call with exact location/format and stay visible until rescue arrives.
Z11-P68:failure Treating map reading, weather monitoring, group pacing and rescue signaling as disconnected tasks until a compound failure hits at dusk.
Z11-P68:verify Walk through all three stages (pre-trip, checkpoint/weather, STOP/rescue) cleanly before stepping away from the trailhead.
Z12-P32:action1 Stay with the disabled vehicle on established roads—cars are vastly easier for searchers and passing motorists to spot than a lone hiker, and walking miles in 110°F+ heat rapidly proves fatal.
Z12-P32:action3 Signal visibility clearly (raise the hood, display bright cloth, check cell/satellite signal from safe open ground) and conserve safe water by resting completely motionless in shade during peak heat.
Z12-P62:action3 Clip a pea-less safety whistle and small waterproof strobe/signal light directly onto the PFD chest where hands reach them while floating.
Z12-P67:action2 Save visual signals (daylight orange smoke, signal mirror, dye marker; nighttime red flares or USCG-approved electronic LED distress light) for when a rescuing vessel or aircraft is actually in sight—do not burn through finite flares with an empty horizon.

Z11-P59:action3 Follow federal licensing rules strictly—FRS is license-free at low power, whereas GMRS, amateur radio and specific marine/aviation frequencies carry legal licensing and lawful-use requirements.
Z12-P55:stop If incoming surf begins closing a rocky pass, retreat immediately BEFORE waves wash across footing—if already trapped on a safe high ledge above water, stay put, avoid jumping into crashing surf and call 911/Coast Guard.
Z12-P63:action1 Leave a complete **float plan** with a trusted onshore contact before launching: vessel description/color/registration, number and names of passengers, departure ramp, exact destination, onboard communications/EPIRB/PLB and overdue call-Coast-Guard cutoff time.
Z12-P63:action2 Monitor official NOAA Marine Weather forecasts (VHF Weather channels or NOAA NWR) BEFORE and DURING trips—large open water builds hazardous wind waves much faster than sheltered shore trees reveal.
Z12-P63:action3 Where carrying a marine VHF radio, know how to hail distress properly on **VHF Channel 16** (and register your MMSI number for one-button VHF-DSC digital distress alerting where equipped) and follow federal marine radio rules.
Z12-P63:failure Launching a kayak or fishing boat onto Lake Superior with zero float plan, relying solely on a phone that loses signal two miles offshore.
Z12-P63:verify Confirm onshore contact holds the float plan and overdue time, marine forecast is checked and VHF/weather channels receive cleanly before departure.
Z12-P63:stop Cancel or postpone launching if marine weather warnings are active, communications fail pre-launch checks or onshore check-in coverage is missing.
Z12-P64:action1 Respect official marine warning tiers strictly: **Small Craft Advisories** signal hazardous wind/wave conditions for smaller vessels; **Gale**, **Storm** and **Hazardous Seas Warnings** signal severe life-threatening open-water conditions—stay in port or off the water.
Z12-P64:verify Check marine zone advisories, wind direction relative to fetch/tides and sheltered shoreline bailouts before pushing off shore.
Z12-P64:stop Active Small Craft Advisories for light paddlecraft, building whitecaps, darkening squall lines or steep breaking inlet bars require staying ashore or landing immediately at the nearest safe lee shore.
Z12-P65:action1 Protect the airway, control breathing as able and use a buoyant craft for support when it remains safe to do so. Do not assume a flooded craft will remain stable or afloat.
Z12-P65:action2 Get as much of your body out of the water as you safely can without losing flotation or destabilizing the craft. Keep signaling for rescue.
Z12-P65:action3 Avoid swimming away from flotation unless remaining creates immediate danger or you can reliably reach immediate safety. Do not estimate swimming range from a fixed cold-water time window.
Z12-P65:failure Leaving an overturned floating aluminum boat half a mile offshore in 45°F water to swim for land, losing muscle control halfway and drowning.
Z12-P65:verify Confirm all passengers stay together holding or atop the buoyant hull wearing buckled PFDs and activate VHF/PLB/visual signals.
Z12-P65:stop Never dive back underwater inside a sinking cabin or swim away from a buoyant hull into distant cold open water.
Z12-P67:action1 Activate electronic distress FIRST when in grave danger: broadcast MAYDAY on VHF Channel 16 / trigger VHF-DSC distress AND activate a registered 406 MHz EPIRB or PLB upright to clear sky so rescue centers receive immediate coordinates.
Z12-P67:action2 Save visual signals (daylight orange smoke, signal mirror, dye marker; nighttime red flares or USCG-approved electronic LED distress light) for when a rescuing vessel or aircraft is actually in sight—do not burn through finite flares with an empty horizon.
Z12-P67:action3 Handle pyrotechnic flares strictly per label downwind over water away from fuel tanks, fiberglass decks, eyes and faces—hot dripping slag causes severe burns and boat fires; check USCG expiration dates regularly.
Z12-P67:failure Firing all three handheld flares at dusk with no boats in sight, or holding a burning flare upwind where hot slag drips onto hands and fuel hoses.
Z12-P67:verify Confirm current NOAA beacon registration, unexpired USCG visual signals and downwind-over-water handling knowledge before launching.
Z12-P67:stop Firing marine distress signals or triggering EPIRB/PLB/MAYDAY in non-emergency situations is unlawful and endangers real rescues; cancel any accidental trigger immediately with the Coast Guard.
Z12-P68:action1 Stay completely outside marked commercial shipping channels, ferry tracks and harbor fairways whenever fog threatens—large ships cannot stop quickly, cannot see low kayaks on radar and travel silently until dangerously close.
Z12-P68:action2 Before crossing any open bay when fog may roll in, take a verified magnetic compass course to shore and keep a loud horn/whistle ready to sound navigation fog warnings per maritime rules.
Z12-P68:failure Paddling across a busy harbor entrance as coastal fog rolls in without a compass bearing, radar reflector or horn.
Z12-P68:verify Confirm compass heading to safe shore, bright visibility gear, working whistle/horn and clear separation from commercial shipping lanes.
Z12-P68:stop Dense zero-visibility sea fog ends open-water crossings immediately—land safely on nearest dry shore or hold clear of all traffic lanes and monitor VHF 16.
Z12-P69:action1 Pack ALL spare dry warm layers, sleeping gear, first-aid supplies and paper charts inside double-sealed roll-top dry bags, securing them cleanly inside hatches or tied neatly so loose floating ropes cannot entangle swimmers during a capsize.
Z12-P69:action2 Carry verified potable freshwater inside tough, sealed, saltwater-tight containers—never assume nearshore sea/estuary water can be treated in an emergency without desalination.
Z12-P69:action3 Keep life-critical emergency items (whistle, VHF/PLB in waterproof case, signal light, small knife) attached DIRECTLY to your worn PFD—not inside the boat hull—so a separated craft never strips away your ability to summon rescue.
Z12-P69:failure Leaving the waterproof VHF radio, PLB and spare fleece loose in an open canoe that sweeps downstream away from capsized paddlers.
Z12-P69:verify Confirm personal SOS tools ride on your PFD, dry bags seal watertight without tangle loops and freshwater jugs are locked salt-tight.
Z12-P69:stop Damaged dry-bag seams, missing hatch covers or unsecured heavy loose gear that can sink or swamp a craft require correction before launching.
Z12-P75:action1 Recognize that high-consequence environmental procedures—including ice self-rescue, shore witness rescue, cold-water immersion care, avalanche avoidance, high-altitude HAPE/HACE recognition and maritime distress—carry fatal risk if misapplied and remain strictly on **publication: HOLD**.
Z12-P75:action3 Pursue formal hands-on certified training (wilderness first aid, avalanche Level 1, coastal/maritime boating safety, swiftwater/ice rescue) from qualified human instructors before entering extreme environments.
Z12-P75:failure Treating an unapproved draft encyclopedia card as a substitute for certified avalanche, boating, desert or wilderness medical training.

Z11-P46:action1 Recognize **foreshortening**: looking across a clear desert basin, wide lake or steep ridge hides intervening gullies, rolling sub-ridges and sheer mileage, making distant peaks or shores look far closer than map scale proves.
Z12-P26:action1 Schedule active desert movement strictly during cool pre-dawn and early-morning hours, resting completely in deep shade during peak midday heat (typically late morning through late afternoon).
Z12-P26:action2 Carry far more potable water than cool-climate norms—desert exertion in extreme heat drives massive sweat loss where natural springs are often dry, alkaline or miles apart—and turn back BEFORE half your carried water is gone.
Z12-P26:action3 Check vehicle cooling, tires, fuel and paper maps before leaving paved highways because cell signal is broadly absent across arid backcountry basins.
Z12-P26:failure Starting a desert canyon hike at 11 a.m. in 108°F heat carrying one small bottle while expecting a mapped seasonal tinaja to hold water.
Z12-P26:verify Confirm early-morning start, midday shade refuge, half-water turnaround rule and verified off-trip contact before entering arid terrain.
Z12-P26:stop Reaching your half-water mark, losing shade access or noticing heat-exhaustion symptoms (dizziness, nausea, heavy fatigue) terminates forward travel immediately.
Z12-P27:action1 Cover skin with loose, light-colored, breathable long sleeves, long pants and a wide-brim hat—direct sunlight baking bare skin raises radiant heat gain, causes painful sunburn and impairs normal sweat cooling.
Z12-P27:action2 Protect against upward ground radiation: light desert sand and slickrock reflect intense solar heat and UV from underneath while dark ground surfaces can exceed 140°F–160°F, burning thin sandals and dog paws.
Z12-P27:action3 Elevate rest spots slightly off scorching sand/rock inside ventilated shade so hot ground conduction and still trapped air do not overheat resting travelers.
Z12-P27:failure Hiking shirtless in 105°F dry desert sun believing bare skin stays cooler, suffering severe sunburn and accelerating dehydration.
Z12-P27:verify Confirm loose breathable full-coverage clothing, shaded neck/face brim, sturdy thick-soled boots and elevated ventilated midday rest shade.
Z12-P28:action1 Drink safe water steadily to thirst and sweat loss rather than hoarding water in your pack until faint—rationing water while dehydrating impairs judgment and accelerates fatal heat stroke ("drink your water, don't carry it into collapse").
Z12-P28:action2 Pair high water intake during long hot exertion with regular salty snacks or balanced electrolyte solutions—guzzling huge volumes of plain water over many hours without replacing lost sodium can trigger dangerous hyponatremia (nausea, headache, swelling, confusion).
Z12-P28:action3 Cut water loss dramatically by stopping midday exertion, resting in shade and keeping mouth closed/breathing calmly rather than trying to find questionable desert plant juices (most cacti/desert plants cause vomiting and worse dehydration).
Z12-P28:failure Hoarding two full liters in a backpack until collapsing from heat stroke, OR forcing gallons of plain water with zero food/salt until confused and vomiting.
Z12-P28:verify Confirm steady safe drinking matched to exertion, regular salty snack intake and strict avoidance of midday heat effort.
Z12-P31:action1 Check the weather forecast for the ENTIRE upstream mountain or mesa watershed—not just your immediate trailhead—because hard sun-baked desert soils cannot absorb rain and funnel runoff into walls of water miles downstream under blue skies.
Z12-P31:action2 Never camp inside dry streambeds, sandy canyon bottoms or narrow slot canyons, and stay out of constricted narrows whenever any thunderstorm chance exists anywhere upstream.
Z12-P31:action3 Watch and listen for distant dark clouds upslope, sudden muddy trickles, floating twigs or a rising rushing roar—climb immediately perpendicular onto high rocky canyon walls or benches.
Z12-P31:failure Pitching a tent on soft flat sand inside a dry desert wash because local skies look crystal clear while a thunderstorm dumps rain 15 miles upstream.
Z12-P31:verify Confirm clear watershed-wide forecast before entering narrow canyons and always pitch camps well above high-water canyon debris lines.
Z12-P31:stop Any Flash Flood Watch/Warning, upstream storm buildup or sudden trickle of muddy water demands climbing to high ground immediately and leaving gear behind.
Z12-P32:action1 Stay with the disabled vehicle on established roads—cars are vastly easier for searchers and passing motorists to spot than a lone hiker, and walking miles in 110°F+ heat rapidly proves fatal.
Z12-P32:action2 Never sit inside a closed parked car in desert sun—cabin temperatures soar past 140°F within minutes; open doors/windows for cross-breeze or rig an external shade tarp beside the vehicle's shaded side off scorching asphalt.
Z12-P32:action3 Signal visibility clearly (raise the hood, display bright cloth, check cell/satellite signal from safe open ground) and conserve safe water by resting completely motionless in shade during peak heat.
Z12-P32:failure Leaving a broken-down car on a park road at 1 p.m. to walk ten miles in 112°F heat, or leaving children/pets inside an un-running parked car.
Z12-P32:verify Confirm everyone stays out of closed hot cabins, sits in external ventilated shade beside the visible vehicle and monitors water/symptom status.
Z12-P32:stop Never leave a disabled vehicle on a traveled road unless a verified occupied building is plainly visible within a short safe walk; call 911/SOS immediately if heat illness appears.
Z12-P34:action1 Expect massive diurnal temperature swings of 30°F–50°F+ after sunset in dry high deserts—dry air and clear skies radiate daytime warmth straight to space within hours of dusk.
Z12-P34:action2 Pack a lightweight warm insulating layer, wind shell and ground barrier even when trailhead afternoon temperatures feel hot, especially if any risk of delay or overnight stranding exists.
Z12-P34:action3 Remember that thin cotton soaked with afternoon sweat chills the core rapidly as desert evening winds turn cold.
Z12-P35:action1 Protect phones, GPS devices and lithium power banks from direct dashboard sun—modern devices trigger automatic thermal shutdown rapidly in direct 105°F+ sun, wiping out digital maps and 911 access right when needed.
Z12-P35:action2 Check vehicle tire pressure/tread, coolant level and belts before remote desert stretches, turning off air conditioning on long steep grades if the engine temperature gauge climbs toward red.
Z12-P35:action3 Keep stored water jugs, medications (such as insulin or epinephrine) and pressurized camp fuel canisters out of direct scorching sun and hot closed trunks where pressure and thermal spoilage spike.
Z12-P35:failure Leaving a smartphone navigating on a sunlit dashboard until thermal shutdown locks it out right as an overheated car stalls on an unpaved desert road.
Z12-P35:verify Confirm electronics stay shaded, paper backup maps are on hand, medications have thermal protection and vehicle cooling/tires pass pre-trip checks.
Z12-P35:stop If a vehicle temperature gauge climbs sharply or tires show heat-blister damage, pull safely off-road in shade early before engine seizure or blowout occurs.
Z12-P36:action1 Watch every step and handhold closely—NEVER reach blind fingers onto rocky ledges, under flat boulders, inside shaded log crevices or into boots/gloves left outside overnight without shaking them out first.
Z12-P36:action2 Step ONTO logs or rocks first so you can see the shaded backside rather than stepping blindly over them where resting rattlesnakes or scorpions shelter from midday heat.
Z12-P36:action3 Use a bright headlamp after sunset when nocturnal snakes and scorpions become active along warm trails and camp paths, and keep sturdy boots on rather than walking barefoot.
Z12-P36:failure Reaching blindly into a cool rock overhang to sit down during midday heat or putting on unshaken camp shoes at dawn.
Z12-P36:verify Confirm visual inspection before sitting, stepping or grabbing ledges, and shake out boots/clothing before dressing in desert camps.
Z12-P36:stop If a venomous snakebite or severe allergic sting reaction occurs, move calmly away from the animal, keep the affected limb still at a comfortable level, remove rings/tight bands and call 911 immediately—NEVER cut, suck or tourniquet a snakebite.
Z12-P70:action1 Audit power, hydration and fuel against climate extremes: bitter cold drains batteries/butane and cracks wet filters; desert heat triggers phone thermal shutdown and tire/coolant failure; high altitude cuts boiling temp (3 min >6,500 ft) and increases stove CO.
Z12-P70:action2 Audit fabrics, fasteners and metals: wet marshes drive trench foot and soak down loft; coastal salt spray pits carbon steel and windblown sand jams zippers and stove jets; UV desert sun degrades nylon and plastics rapidly.
Z12-P70:failure Bringing an unchanged fair-weather three-season backpacking kit into a −10°F winter plain, a 112°F desert canyon or a salty rocky coast.
Z12-P74:action1 Set FOUR objective abort limits before starting: (1) **Resource limit** (half water in deserts, fuel reserve in winter, half battery/daylight), (2) **Weather/Water limit** (active Warnings, lightning, whiteout, Gale/Small Craft Advisory, rising tide/creek).
Z12-P74:failure Reaching the half-water mark or hearing afternoon thunder above treeline and deciding to push twenty more minutes for the summit view.
Z15-P39:action1 NEVER leave a child, dependent adult, or pet alone inside a parked vehicle for even **"just two minutes"**—greenhouse solar heating spikes cabin temperatures by roughly 20°F in 10 minutes and can reach fatal temperatures above 120°F even when outdoor air is a mild 70°F and windows are cracked open.
Z15-P39:failure Cracking car windows an inch in a 75°F sunny parking lot for ten minutes while running into a store with a sleeping toddler or dog in back.

Z10-P48:action2 Recognize delayed snow-blindness symptoms appearing 4 to 12 hours after exposure: severe gritty burning pain, tearing, swollen lids, headache, and extreme light sensitivity that can leave a traveler temporarily unable to open their eyes.

Z12-P08:action1 Wear UV-rated wrap-around sunglasses or goggles with side shielding whenever traveling over sunlit snow—fresh snow reflects up to ~80% of UV upward into unprotected eyes, and thin bright clouds still transmit burning UV.
Z12-P08:failure Leaving sunglasses in the car on a bright March snowshoe trip because air temperature feels cold or skies look lightly hazy.
Z12-P37:action1 Expect air temperatures to drop roughly 3°F–5°F for every 1,000 feet of elevation gain (plus severe wind chill on open passes)—a 75°F valley trailhead routinely meets 40°F sleet and freezing gusts at an alpine pass.
Z12-P37:action2 Protect skin and eyes against stronger ultraviolet intensity in thinner high-altitude air using UV sunglasses, brimmed hat and sunscreen even when air feels cool.
Z12-P37:action3 Expect clear blue alpine mornings to build rapidly into lightning, hail or sudden summer snow squalls by early afternoon—carry full cold-wet shelter layers on EVERY mountain trip regardless of morning sun.
Z12-P37:failure Packing only a light windbreaker for a sunny July 12,000-foot pass hike and getting caught in a 35°F afternoon hailstorm.
Z12-P37:verify Check the summit/pass elevation forecast (not valley town weather) and pack warm/waterproof layers plus UV protection before departing.
Z12-P37:stop Rapid temperature drops, sleet, hail or building clouds above treeline trigger immediate descent back into sheltered forest before hypothermia or lightning strikes.
Z12-P38:action1 Start early (often at or before dawn) on above-treeline objectives so your party crosses high passes and starts descending WELL BEFORE midday convective cumulus clouds build into storms.
Z12-P38:action2 Set a hard clock turnaround time before leaving the trailhead—if you have not reached the summit or pass by that hour, TURN AROUND immediately regardless of how close the top looks.
Z12-P38:action3 Remember that once thunder is heard above treeline, NO outdoor ridge, boulder or isolated tree is safe from lightning; descend promptly off high points toward dense lower terrain or trailhead vehicles/buildings and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
Z12-P38:failure Lingering on an exposed 12,000-foot summit at 1:30 p.m. for photos as dark anvil clouds build directly overhead.
Z12-P38:verify State your dawn start time, hard summit turnaround clock and fastest descent route below treeline before departing.
Z12-P38:stop Towering dark cumulus, audible thunder, hair standing on end or buzzing metal gear require immediate rapid descent off ridges and away from isolated trees/water.
Z12-P39:action1 Ascend gradually above 8,000 feet (sleeping at moderate intermediate elevations first and limiting daily sleeping-elevation gain) because high physical fitness does NOT protect against altitude illness.
Z12-P41:action1 Check the official regional avalanche forecast daily before winter mountain travel—remembering most human-triggered avalanches release on slopes between roughly 30 and 45 degrees (and steep wind-loaded convex rolls).
Z12-P43:action1 Avoid unstable talus or routes with exposed people below when possible. Keep companions out of the fall line rather than clustering beneath unstable material.
Z12-P43:action2 Shout **"ROCK!"** loudly and instantly if ANY stone dislodges—people below should duck cleanly against uphill cover and protect their head rather than looking straight upward into the falling rock's path.
Z12-P43:action3 Avoid wet lichen-covered granite slabs, steep snow-choked chutes without traction/training and shortcuts cutting off switchbacks (which erode trails and knock rocks onto hikers below).

Z12-P45:action1 Assess from a stable bank. Heat, rain and upstream releases can alter snowmelt flow. Do not infer a safe hour or wading depth.
Z12-P45:failure Stepping into a rushing thigh-deep icy snowmelt stream at 3 p.m. with a heavy backpack buckled tightly around the waist and a logjam thirty feet downstream.
Z12-P46:action1 Follow the CDC altitude boiling rule: above 6,500 feet water boils at a lower temperature, so maintain a full rolling boil for **3 FULL MINUTES** (rather than 1 minute below 6,500 feet) to reliably kill microbes after screening out chemical hazards.
